"An Image Won't Save Black Holes" is an article by Stephen John Crothers published on 13 April 2019 on Beyond Mainstream .
Crothers rejects the black hole image as a discovery at all, and states his objection as a matter of internal contradiction rather than evidence. A black hole is said to concentrate a finite mass in a singularity of zero volume, infinite density and infinite gravity, though no finite mass has any of those properties; and the event horizon is assigned an escape speed of zero, an escape speed equal to c , and no capacity for escape at all, simultaneously and in the same place. He argues no image can rescue a definition that is self-contradictory.

No more detailed treatment of the subject has yet been found among Dr. Waldron's papers. Any model of the universe must accommodate two features; it must account for the redshift and it must give an answer to Olbers's paradox. Abstract
This revision is much better than the original paper I wrote in 2012, especially from Section XXV on. In it I tell of Einstein’s struggles to put his theories into words. I also tell how he used some of his thought experiments to try to help him do this. They turned out to be of little use however. In one of them the participant believed he was feeling the force of gravity when it was really the force of acceleration. In another one the gravity he believed he was feeling turned out to be centrifugal force. And in still another, instead of being based on real-world things like gravity, it worked through abstractions like curved lines that were infinitely close to each other, thus being of no practical use for anything.
The format of this paper is twofold. When quoting or paraphrasing what I believe to be are Einstein’s key points in each chapter (Section) of his book, I use a Regular Cambria font. My comments, analysis, criticism and questions are made in a Bold Face Italic Cambria font. When in the latter mode, I occasionally take the liberty of expanding his own wording when I believe that he is being too terse or compressed in his narrative.

Abstract
The following report summarizes an analysis of the magnet plate drop test data provided by Don Kelly. It indicates that significantly slower drop times can be produced by a falling plate being tilted such that one edge will impact first, delaying the time at which the impact switch will be triggered. In addition, there are a number of variables not isolated that could cause widely scattered data. To this extent, the experiment needs to be more tightly controlled. The slower drop times reported by Kelly, as a result do not establish a magnetic-gravitational interaction.

Andraz Pibernik is a Slovenian independent researcher known for a self-developed theory he calls "E=mQ²", presented as a grand unification of gravity and electromagnetism. His writings have been posted on the General Science Journal and viXra. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Ideas
Pibernik proposes to reformulate mass–energy relationships in terms of what he labels a "Q²" quantity, which he connects to squares of time and of acceleration, and argues that this yields a unified description of gravity and electricity of the kind he says Einstein sought in his later years. He has authored several related essays and papers, including "E=mQ² The Grand Unification of Gravity and Electromagnetism" (2013), and has extended the framework to speculative claims about consciousness, light and torsion fields. In this work he acknowledges the influence of the amateur theorist Al ("Alan") Zeeper.
These proposals are self-published outside the peer-reviewed physics literature and lie well outside the scientific mainstream.

André Koch Torres Assis (born August 11, 1962) is a Brazilian physicist and historian of science, and a Professor of Physics at the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP), Brazil. He is best known for his work reviving and extending the electrodynamics of Wilhelm Eduard Weber , for his theory of Relational Mechanics — a quantitative implementation of Mach's Principle intended to replace Newtonian mechanics and Einstein's theories of relativity — and for a large body of work on the history and foundations of electricity, magnetism and mechanics. Over more than three decades he has authored or co-authored more than twenty books (in Portuguese, English, German, Italian, French and Russian) and several hundred papers, and has led a multi-volume project translating the complete electrodynamic works of Wilhelm Weber into English.
His research spans several interconnected areas: gravitation (Relational Mechanics, Mach's principle and the origin of inertia, the absorption of gravity); electromagnetism (Weber's electrodynamics, Ampère's force between current elements, the electric field outside resistive wires carrying steady currents, and the propagation of electromagnetic signals); cosmology (Hubble's law of redshifts, the cosmic microwave background radiation, Tired Light , and an infinite universe in space and time); and the history and philosophy of science . He is also known for advocating hands-on physics experiments performed with simple, easily accessible materials.

André-Marie Ampère (20 January 1775 – 10 June 1836) was a French physicist and mathematician who founded the science he named electrodynamics , and who wrote down a force law between current elements that is still argued over on this wiki two centuries later.
Ampère was largely self-taught, reading his way through his father's library as a boy. His father was guillotined in the Terror of 1793, an event that marked him for life. He became professor at the École Polytechnique in 1809 and at the Collège de France in 1824.
His decisive work occupied a few extraordinary weeks. On 4 September 1820 Ampère heard of Ørsted's discovery that a current deflects a magnetic needle; by 18 September he had shown that two parallel currents attract one another and two antiparallel currents repel. He invented the helical winding he named the solenoid and showed it behaves as a magnet, and proposed that all magnetism is due to circulating molecular currents — a hypothesis vindicated a century later by electron orbital and spin magnetism. He devised the astatic needle and the first galvanometer.
The results were consolidated in his Mémoire sur la théorie mathématique des phénomènes électrodynamiques uniquement déduite de l'expérience (1826), whose subtitle — "uniquely deduced from experiment" — states his method. search_text:
Antimatter is matter composed of antiparticles — particles carrying the same mass as their ordinary counterparts but opposite electric charge and opposite values of the other additive quantum numbers. When a particle meets its antiparticle the pair can annihilate, converting their rest mass into radiation.
The standard account
Antimatter entered physics through Dirac's 1928 relativistic wave equation for the electron, whose solutions included negative-energy states. Dirac's initial interpretation was a filled "sea" of negative-energy states whose holes appeared as positive particles; by 1931 he had identified the hole as a new particle of electronic mass and opposite charge. Carl Anderson found it in cloud-chamber cosmic-ray tracks in 1932 and named it the positron. The antiproton followed at the Bevatron in 1955, and antihydrogen atoms were first assembled at CERN in 1995, with trapped antihydrogen produced by the ALPHA experiment from 2010 onward.
Annihilation is the practical signature: an electron and a positron at rest annihilate into two 511 keV gamma rays, the basis of positron emission tomography. Antimatter is routinely produced in accelerators and in cosmic-ray showers, and appears in beta-plus decay.
The genuine open problem is the baryon asymmetry : the observed universe is made almost entirely of matter, yet the standard hot Big Bang picture starts from conditions that should have produced matter and antimatter in nearly equal amounts. CP violation, discovered in neutral kaon decays in 1964, is real but too small to account for the asymmetry, and the Sakharov conditions for baryogenesis are not satisfied by the Standard Model alone. Whether antimatter falls up or down under gravity was an open experimental question until very recently, when CERN's ALPHA-g experiment reported that antihydrogen falls downward.

Antirelativity part 2: Does the Sagnac experiment disprove special relativity?
Summary
The second of Roger J Anderton 's anti-relativity sessions, hosted by Franklin Hu and given over to a recorded lecture by Albrecht Giese of Hamburg, "The Sagnac effect disproves Einstein's relativity". Getting the video to play with sound took some time. Anderton's own position was stated at the outset and repeated throughout: he does not think the question can be settled, because special relativity is not a precisely defined theory and is vague about how it treats the experiment — but others think otherwise, and Giese is one of them.
Giese's lecture
Giese's framing is that the Sagnac experiment decides between two versions of relativity. Einstein's is built on a principle — the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame — and requires contraction and dilation to be defined so that the principle holds. The two give the same results, but Lorentz's mathematics is dramatically simpler.

The Allais effect is the claim that a pendulum's period changes measurably during a solar eclipse. The paper works against a specific dataset: the torsion-pendulum measurements made by Erwin J. The shadowing mechanism
In Autodynamics gravity is the pressure of pico-gravitons absorbed by matter. The Sun, absorbing them, casts a cone of umbra and penumbra in which the flux is depleted. When the Moon enters that cone it receives a reduced flux, so its own gravitational pull on the Earth's surface weakens — and since the Moon's pull ordinarily reduces the net downward acceleration at the Earth's surface, weakening it makes the net acceleration increase . The prediction is therefore that gravity at the surface rises slightly during totality, shortening a Foucault pendulum's period and lengthening a torsion pendulum's.

Are Constants Arbitrary? Or will aliens find the same ones? was a live session presented by David de Hilster on 5 November 2022 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Would intelligent aliens on other worlds find the same physics and cosmological constants? Or are they arbitrary? Join this fascinating discussion live with other like-minded critical thinkers from the CNPS and around the world!
Summary
A panel discussion led by David de Hilster on whether the fundamental constants are arbitrary, framed by a question he kept returning to: at an intergalactic science conference, which of our results could we present without embarrassment, and which would we hide?
His starting point was the Wikipedia list of fundamental physical constants, and in particular its own admission that there is no single correct way of enumerating them and that which are taken as fundamental and which as derived is a matter of arbitrary choice. He was cheerful about where his own embarrassment would lie: the gravitational constant, the speed of light and Planck's constant he could imagine anyone finding; the Yukawa couplings for quarks and leptons, the two parameters of the Higgs potential, the four of the quark mixing matrix and the three gauge coupling constants he would keep under the table. He recommended Alexander Unzicker 's The Higgs Fake and an interview on Unzicker's channel with a Nobel laureate who claimed to have reduced the constants to four, and who grew visibly uncomfortable as the questions became basic.

Title Are Quasars Manifesting a de Sitter Redshift?
Author(s) John B Miller , Thomas E Miller
Keywords quasars , de Sitter, redshift , velocity, distance, gravitational
Published 1994
Pages 67-71
Abstract
In 1929, Edwin Hubble wrote in his classic paper demonstrating a correlation between redshift and distance. "The outstanding feature, however, is the possibility that the velocity-distance relation may represent the de Sitter effect...." Since the discovery of quasars more than thirty years ago, many more-or-less plausible explanations for the quasar redshift have been proposed. Although the de Sitter redshift was the first known cosmological redshift, it hs not yet been considered as a possible etiology for the redshift of quasars. We address the question, "Is it possible that the quasar redshift is a de Sitter redshift?" Perhaps the asymptotic character of a gravitational de Sitter redshift could help explain the quasar phenomenon: objects with high redshifts that appear to be almost as bright as objects with intermediate redshifts. Reconsidering the possibility of a nonlinear de Sitter redshift-distance relation, we find quasar intrinsic brightness to be rather ordinary. Given a de Sitter redshift-distance law, intrinsic brightness is found to be independent of redshift over five orders of magnitude.

Abstract
Several arguments favouring instantaneous action at a distance are presented. The action at a distance laws of Newton, Coulomb, Amp're and Weber are analysed. Historical evidence that Weber's electrodynamics led to the propagation of electromagnetic signals with finite velocity prior to the development of Maxwell's equations are emphasized. The implementation of Mach's principle with Weber's law applied to gravitation is discussed.
Overview
This is a philosophical and historical paper rather than a technical one, and it is unusual in this collection for the way it is framed: as an intellectual autobiography, tracking the author's changing view over two decades and arriving at a position he describes as a growing sympathy rather than a conviction.
The argument is for instantaneous action at a distance as a serious option in physics, against the near-universal preference for contact action mediated by fields. Four historical force laws are examined — those of Newton , Coulomb, Ampère and Weber — together with the historical claim that Weber's electrodynamics yielded finite propagation of electromagnetic signals before Maxwell's equations existed, and the use of Weber's law applied to gravitation as a way of implementing Mach's principle .

Ari Lehto (born 16 September 1942) is a Finnish physicist who has argued since the 1980s that the measured properties of matter can be derived from the Planck scale by period doubling — the universal route to chaos in nonlinear dynamical systems described by Mitchell Feigenbaum.
His work is unusual in this collection for two reasons. It is quantitative and falsifiable in a direct way: it predicts specific numbers — particle rest energies, the elementary charge, planetary orbital radii — which either match measurement or do not. And a substantial part of it has appeared in ordinary peer-reviewed journals , including Astrophysics and Space Science in 1996 and Nonlinear Dynamics in 2008, rather than only in dissident venues. He worked at the Laboratory of Materials Science of the Helsinki University of Technology, now part of Aalto University.
The idea
The Planck scale is built from the natural constants h , c , G and ε 0 alone, which is what makes it attractive as a starting point: it is, in Lehto's words, "absolute and unadjustable". The obstacle is one of magnitude. The Planck energy is about 10 22 MeV against 0.511 MeV for the electron and 938 MeV for the proton, and the Planck length is 10 −35 m — too far from anything measurable for a direct connection to be obvious.
Lehto's proposal is that the connection is made by a process that generates subharmonics rather than harmonics , stepping the Planck quantities down rather than up. Arp 220 is the result of a collision between two galaxies which are now in the process of merging. It is the 220th object in Halton Arp 's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies .
Features
Wider angle (2.4′ ) view by Hubble Space Telescope
Compound view shows a ALMA Band 5 image of the colliding galaxy system Arp 220. [ 1 ]
Arp 220 is the closest Ultraluminous Infrared Galaxy (ULIRG) to Earth. Its energy output was discovered by IRAS to be dominated by the far-infrared part of the spectrum. [ 2 ]
It is often regarded as the prototypical ULIRG and has been the subject of much study as a result.
Most of its energy output is thought to be the result of a massive burst of star formation, or starburst , probably triggered by the merging of two smaller galaxies.
Recent (2002 and 1997) HST observations of Arp 220, taken in visible light with the ACS , and in infrared light with NICMOS , revealed more than 200 huge star clusters in the central part of the galaxy.
The most massive of these clusters contains enough material to equal about 10 million suns. [ 3 ]
X-ray observations by the Chandra and XMM-Newton satellites have shown that Arp 220 probably includes an active galactic nucleus (AGN) at its core, which raises interesting questions about the link between galaxy mergers and AGN, since it is believed that galactic mergers often trigger starbursts, and may also give rise to the supermassive black holes that appear to power AGN.
Luminous far-infrared objects like Arp 220 have been found in surprisingly large numbers by sky surveys of submillimetre wavelengths using instruments such as the Submillimetre Common-User Bolometer Array (SCUBA) at the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT).
Arp 220 and other relatively local ULIRGs are being studied as equivalents of this kind of object.
Astronomers from the Arecibo Observatory have detected organic molecules in the galaxy. [ 4 ]
Arp 220 contains at least two bright maser sources, an OH megamaser , and a water maser .

The arrow of time is the problem that the fundamental laws of physics are, with one small exception, symmetric under reversal of the time coordinate, while almost everything we observe is not. Cups break and do not unbreak; heat flows from hot to cold; we remember the past. Nothing in Newton's equations, Maxwell's equations, general relativity or the Schrödinger equation distinguishes one direction of time from the other, yet the world plainly does.
The several arrows
It is usual, following Eddington, who coined the phrase in 1927, to distinguish:
The thermodynamic arrow — entropy of an isolated system increases toward the future.
The cosmological arrow — the universe is observed to be expanding, in one direction of time.
The radiative arrow — Maxwell's equations admit both retarded and advanced solutions, but we observe outgoing waves from sources and never converging ones.
The psychological arrow — we have records of the past and not of the future.
The causal arrow — effects follow causes.
The one genuine asymmetry in the microscopic laws is in the weak interaction. CP violation was discovered in neutral kaon decays by Christenson, Cronin, Fitch and Turlay in 1964; direct time-reversal violation was demonstrated by CPLEAR in 1998 and by BaBar in the B-meson system in 2012. This asymmetry is real, but it is far too feeble and far too specific to explain why coffee cools.
The standard resolution of the thermodynamic arrow does not locate it in the dynamics at all. Boltzmann's statistical account explains why entropy increases toward the future given that the system is now in a low-entropy state, but the same argument run backwards would predict higher entropy in the past, which is false. The repair — the past hypothesis — is to postulate that the universe began in a state of extraordinarily low entropy. Arthur Stanley Eddington (28 December 1882 – 22 November 1944) was a British astrophysicist, Plumian Professor of Astronomy at Cambridge from 1913 and director of the Cambridge Observatory from 1914. He did more than anyone else to establish general relativity in the English-speaking world, founded the theory of stellar interiors, and spent his last fifteen years on a numerological unification of physics that his colleagues could not follow.
Eddington's astrophysics is uncontested and permanent. In The Internal Constitution of the Stars (1926) he treated a star as a gas sphere in radiative equilibrium, derived the mass–luminosity relation, and established the Eddington limit — the luminosity at which radiation pressure on the outer layers balances gravity, above which a star cannot be stable. He also showed that stellar energy output could not be gravitational contraction and had to be subatomic in origin, before the fusion mechanism was known.
He was a Quaker and a conscientious objector during the First World War, and his advocacy of the theory of a German physicist to a British audience in 1919 was in part a deliberate act of scientific internationalism.
The 1919 eclipse
On 29 May 1919 two British expeditions photographed the star field around the eclipsed Sun: Eddington on Príncipe, and a second party at Sobral in Brazil. General relativity predicted a deflection of starlight at the solar limb of about 1.75 arcseconds — twice the value obtained from a Newtonian corpuscular calculation. Three data sets resulted. Arthur Zinzen (29 September 1893 – 4 January 1965) was a German engineer, standards expert and university teacher. In mainstream engineering he is remembered for the Zinzen diagram , a phase diagram for the melting of fuel ashes, and for his long leadership of the German Standards Committee. Late in his career he turned to foundational questions in physics and its philosophy, publishing in 1962 on the nature of inertia and on the classification of the fundamental physical quantities — the work for which he is catalogued here.

Astronomy is the observational study of objects beyond the Earth. On this wiki it is the discipline that supplies most of the evidence in dispute: nearly every argument about cosmology , redshift and gravitation catalogued here rests on an astronomical measurement, and the disagreements are usually about what those measurements mean rather than about the numbers themselves.
Category: Astronomy holds over 260 items.
What is disputed
Astronomical observation is indirect. Almost nothing beyond the Solar System can be sampled, weighed or repeated; distances, masses and ages are all inferred through a chain of assumptions, and the criticism collected here generally attacks a link in that chain rather than the observation at its end.
Distance — the redshift –distance relation underpins the extragalactic distance scale. Halton Arp 's intrinsic redshift work argues from physically associated objects with discordant redshifts that the relation cannot be read as a simple distance indicator.
Age and evolution — the Hubble Deep Field and its successors are argued to show galaxies more mature at high redshift than the standard chronology permits.
Mass — galactic rotation curves are explained in the standard model by dark matter ; the alternatives catalogued here modify gravitation instead.
Compact objects — the interpretation of black holes and of the objects identified as them is contested.
Light propagation — whether deflection near the Sun occurs in curved spacetime or in the solar plasma, a case argued by Edward Henry Dowdye .
Solar System work
A distinct and more testable strand concerns the Solar System, where measurement is direct enough to constrain theory sharply: planetary radar ranging, the Allais effect during solar eclipses, the Pioneer anomaly, lunar laser ranging, and satellite orbital dynamics. Tom Van Flandern 's arguments on the speed of gravity draw on this material, as does Ioannis Iraklis Haranas 's work on modified gravitational potentials.

On this wiki the disputes concern the models applied to the observations rather than the observations themselves: the photometry, the spectra and the redshift catalogues are largely common ground, and the argument is about what they are evidence for .

How the subject is divided here
Astrophysics on this wiki overlaps heavily with cosmology and shades into it at almost every point, because most of the disputes turn on the same question — whether an observed feature is intrinsic to the object or an artefact of the expanding-universe interpretation. As a rough division of labour:
Astronomy (298 catalogued pages) — observation, instruments and measurement.
Astrophysics — the physics of individual objects: stars, quasars, compact objects, galaxies.
Cosmology (805 catalogued pages) — the universe as a whole, its origin and its large-scale structure.

Athanassios A. Nassikas (born 1947) is a Greek mechanical engineer and emeritus professor whose work begins from an unusual place: not from an experiment, and not from a defect in a particular theory, but from a claim about the language in which every physical theory must be written.
His argument is that any theory of physics has to be stated through a basic communication system — classical Aristotelian logic, the Leibniz principle of sufficient reason, and a usually unnoticed axiom that there is an anterior and a posterior. He offers a theorem purporting to show that this system is inherently contradictory . If that is right, then no perfect theory is available to anyone, and the most that can be sought is a least contradictory one. That is the Claim for Minimum Contradictions , and from it he derives a physics in which space-time is stochastic and is itself matter, gravitational and electromagnetic space-time coexist with the latter's magnitudes imaginary, and general relativity and quantum mechanics both emerge as simplifications.
The position has a striking consequence he accepts openly: the theorem cannot be stated consistently either, since it is stated inside the system it condemns. Strict rigour, he concludes, imposes silence — and the claim for minimum contradictions is what licenses speaking anyway.

The Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies is a catalog of peculiar galaxies produced by Halton Arp in 1966. A total of 338 galaxies are presented in the atlas, which was originally published in 1966 by the California Institute of Technology . [ 1 ]
The primary goal of the catalog was to present photographs of examples of the different kinds of peculiar structures found among nearby galaxies. Arp realized that the reason why galaxies formed into spiral or elliptical shapes was not well understood. He perceived peculiar galaxies as small "experiments" that astronomers could use to understand the physical processes that distort spiral or elliptical galaxies. With this atlas, astronomers had a sample of peculiar galaxies that they could study in more detail. The atlas does not present a complete overview of every peculiar galaxy in the sky but instead provides examples of the different phenomena as observed in nearby galaxies.
Because little was known at the time of publication about the physical processes that caused the different shapes, the galaxies in the atlas are sorted based on their appearance. Objects 1–101 are individual peculiar spiral galaxies or spiral galaxies that apparently have small companions. Objects 102–145 are elliptical and elliptical-like galaxies. Individual or groups of galaxies with neither elliptical nor spiral shapes are listed as objects 146–268. Objects 269–327 are double galaxies. Finally, objects that simply do not fit into any of the above categories are listed as objects 332–338. Most objects are best known by their other designations, but a few galaxies are best known by their Arp numbers (such as Arp 220 ).

An atom is the smallest unit of a chemical element that retains that element's identity: a dense positively charged Nucleus surrounded by electrons .
The standard account
The modern picture was assembled in about thirty years. J. J. Thomson identified the electron in 1897. Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiments, reported in 1911, showed that the positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a nucleus some hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself — an atom is roughly 10 −10 m across, a nucleus roughly 10 −15 m. Bohr's 1913 model quantised the electron's angular momentum and reproduced the Hydrogen Atom spectrum, but it was an admitted hybrid: it forbade by fiat the radiation that classical Electrodynamics demands of an accelerating charge. The wave mechanics of de Broglie, Schrödinger and Heisenberg replaced the orbits with stationary states in 1925–1926, and Pauli's exclusion principle explained why electrons stack into shells and hence why the periodic table has the structure it does.
The quantum-mechanical account is quantitatively extraordinary: atomic transition frequencies are predicted and measured to more than ten significant figures, and atomic clocks built on them define the second. What it does not supply is a picture — the electron in a stationary state is described by a probability amplitude, not a trajectory — and that absence is the starting point for most of the alternatives catalogued on this wiki.

Autodynamics ( AD ) is an alternative theory of relativistic mechanics developed by the Argentine physicist Ricardo L. Carezani beginning in the 1940s, and promoted since 1994 by the Society for the Advancement of Autodynamics (SAA). Its central claim is that Einstein's special relativity is built on a redundant use of two reference frames, and that removing the redundant frame yields a simpler, single-frame mechanics which Carezani held to replace both special and general relativity. Autodynamics is not accepted by mainstream physics, which regards it as a fringe or pseudoscientific theory; on this wiki it is documented as a dissident alternative to relativity.
Core ideas
Frame reduction. Carezani argued that the Lorentz "systems in relative motion" from which special relativity is derived contain a second reference frame that is mathematically and physically redundant. Removing it — the Carezani Frame Reduction — is said to give a new set of transformation equations that remain finite at the speed of light, reduce to Newtonian mechanics at low speed, and contain no paradoxes.
Mass decreases with velocity. In place of the "relativistic mass increase" of special relativity, Autodynamics holds that a moving body must eject part of its mass in order to accelerate — much like a rocket — so that its rest mass decreases and the lost mass is converted to kinetic energy.
No neutrino. Carezani held that the neutrino was invented only to preserve energy conservation within the relativistic equations of beta decay. Autodynamics claims to describe beta decay and nucleus–nucleus collisions without invoking a neutrino.

An alternative approach to relativistic physics is reviewed, based on an invariant formulation of electromagnetic field theory due to Hertz. This paper sums up a half-century of my dissident thinking in physics and forms a concluding testament.

Bankrupting Physics: How Today's Top Scientists are Gambling Away Their Credibility is a 2013 book by the German physicist Alexander Unzicker and the Canadian science writer Sheilla Jones , published by Palgrave Macmillan in its MacSci series. It is a polemic against what the authors regard as the drift of fundamental physics away from experiment and toward untestable mathematics.
It is the first of Unzicker's book-length critiques, preceding The Higgs Fake and Einstein's Lost Key .
Origins
The book is the English edition of Unzicker's German work Vom Urknall zum Durchknall: Die absurde Jagd nach der Weltformel — roughly "From the Big Bang to the Big Crackup: the absurd hunt for the world formula" — published by Springer Spektrum in July 2010 and reworked with Jones for the English-language edition.
The German original was named science book of the year 2010 by Bild der Wissenschaft in the category Zündstoff ("incendiary material") — awarded to the book judged to present a controversial subject most competently. It is worth noting that the award was for being provocative and well-argued rather than for being correct, which is close to the book's own self-description.
The argument
Unzicker and Jones take the reader on a tour of contemporary theoretical physics and argue that a series of heavily publicised programmes have reached dead ends. The principal targets are:
String theory — decades of effort with no experimental prediction that has been tested;
The multiverse and parallel universes — treated as an abandonment of falsifiability;
Cosmic inflation — flexible enough, they argue, to accommodate almost any observation;
The standard models of particle physics and cosmology — criticised as over-parameterised and unexplanatory;
Dark matter and dark energy — described as names for ignorance rather than disco

Before the Big Bang: The Origins of the Universe is a 1997 book by the physicist Ernest J Sternglass , published by Four Walls Eight Windows / Basic Books.
Overview
Sternglass proposes a cosmology in which, before the Big Bang, all the mass of the universe was contained in a single ultramassive "primeval atom" — an electron and a positron orbiting each other at nearly the speed of light — a modern development of Georges Lemaître's primeval-atom idea. Over vast times this system divided repeatedly, laying down the dense "seeds" of galaxies and superclusters, until "motional energy" set off the Big Bang. Along the way the book offers a tour of modern particle physics and cosmology and recounts Sternglass's personal exchanges with Einstein, de Broglie, Bohr, and Feynman. His theory has not been accepted by mainstream cosmologists.
About the author
Ernest J. Sternglass (1923–2015) was an American physicist (electron optics and low-light imaging) and professor emeritus of radiological physics at the University of Pittsburgh. He was also widely known as an anti-nuclear activist studying the health effects of low-level radiation.

Benjamin B. Dayton is a researcher and author known for proposing a hydrodynamic model of elementary particles, atomic structure, and fields, published in the journal Physics Essays . He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Ideas
Dayton proposes a hydrodynamic theory of particles and fields in which the only basic particles carrying mass are the positron and the electron. In his model the positron acts as a source and the electron as a sink for the flow of an ideal, incompressible "primordial fluid," with the fluid returning from a sink to a source through a channel at velocity c . He develops this framework further into a hydrodynamic model of the electron structure of atoms, in which electron cores are subject to a virtual orbital motion relative to the primordial fluid and arrange themselves into nested concentric shells.
These proposals lie outside the accepted framework of quantum mechanics and the Standard Model, which do not treat particles as sources and sinks in a fluid medium. Dayton's articles on the subject appeared in Physics Essays , including "Hydrodynamic model of the electron structure of atoms" ( Physics Essays , Vol. 28, No. 4, 2015).

Benjamin F. Bush is a chemist and researcher known for his work in cold fusion (low-energy nuclear reactions), particularly the reported correlation between excess heat and helium-4 production in deuterated systems. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Work
Bush collaborated with Melvin H. Miles and co-workers on electrolysis experiments using palladium and heavy water carried out at the Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division (China Lake). This research reported the formation of helium-4 during episodes when the electrolytic cells produced more energy than they consumed, with the measured helium production rate said to be of the magnitude expected for reactions yielding helium. To address criticism that atmospheric helium might diffuse into glass sample containers, metal flasks were used in later runs.
Bush is a co-author, with Miles and K. B. Johnson, of the report Anomalous Effects in Deuterated Systems (NAWCWPNS TP 8302, 1996) and of related papers analyzing excess heat, tritium, and helium in cold fusion experiments. Cold fusion claims of this kind are not accepted by the mainstream physics and chemistry communities, which have not reproduced the effects to general satisfaction.

Bertrand Wong is an author known for his speculative writings on fundamental physics, including proposals toward a grand unified theory and the role of consciousness in physical theory. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Work
Wong published the paper "The Ultimate Law of Nature" in Physics Essays (Vol. 22, No. 3, 2009), in which he reviews historical attempts to formulate a theory of everything (TOE) or grand unified theory (GUT) and discusses how frameworks such as superstring theory and M-theory might yield an ultimate law governing nature.
He has also authored numerous papers hosted by the General Science Journal, including "Quantum Particles, Consciousness, Unified Field Theory and Relativity," "On the Unified Field Theory," "Quantum Entanglement," and "On the Special Theory of Relativity." In this body of work he argues that consciousness may be a fundamental element of physics and central to any complete unification of nature — positions that fall outside the scientific mainstream.

Beyond Newton is a 1964 book by Dewey B Larson , published by North Pacific Publishers. It focuses on gravitation within the framework of Larson's Reciprocal System of theory.
Overview
Larson applies the Reciprocal System — in which the universe is composed of motion, with space and time as its reciprocal aspects — to the problem of gravity and atomic structure. He argues that conventional, matter-based physics rests on erroneous assumptions, and that his system resolves outstanding problems of gravitation more consistently, presenting it as the kind of unified theory that Einstein and others had sought. The book is a shorter, focused companion to his larger works such as Nothing But Motion .
About the author
Dewey B. Larson (1898–1990) was an American chemical engineer and independent theoretician, the originator of the Reciprocal System of theory. See also his New Light on Space and Time .

Bibhas R. De is a physicist and author known for his alternative theoretical work on electromagnetism and his criticism of Big Bang cosmology. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Background
De studied astronomy at the University of Michigan and received a Ph.D. from the University of California, San Diego, where he was a doctoral student of the plasma physicist Hannes Alfvén.
Ideas
De proposes the concept of a "source-free magnetic structure," which he describes as a finite, static configuration of magnetic field lines existing in empty space with no currents or sources within it, obtained as a solution of Maxwell's equations. He argues that such a magnetostatic field constitutes the physical presence of something possessing mass, and that the relationship between this mass and the field energy does not follow the usual mass-energy relation, a departure he labels "TransEinsteinian" and "TransMaxwellian" physics. These claims lie outside mainstream physics.
De has also been a vocal critic of Big Bang cosmology. In his book The Falsifiers of the Universe: Big Bang Cosmology — The First Fraud in the Final Frontier , he disputes the standard interpretation of cosmological observations, including data from the COBE mission and the cosmic microwave background.

Big Bang is the prevailing mainstream cosmological model for the origin and evolution of the observable universe. In its standard form it holds that the universe began roughly 13.8 billion years ago in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since, with galaxies, stars, and atoms forming as it evolved. In mainstream physics and astronomy the model is regarded as well supported by several independent lines of observation; this wiki documents a substantial body of work that disputes it, collected in the criticisms section below .
Overview
The core claim of the standard model is that the universe is not static but is expanding, so that in the past it was smaller, hotter, and denser. Extrapolating the observed expansion backward in time leads to a state of enormous density and temperature — often described as an initial singularity — from which space, time, matter, and energy are said to have emerged. As the universe expanded it cooled, passing through a sequence of epochs in which the fundamental forces separated, subatomic particles formed, the lightest atomic nuclei were synthesized, neutral atoms appeared, and matter gradually clumped under gravity into the large-scale structure of galaxies and galaxy clusters seen today.

We are all so accustomed to reading that the universe "began" once a time with the Big Bang that most people no longer think it necessary to question or scrutinize it. A detailed analysis of the Big Bang theory, however, leads to consequences and implications that are inconsistent, or are contradicted by astrophysical observations, including important ones. At the same time, one of the pillars of the model, the all important cosmic redshift- the shifting of spectral lines toward the red end of the spectrum, in proportion to the distance of the source from us- can be explained without invoking the Doppler velocity interpretation(1) so dear to Big Bang theorists. The redshift is explained instead by taking the intergalactic medium into account, and correcting our understanding of how light interacts with such a medium on its way to the observer. Two different theoretical approaches, semi classical electrodynamics and quantum electrodynamics, have shown that all interactions or collisions of electrodynamics waves (photons) with atoms are inelastic; that is, the photons lose a very small part of their energy as a result of the interaction. Hence, the greater the depth of the intergalactic medium through which a galaxy's light must pass, the more toward the low-energy end of the spectrum - that is, toward the red - is the light frequency shifted. These considerations eliminate the limit on the size of the universe imposed by the Big Bang theory. Indeed one can say that the universe far greater than imagined.

Abstract
?Hubble's Law' states that the further away a galaxy is, the faster it is receding from Earth. But, the red shift of light from galaxies in-dicates their recession speeds, at the time of emission of the light. The correct interpretation is, therefore, that the farther away a galaxy was at the time of emission of the light, the faster it was recessing. The nearest galaxies give us the most recent information; the more recent the information, the slower the recession. A logical conclusion is that the recession of galaxies has decreased gradually to a present steady state. This means that the ?Big Bang' theory is not sustainable and that the Universe is not expanding.

Birkeland currents are electric currents that flow along magnetic field lines — in the original and best-established case, along the Earth's field into and out of the polar ionosphere, carrying charge between the ionosphere and the outer magnetosphere. They are named after the Norwegian physicist Kristian Birkeland (1867–1917), who proposed them to explain the aurora, and the name was given by Hannes Alfvén .
They occupy an unusual position in the material catalogued on this wiki. The currents themselves are not a heterodox idea: they were rejected for six decades, then measured directly by satellite in the 1970s, and are now ordinary space physics. What remains disputed is how far the same picture can be carried — to stars, to galaxies, and to the structure of the universe.
The standard account
Birkeland's proposal
Birkeland argued from the aurora. In a series of experiments beginning in the 1890s he built a terrella — a magnetised sphere suspended in an evacuated chamber — and directed a beam of cathode rays at it. The discharge did not strike the sphere evenly: it was steered by the magnetic field into glowing rings around the magnetic poles, reproducing the shape and position of the auroral ovals. From this he concluded that the aurora is produced by charged particles from the Sun guided down the Earth's magnetic field into the polar regions, and that the associated currents flow along the field lines rather than across them.
He set out the argument with data from his Norwegian Aurora Polaris Expedition of 1902–1903, published in two volumes from 1908. The theory was rejected. The principal opposition came from Sydney Chapman, whose account of geomagnetic storms placed the currents entirely within the ionosphere and required no current flowing along the field into space; the prevailing view held that the intervening space was effectively empty and could not carry a current at all. A black hole is, on the standard account, a region of spacetime in which gravitation is so strong that no matter and no light can escape from it. It is bounded by an event horizon , a one-way surface at which the escape speed is said to equal the speed of light, and it is held to contain at its centre a singularity — a point or ring of infinite density at which the known laws of physics cease to apply. Black holes are today part of the standard furniture of astrophysics: they are said to form when massive stars collapse, to sit in supermassive form at the centres of most galaxies, and to have been detected by the gravitational waves given off when two of them merge.
The literature collected on this wiki does not accept that account, and the black hole is probably the sharpest single point of disagreement between the researchers documented here and mainstream astrophysics. The objection is unusual in its form. It is not, in the main, that the observations have been misread — though that charge is made too — but that the object itself is a mathematical artefact: that the solution of Einstein's field equations from which the black hole was extracted does not contain one, and that the theory in which it is said to live forbids it. As Stephen John Crothers puts the position, "there is no black hole in Schwarzschild's solution. Indeed, his solution precludes the black hole, and for this reason he never spoke of the black hole."
This article sets out the mainstream account first, then the history of the idea as the critics reconstruct it, then the dispute over the Schwarzschild solution, over singularities and horizons, over the observational claims and over the gravitational-wave detections, and finally the alternative models of compact objects proposed in the archive.

It offers an account of black holes in which they are neither singular nor bounded by an event horizon: they are simply very large, very dense, but entirely finite bodies of ordinary matter, dark because light cannot get out of the region they occupy.

The central philosophical claim of the field approach is that the Coulomb field is the only real, physical field . Robert J. "Bob" Johnson is an independent researcher based in Oxford, England, and a long-standing advocate of the Electric Universe and Plasma Universe view. He wrote the original outline for the Essential Guide to the Electric Universe , the introductory reference issued by the Thunderbolts Project, and has presented at Electric Universe conferences and at Natural Philosophy Alliance meetings between 2011 and 2013.
Approach
The Electric Universe position Johnson works within holds that electromagnetic forces, and plasma behaviour in particular, play a far larger role in astrophysics and geology than conventional accounts allow, with gravity correspondingly demoted. Johnson's own papers apply that outlook in two quite different directions, and both share a method: he takes a phenomenon whose standard explanation he judges incomplete, and proposes an alternative drawn from outside the relevant discipline.
Evidence for the Anisotropy of the Speed of Light (2011) joins Petr Beckmann 's proposal that light propagates relative to the locally dominant field to the Electric Universe contention that the Earth carries a net charge, and reads the small non-zero drift velocities reported in Michelson–Morley-type interferometry as an electromagnetically induced anisotropy rather than an ether wind.
The Origin of Nodular Flint (2012) turns to geology, arguing that the diagenetic account of flint formation in chalk leaves the banding and the shapes of nodules unexplained, and proposing instead that flint is produced directly from chalk by biological transmutation — the Kervran effect — converting calcium to silicon and carbon.
Both papers end by proposing tests rather than declaring the case closed, which is a consistent feature of his writing.

"Bohr's Atom" is a four-part paper by Ricardo L Carezani , dated July 1996, applying the Autodynamics equations to the hydrogen atom. It is published at autodynamics.org across four pages — The Hydrogen Atomic Spectrum , Wilson and Sommerfeld Elliptic Orbits , The Sommerfeld Fine Structure and AD's Approach — and its claimed result is the recovery of the Dirac equation for the hydrogen energy levels, with its four quantum numbers, without wave mechanics.
Overview
The paper is structured as a historical reconstruction followed by a substitution. Carezani retraces the standard development — Bohr 's quantisation of the orbital action, the Wilson–Sommerfeld extension to elliptical orbits, and Sommerfeld's relativistic treatment yielding the fine structure — and then repeats Sommerfeld's calculation with the Autodynamics energy relation in place of the relativistic one. His conclusion is that the substitution produces Dirac's formula directly.
The site's own summary states the claim: "In another triumph, Dr. Ricardo Carezani derives Bohr's Atom without wave equations."
The argument
Part 1: the hydrogen spectrum
Carezani sets out Bohr's 1912 application of classical mechanics to the hydrogen term scheme, and stresses a point of interpretation he regards as widely misunderstood. What Bohr quantised was the action of the orbital motion, in units of h / 2 π — not the energy of an independent particle. "AD students must scrutinize this idea carefully … many professionals of the Conventional Wisdom hold that Quantum Mechanics describes a quantum of energy for an independent particle." The energy absorbed or emitted is quantised only as a consequence of the quantised orbital motion.

On May 16 1994, a distinguished physicochemist, a Member of the Russian Academy of Sciences Boris Vtadimirovich Deryagin deceased at the age of 91. A whole epoch in the development of the physical chemistry of surface phenomena is associated with his name. Classical works on the theory of the stability of colloids and thin films of liquids brought him world-wide fame. B. V. Deryagin made a considerable contribution to the development of the theory of surface forces, diffusiophoresis, and thermoosmosis. Being a brilliant experimenter, he was the first to accomplish direct measurements of long-range molecular forces. The concept of disjoining pressure of thin interlayers and its various constituents introduced by B. V. Deryagin made it possible to pass from the two-dimensional Gibbs thermodynamics to three-dimensional thermodynamics of multiphase systems, which takes into account finite thicknesses and peculiar properties of interface layers.
While studying the processes of adhesion of solids, B. V. Deryagin discovered that disruption of an adhesion linkage results in the formation of fresh surfaces covered with oppositely charged dense layers, which leads to the appearance of electronic adhesion. The theory of the forces of the interaction of nonplanar surfaces, which was developed by B. V. Deryagin as early as in 1934 and found wide application, occupies a special place in tile science of colloids and surface phenomena. Under the leadership of B. V. Deryagin, a series of work on the synthesis of diamond at low pressures was begun in 1950. The development of experimental methods and theoretical views on the influence of atomic hydrogen on gasification of non-diamond forms of carbon enabled preparation of diamond from the gaseous phase on various supports.

Abstract
New interpretations are given to stellar aberration and Sagnac effect. By strict following the wave model for light it is demonstrated that the wave motion depends on the ether-wind in one dimension only. This means that we cannot describe wave motion by the vector sum of ether-wind and wave velocity. Stellar aberration is therefore silent about the ether-wind, and the entrained ether is not ruled out. By utilizing the fact that the Sagnac effect can be locked in inside an optical fiber it is demonstrated that Sagnac effect is in reality a translational effect. The problem of synchronizing separated clocks forced Sagnac to use a rotating equipment to detect a translational effect. Together with the experiences from the Global Positioning System (GPS) we can find support for an ether that is entrained by our planet. Further confirmation can be found by detecting the ether-wind by translational equipment in a lab or in a satellite.
Overview
This is the earlier of two papers by John-Erik Persson in this collection, and it develops the same central thesis as Physics without Paradoxes — that a wave's motion depends on the ether wind in one dimension only, so that the vector sum of wind and wave velocity is not the right description. Here the argument is applied to two specific phenomena.
The first is stellar aberration. If only the longitudinal component of the wind matters, then a transverse wind cannot tilt a wave front, and aberration measures nothing about the ether. It follows, Persson argues, that Bradley's 1728 observation does not rule out an ether entrained by the Earth — the objection that has stood against entrainment for three centuries is withdrawn.

Bridge From Nowhere: A Story of Space, Motion, and the Structure of Matter is a 1989 book by the chemist William Day . It is the founding statement of what he later called holistic physics : the claim that matter and motion are inseparable, that motion is a structural feature of matter rather than something matter does, and that the material world is built as a three-storey hierarchy of orbital systems — particles, atoms, gravitating systems — each obeying the same pattern at its own scale.
The book is unusual in this literature for who wrote it. Day was not an outsider to peer review: a decade earlier he had published Genesis on Planet Earth , an origin-of-life book taken up by Yale University Press for its Bio-Origins series with a foreword by Lynn Margulis, and reviewed by such figures as Sidney W. Fox and Hyman Hartman. Bridge From Nowhere is what happened when he turned the same interest — how ordered structure arises out of a featureless beginning — from biology to physics.
Its thesis is stated on the jacket:
In this remarkable book the author challenges the traditional definition of motion. He contends that matter and motion are fundamentally inseparable. At each level of matter's hierarchy — particles, atoms, gravitational systems — motion is a structural feature; and as objects move in space, they behave as components conforming to a basic composition of kinematic systems.
— Jacket copy, Bridge From Nowhere (1989)
The argument
Motion as structure
The book's point of departure is a complaint about what physics chose to measure. Dynamics treats motion as something that happens to a body when a force is applied, and describes it with mass, momentum and energy. Day's contention is that this gets the order backwards: at every level of matter, motion is already there

Scientific career
Fields Psychology, Physics, Biofeedback
Buryl Richard Payne (29 May 1932 – 17 August 2017) was an American psychologist and physicist, an early researcher in biofeedback instrumentation, and later an author and inventor in the fields of magnetic healing, geomagnetism and what he called the "spin force." He founded the Academy for Peace Research and devoted much of his later life to the study of solar, geomagnetic and planetary influences on human behavior. His ideas about a measurable biological "spin force" and about the ability of collective thought to affect solar activity are not accepted by the scientific mainstream.
Education
Ph.D. — Payne trained in both psychology and physics and held a doctorate, working across the two fields throughout his career.
Biography
Payne began his career in the emerging field of biofeedback, working with instruments such as the galvanic skin response (GSR) meter and the electroencephalogram (EEG) to measure and train physiological states. He directed a graduate science-writing program at Boston University and wrote widely for both scientific and popular audiences, combining a physicist's interest in instrumentation with a psychologist's interest in consciousness. His 1973 book Getting There Without Drugs: Techniques and Theories for the Expansion of Consciousness and his Bio-Meditation: The Scientific Way to Use the Energy of Your Mind (1978) grew out of this period.
From the 1980s onward Payne turned increasingly to magnetism and to the influence of the Sun and planets on living systems, publishing a series of self-issued books and building the instruments he used in his experiments. He remained an active writer and experimenter into his eighties, and died on 17 August 2017.

Summary
Franklin Hu hosted with Ian Cohen, Bob Gray , Alistair Riddoch and Cornelis Verhey in the chat, and David de Hilster joining for most of the hour. Two arguments ran side by side: whether the medium filling space is a solid, and how the society should run its own wiki.
Is space a solid?
Hu began by reading out the week's email exchange. Akinbo Ojo had argued that the fundamental medium must be an elastic solid rather than a fluid — the position he attributes to Newton, Maxwell, Kelvin and Einstein — the reason being transverse waves. Light and radio waves are transverse; only a medium whose parts keep fixed positions relative to one another can carry a transverse disturbance; therefore the medium is solid.
Hu's objection was the one he pressed all session. The defining property of a solid is that its parts hold their relative positions, which is exactly why one solid cannot pass through another. If space were solid and we are solid, we would be frozen in it like ice. Since we plainly are not, it cannot be a solid; a fluid, in which the parts move aside freely, accounts for the same experience without further invention. He challenged the list to produce any definition of solid on which two solids may pass through each other undisturbed, and treated the failure to do so as a case of what happens when the role of logic is set aside. Verhey's reply on the list — that the right conclusion is that what Hu thinks a solid is, is not one — he rejected as inverted: conclusions come from observation.

The subject was light, and specifically polarization. Hu was replying to a video from Gary of the Draft Science channel, who had responded to his earlier remarks.
Where the two agree
Hu played Gary's account of radio polarization and endorsed it without reservation: a receiving antenna picks up the strongest signal when it has the same shape and orientation as the transmitting one; turn it through ninety degrees and it intercepts almost nothing. That, he said, is exactly how he thinks polarization works.
He also thought Gary had made an important distinction that is usually elided. Radio waves and light waves behave differently, though both are called electromagnetic. A radio antenna produces a continuous sinusoidal train, which one can watch rising and falling on an oscilloscope. Light is produced by an electron moving between levels, which is a discrete event, and arrives in packets. Hu's picture of a photon is a single bump — one flick of a rope rather than a train — whose width is its frequency; and he suggested that if one could put a photon on an oscilloscope one would see nothing, one bump, and nothing again.

Lucas on quantized gravity
Lucas previewed five papers he is writing for the Common Sense Science newsletter on the quantization of gravity, due in early 2020, and set out the problem they address.
The quantization of orbital spacing predates Newton in the form of Bode's law, which worked for the planets known at the time and then failed for the outer ones; applied to the moons of the planets it works for many and not others. Nobody has derived it — not from Newton's law and not from general relativity — and he takes that failure as a sign that something is wrong. He now has some 2,600 measured exoplanets to test against, and says his account handles the data.

"Calorimetric Test of Special Relativity" is the 1984 Physical Review A paper by D. R. Walz, H. P. Noyes and Ricardo L Carezani reporting the only accelerator experiment ever conducted to test Autodynamics against special relativity . It was carried out at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, and its result agreed with special relativity. The page of that name at autodynamics.org is Carezani's retrospective account, written some twenty years later, of why he regards the outcome as consistent with his theory rather than against it.
Overview
Carezani had reached Stanford by correspondence in the 1970s and met the theoretical physicist H. P. Noyes there after moving to California. Noyes wrote the paper; Walz was technically responsible for the experiment; Carezani supplied the theory under test and, by his own account in the endnotes to Muon Decay and Autodynamics , "only participated in writing the short explanation about the theory and discussing the experiment."
The measurement compared the kinetic energy of accelerated electrons , determined calorimetrically, against the energy inferred from their velocity. The relativistic expression was confirmed. Noyes's paper states the motivation plainly: "The alternative theory which led to the test presented here was developed by one of us (RLC) in an effort to understand why the energy expected from beta decay did not show up in a calorimeter."

"Can Dimensionful Constants Have a Fundamental Meaning?" is an article by Alexander Unzicker published on 12 April 2019 on Beyond Mainstream .
Unzicker answers his own title in the affirmative, against the received view that only dimensionless constants can carry fundamental meaning. He accepts the starting observation — that the metre and the second are arbitrary, and that h , c and G are expressed in those arbitrary units — but argues the conclusion drawn from it is mistaken, and typical of a methodology in which calculating has replaced thinking. He points to the history of the subject, particularly Whittaker's A History of the Theories of Aether and Electricity , and to the debate over a variable speed of light.

Title Can Photon-Particle Interactions be Explained with Varying Light Speed?
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) Raymond H Gallucci
Keywords Tired Light , Compton Scattering, Ashmore, Light Speed
Published 2015
No. of pages 4
Abstract
Photon-particle interactions, both ‘classical,’ such as Compton Scattering, and ‘speculative,’ such as ones associated with ‘tired light’ theories of the cosmological red-shift, are explained with the assumption of the constancy of the speed of light. For classical interactions, reciprocal variations in light frequency and wavelength occur under the constraint that their product always equals constant speed ‘c.’ Proponents of a cosmological red-shift claim that the universe is expanding due to expansion of space (or space-time) itself as light, traveling at ‘c,’ is stretched as the distance between the source and observer increases due to this space (or space-time) expansion. Counter arguments to this interpretation often fall into the realm of ‘tired light,’ dismissed by mainstream physicists for various reasons, but still advocated by various ‘dissident’ physicists, since the term was first coined by Zwicky in 1929. In this paper, I examine a classical photon-particle interaction, Compton Scattering, and one of the more popular ‘tired light’ theories to show that the assumption of a constant speed of light is unnecessary, i.e., similar results evolve from assuming a variable light speed.

search_text:
The Casimir effect is an attractive force that appears between two closely spaced, uncharged, parallel conducting plates in a vacuum, and which is conventionally attributed to the fluctuations of the quantum electromagnetic field in the space between and around them.
The effect was predicted in 1948 by the Dutch physicist Hendrik Casimir, then at Philips Research Laboratories in Eindhoven, in the course of work with Dirk Polder on the forces between neutral atoms. Casimir's argument is that the presence of the plates restricts which electromagnetic field modes can exist in the gap: only wavelengths that fit between the plates survive, while the region outside supports the full continuum. The resulting imbalance in mode density produces a net inward pressure. For idealised perfectly conducting plates separated by a distance a , the predicted force per unit area is proportional to 1/ a 4 , so it is utterly negligible at everyday separations but becomes appreciable — of order atmospheric pressure — at separations of a few tens of nanometres.
The force was first measured with reasonable precision in 1997 by Steve Lamoreaux, using a torsion pendulum in a sphere-and-plate geometry, and confirmed in 1998 by Umar Mohideen and Anushree Roy with an atomic force microscope. Later measurements have tested the geometry, temperature and material dependence of the force. It is now a standard laboratory phenomenon and a practical nuisance in micro- and nano-electromechanical devices, where it can cause moving parts to stick together.
A genuinely open question in the standard account
The measurement of the force is not in dispute; its interpretation is. Casimir's own derivation is framed in terms of the zero-point energy of the vacuum, and the effect is very widely presented in textbooks and popular accounts as direct proof that empty space contains energy. Centaurus A or NGC 5128 is a galaxy in the constellation of Centaurus . It was discovered in 1826 by Scottish astronomer James Dunlop from his home in Parramatta, in New South Wales, Australia. There is considerable debate in the literature regarding the galaxy's fundamental properties such as its Hubble type ( lenticular galaxy or a giant elliptical galaxy ) [ 1 ] and distance (10–16 million light-years ). [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ] [ 6 ] NGC 5128 is one of the closest radio galaxies to Earth , so its active galactic nucleus has been extensively studied by professional astronomers. [ 7 ] The galaxy is also the fifth-brightest in the sky, [ 7 ] making it an ideal amateur astronomy target, [ 8 ] although the galaxy is only visible from low northern latitudes and the southern hemisphere.
The center of the galaxy contains a supermassive black hole with a mass equivalent to 55 million solar masses , [ 9 ] which ejects a relativistic jet that is responsible for emissions in the X-ray and radio wavelengths. By taking radio observations of the jet separated by a decade, astronomers have determined that the inner parts of the jet are moving at about half of the speed of light . X-rays are produced farther out as the jet collides with surrounding gases resulting in the creation of highly energetic particles. The X-ray jets of Centaurus A are thousands of light-years long, while the radio jets are over a million light-years long. [ 10 ]
Like other starburst galaxies , a collision is suspected to be responsible for the intense burst of star formation. Models have suggested that Centaurus A was a large elliptical galaxy that collided and merged with a smaller spiral galaxy. [ 11 ]

NGC 5128 was discovered on 29 April 1826 by James Dunlop during a survey at the Parramatta Observatory. [ 12 ]

search_text:
For David Tombe's 2011 paper of the same name, see Centrifugal Force (2011 paper) .
Centrifugal force is the outward effect associated with rotation — the pull felt in a swung sling, the outward thrust in a centrifuge, the tendency of an orbiting body to recede from its centre. In modern textbook mechanics it is classed as a fictitious or pseudo force: an artefact of describing motion from a rotating frame of reference, with no physical cause behind it. A body in curved motion is held to experience only an inward centripetal force; what looks like an outward force is said to be nothing but inertia, the body's tendency to continue in a straight line.
That classification is the point of dispute in the literature archived on this wiki. Most of the papers collected here treat centrifugal force as a real outward force with a physical cause, and regard its demotion to a fictitious status as a twentieth-century error that severed classical mechanics from the medium in which the older physicists believed it operated. The topic is dominated by David Tombe , who has returned to it in paper after paper, and whose position — that centrifugal force is an aether pressure, and that the same pressure appears in electromagnetism — supplies most of the argument set out below. Other lines are represented by Charles William Lucas , who derives inertia and centrifugal force from an electrodynamic force law, by Nainan K Varghese , who denies that curved motion is a single motion at all, and by Nassim Haramein and Elizabeth A. Abstract
It is nowadays taught that centrifugal force is a fictitious force that can only be observed from a rotating frame of reference. This teaching is based on the argument that when no inward centripetal force is acting, a particle will proceed in its straight line inertial path. In situations where the physical effects of centrifugal force are detected, this is dismissed as being merely the effects of inertia. Polar coordinates relative to a point origin expose a centrifugal force acting on a particle that is moving in a straight line, but this centrifugal force tends to be masked from view by virtue of the fact that the radial position vector is rotating. This article will examine ways to expose the physical reality of the centrifugal force.
Overview
Centrifugal Force is a four-page paper by David Tombe of Belfast, dated 10 November 2011 and published through the General Science Journal . Its thesis is that centrifugal force is a real physical force rather than a fictitious one visible only from a rotating frame.
The argument opens with Newton's rotating bucket. When a pail of water is rotated relative to the fixed stars the surface rises at the sides, "yet no officially recognized upward force is deemed to be acting on the system." Tombe holds that the standard dismissal — that this is the tendency of particles to follow straight inertial paths — misdescribes what happens: "It is taught wrongly, that when the inward acting centripetal force yields, only tangential motion ensues, and that no outward radial motion is involved. Later in life he founded Electric Spacecraft, Inc. and published the Electric Spacecraft Journal , a periodical devoted to the study of electric field propulsion and related fringe-science topics including electrostatics, electrogravitics, and aether concepts.

Yost was born on July 10, 1933, in Boston, Massachusetts, the son of Charles William Yost and Winnie (Tuminski) Yost. As a teenager he became an accomplished amateur astronomer, designing and building a ten-inch reflector telescope and an observatory cover for his high school, and he developed early interests in rocketry, electrostatics, and the work of Nikola Tesla . He later recalled deciding at age 17, in 1950, that a "flying saucer" could in principle be designed to operate on electrostatic principles.

As a research engineer on NASA projects, Yost developed and analyzed parachute recovery systems for the Apollo spacecraft and ejection seating for military aircraft. From 1966 to 1969 he served as Director of Systems Analysis at Stencel Aero Engineering Corporation (SAEC) in Arden, North Carolina.

From 1941 he argued that the same discharge physics accounts for a wide range of astrophysical phenomena, and he pursued that idea for the rest of his life.
His position is unusual in two ways. His mainstream work was well received — his 1941 paper on the lightning discharge, written with R. H. Golde, is a standard citation in the field and had been cited some 311 times by 2013 — and his astrophysical claim was narrower than the tradition that later grew from it. Bruce accepted the conventional thermonuclear account of where stellar energy comes from. What he proposed was that the violent and sudden events seen in stellar and galactic atmospheres are electrical discharges, not that the stars are electrically powered.

ChatGPT Solves Dark Matter was a live session presented by Franklin Hu on 19 October 2024 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
The proof for Dark Matter in galaxy rotation curves depends on using the formula v = SQRT(GM(enclosed)/r). However, this formula can only be correctly applied to "spherical" mass distributions and cannot be directly applied to anything like a flat disk galaxy. The anomalous dark matter is appearing because we applying a formula that only works on spheres on a disk shaped galaxy. Papers show that you can recover the observed rotation curves if you calculate gravity correctly using a disk shape and no dark matter is needed. Ordinary Newtonian gravity can explain the galaxy rotation curves with no modification.
Summary
Franklin Hu 's claim is that dark matter is an artefact of applying the wrong formula, and that a language model stumbled into the right answer while making an arithmetic mistake. Roger J Anderton hosted and offered his own diagnosis at the outset: what is taught as Newtonian physics is a dumbed-down version, and a fuller one might account for what dark matter was invented to explain.
The wrong formula
The starting point is David de Hilster 's paper and video, which set Hu off. Newton's universal law is a sum over distances between masses; GM / r 2 with a single radius is a result Newton derived for the special case of a sphere, and holds only outside the mass. Hu's illustration was the Great Pyramid: stand on its apex and ask what radius to use. There is none, and the only honest method is to compute the attraction of every block and add them up — which is exactly what Newton did for the sphere, arriving after considerable labour at a formula that looks like the naive one.
Two consequences follow that he thinks decide the matter.

Chris C. King is a researcher formerly associated with the Department of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Auckland, New Zealand, known for work spanning mathematical biology, chaos theory, quantum cosmology and consciousness studies. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Work
King published "Dual-Time Supercausality" in Physics Essays (vol. 2, no. 2, 1989, pp. 128–151), in which he proposes a model of physical causality extending beyond the standard quantum and classical descriptions. In his account, the usual stochastic quantum model is replaced by two complementary causal processes—a symmetric-time process and a directed-time process—whose mode of interaction is intended to avoid temporal paradox. The proposal draws on the transactional interpretation of quantum mechanics, in which time-symmetric advanced and retarded waves form "transactions."
King has extended these ideas into what he terms transactional and "biocosmology," relating the origin of the universe and of life to the anthropic principle and to a proposed interactive role of conscious observers in cosmological evolution. This body of work lies outside the scientific mainstream and is developed largely through self-published preprints and essays rather than peer-reviewed literature. Much of it is collected on his personal research site, dhushara.com, alongside writings on the "hard problem" of consciousness and quantum cosmology.

Chris P. Duif is a Dutch experimental physicist at the Interfaculty Reactor Institute of Delft University of Technology , where he has worked since the 2000s on spin-echo small-angle neutron scattering (SESANS) and the instrumentation behind it. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists on the strength of a single item: a 2004 preprint reviewing the reported gravitational anomalies during solar eclipses.
That listing gives a misleading impression of the balance of his work. Duif's published record is mainstream neutron instrument physics , running from 2007 to the present in Physica B , Review of Scientific Instruments , Journal of Applied Crystallography , ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces and elsewhere — and the eclipse review itself is a cautious survey rather than an advocacy piece.
Neutron scattering at Delft
Duif works in the Delft group built around SESANS , a technique that measures structure in real space over a range from nanometres to tenths of a millimetre without the tight collimation that ordinary small-angle scattering requires. The trick is to encode the scattering angle in the Larmor precession of the neutron's spin rather than in its position on a detector, which allows a wide beam and so a much larger usable flux.
His contributions are largely instrumental. With M. Theo Rekveldt, Wicher Kraan, Jeroen Plomp and Wim Bouwman he worked on polarization optimisation of spin-echo instruments ( Review of Scientific Instruments , 2008), on spatial modulation of a neutron beam by Larmor precession with Roland Gähler ( Physica B , 2009), on combining SANS and SESANS in a single instrument to cover 1 nm to 0.1 mm

Christian Sutterlin (born 1 February 1943) is a French fluid-mechanics engineer, a graduate of ENSEEIHT Toulouse (1967) and a former Navy officer. He works on alternative paradigms in physics, with interests spanning the ether , angular momentum, fluid mechanics, and analytical philosophy. Beyond his own research, he is significant to the dissident-science community as a publisher : he owns ÉDITIONS D'ASSAILLY (Assailly Publishing), the house that issues Jean de Climont 's directory of dissident scientists.
Éditions d'Assailly and the Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists
Through his imprint Éditions d'Assailly, Sutterlin publishes The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists , compiled by the French engineer Jean de Climont . It is the largest catalogue of its kind: a directory of scientists, engineers, and doctors who dispute — or propose alternatives to — mainstream positions in physics, especially relativity , quantum mechanics, and cosmology .
A revised edition released in November 2015 was announced as containing nearly 8,000 dissident names , each with home-page addresses and notes on the person's work; that edition updated most links, added many new entries and email addresses, and removed duplicate or information-less names. The list is issued as a book-length HTML directory and is also available through Google Books. Éditions d'Assailly likewise publishes de Climont's other titles.
The work is a natural companion to this wiki's mission of documenting science outside the mainstream, and it complements the biographical and bibliographic records collected by the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society .
