Christopher J. Arnold is an American inventor known for a patented "pulsed plasma drive" electromagnetic motor-generator and for related claims concerning energy production and nanodiamond synthesis. His work is associated with the Electric Universe and free-energy communities and lies outside the scientific mainstream.
Biography
Arnold is an independent inventor based in the United States. Public records of his activity are drawn primarily from his patent filings and from online forums and promotional material dating to the early 2000s. Beyond his patents and self-published claims, little verifiable biographical detail is documented.
Work
In 1998 Arnold filed a patent application for an electromagnetic motor and generator built around what he termed a pulsed plasma commutator. The device was described as combining a bipolar magnetic rotor of high-energy permanent magnets with a commutator designed to permit, rather than suppress, electrical sparking, so as to generate a plasma discharge and an adjacent coil intended to recapture radiated energy. The patent, US 6,271,614 B1, "Pulsed plasma drive electromagnetic motor generator," was filed on November 15, 1999 (priority date November 20, 1998) and issued on August 7, 2001.
Arnold and associates subsequently promoted the device under the name PlasmaKing Corporation, and around 2004 solicited private investment for its commercialization. In forum postings he asserted that the technology could produce large volumes of hydrogen from oil, remediate toxic waste, convert oil and coal to methane for low-emission power generation, and generate so-called "zero point" or free energy. GRAVIMAGRETISM represents Part IV of Marinov's encyclopaedic CLASSICAL PHYSICS. In Marinov's absolute space-time theory the gravitational phenomena are considered by analogy with the electromagnetic phenomena. Aiming to obtain a complete mathematical similarity in the gravitational and electromagnetic theories, Marinov introduces hypothetically the magretic energy as a space-time companion to the space gravitational energy, in the same manner as magnetic energy is a space-time companion to the space electric energy. For this reason Marinov re-names the gravitational theory "gravimagretism. Until today experiments have not given proofs about the existence or non-existence of magretic energy. Such an experiment (the "cauldron" experiment) is proposed by Marinov in Part V. The results of Marinov's accelerated "coupled-mirrors" experiment (described in Part III) shows that Einstein's principle of equivalence is not valid, i.e. one can make an experimental distinction between a kinematic and a gravitational acceleration. Marinov's high-velocity experiments lead to the conclusion that our universe is static as a whole. Thus Marinov considers the "red shift" of the galaxies as a gravitational effect and not as a Doppler effect due to the "escaping velocities" of the galaxies. Marinov shows that the gravitational treatment of the "red shift" leads to a quadratic dependence on the distance to the galaxies and not to a linear dependence as one obtains at the Doppler treatment. The observational data fit better to a quadratic dependence and not to a linear dependence as was established previously by Hubble.

Abstract
Both the classical and the relativistic composition law for velocities are applied to re-calculate the Sagnac Effect. The ensuing formulae for the fringe shift are found to differ already in first order of v/c. Whilst the classical formula is validated by interferometric measurements and verified by the GPS-system, this is not the case for the relativistic result.
Overview
Wolfgang Engelhardt, retired from the Max-Planck-Institut für Plasmaphysik at Garching, published this short 2013 paper arguing that special relativity, correctly applied, predicts no Sagnac effect — and that since the effect is measured and is used in GPS, the theory's basic postulate is at stake.
The argument is set out in two parallel derivations. Section 2 treats the rotating interferometer classically. Adapting the Galilean transformation to a circular path by writing d s ′ = d s − v ₀d t with d t ′ = d t , he obtains the composition law v φ ′ = v φ − v ₀, and hence travel times L /( c ∓ v ₀) for the two beams and the standard fringe shift ΔZ = 4 A · Ω / cλ ₀. He notes that Michelson and Gale verified this in 1925 by varying the enclosed area, and reads the result as showing "an 'ether wind' must exist due to the rotation of the earth".
Section 3 repeats the exercise with the Lorentz transformation. Writing the differential form d t ′ = γ(d t − v ₀d s / c ²) and d s ′ = γ(d s − v ₀d t ), and dividing, he obtains the relativistic composition law
v φ ′ = ( v φ − v ₀)/(1 − v φ v ₀/ c ²)
which for v φ = c gives v φ ′ = c . He concludes that both beams travel at c in the rotating frame, so Δt′ = L / c − L / c = 0, and that "the SRT correctly applied to a rotating Sagnac Interferometer does not predict the Sagnac Effect."

Claude Poher (born 19 February 1936) is a French astrophysicist and space researcher, known within the dissident literature for the "universons" theory — a corpuscular, "pushing" model of gravitation in the Le Sage tradition — and known publicly as the founder of GEPAN , the French space agency's unit for the scientific study of unidentified aerospace phenomena. He is listed in Jean de Climont 's Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Career
Poher was born in Brittany and holds degrees in space-research engineering and electronics together with a doctorate in astrophysics. He joined the Centre National d'Études Spatiales (CNES) in the 1960s and spent some three decades there in space research and aeronautics, rising to direct the Rockets and Probes division and, by 1976, the division of Scientific Systems and Projects . He contributed instruments and experiments to NASA's lunar programme and to planetary exploration missions.
In May 1977 he established and directed GEPAN ( Groupe d'Études des Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non-identifiés ) in Toulouse — the first official, government-funded scientific body charged with investigating unidentified aerospace phenomena. He began with a secretary and built the group to about ten scientists and engineers. He took a sabbatical on 30 December 1978 and ceased official work on the subject, though he has continued to follow it privately. The unit itself survived under later names and remains part of CNES.

The Special Relativity Theory (SRT) and the General Relativity Theory (GRT) sometimes exhibit clock effects of equal magnitude which cancel and sometimes exhibit clock effects of equal magnitude which are additive. This cannot be coincidence, yet there is nothing within the two disjoint relativity theories to suggest an underlying mechanism. The effects appear to be related to energy, but the SRT treats energy as relative and the GRT treats an orbiting body as following a force-free trajectory. Thus an alternative to the Einstein theories seems to be required. I have proposed what I call a Modified Lorentz Ether Theory (MLET) which extends the Lorentz ether concepts to cover gravitational phenomena. Following a brief review of MLET concepts, it is contrasted with SRT concepts. Current data available from a number of modern experiments are evaluated with regard to both MLET and SRT. In general, MLET provides a more coherent and consistent explanation of the data. In the principal section of the paper it is shown that in the earth-centered inertial (ECI) frame Global Positioning System (GPS) clocks must not be adjusted for the gradient of the sun's gravitational potential. MLET shows that the differential effect of the sun's gravitational potential is absorbed into the clock bias which converts the Selleri transformation into an apparent Lorentz transformation. By contrast, there is no valid explanation for this phenomenon which is consistent with SRT/GRT and they are thereby refuted. This is very strong evidence that some form of Lorentz ether theory is valid and that Einstein's relativity theories are invalid.

Cláudio Nassif (also published as Cláudio Nassif Cruz ) is a Brazilian theoretical physicist working at the Centro Brasileiro de Pesquisas Físicas and in Belo Horizonte, who has developed over two decades a modification of special relativity called Symmetrical Special Relativity (SSR).
Its central idea is a single, elegant addition. Special relativity has an unattainable maximum speed, c . Nassif adds an unattainable minimum speed, V — equally invariant, equally a barrier — so that the range of possible speeds becomes the doubly bounded interval V < v ≤ c instead of 0 ≤ v < c .
The consequence is that rest is abolished . No particle can be at rest, because rest would require v = 0, and V cannot be reached. And since the minimum speed must be the same for all observers, it defines a privileged frame — which means SSR breaks Lorentz symmetry .

Electromagnetic fields, electric charges, and light possess momentum and energy that we can experience with our sense organs. Therefore, these are real physical entities (objects). Summary
The first of two talks by Sankar Hajra of Kolkata — this one on special relativity, its sequel a fortnight later on general relativity. He set out his method in advance, in a letter Ian J Cowan read at the start: he proposes no theory of his own, will use only Newton and Maxwell, and will say nothing about anyone else's alternative. The session was hampered throughout by the speaker's partial hearing loss; he asked for questions in writing, and much of the discussion had to be conducted through the chat.
The premise
The argument rests on one claim stated at the outset. Electromagnetic fields, electric charges and light possess momentum and energy, and are therefore real physical entities. All physical objects are subject to gravity. Therefore so are these. Hajra's contention is that this single consideration collapses both relativities.
Its immediate consequence is that the Earth carries the electromagnetic fields in its vicinity along with it — they translate, rotate and spin with the planet as any other physical object does, and experience the Coriolis force when in motion relative to its surface. The Earth's surface is then exactly equivalent to free space for electromagnetic purposes, which is why every optical and electromagnetic phenomenon observed on it is independent of the planet's motion.

Common Sense Science (CSS) is an American non-profit research and education corporation, founded in 1997 by the electrical engineer David L. Bergman , dedicated to developing a classical, geometric alternative to quantum mechanics in which elementary particles are real physical objects with real shape and size rather than dimensionless points.
The name states the programme's premise: that physical theory should be answerable to ordinary standards of intelligibility — that every effect has a cause, that objects have definite properties whether or not anyone is observing them, and that a model which cannot be pictured is not yet an explanation. Its founding claims are that the universe and all natural phenomena are fundamentally electrical in character , and that matter is best described using geometric models set in absolute time and Galilean space .
CSS is unusual among alternative-physics efforts in three respects: it produced a sustained, multi-decade research programme rather than a single thesis; it published a regular quarterly journal, Foundations of Science , for more than twenty years; and it is openly and explicitly grounded in a Christian creationist worldview , which its members regard as the source of the realist and causal commitments that classical physics once shared and modern physics abandoned.

It is shown that Einstein's proof for E = mc 2 is actually incomplete and therefore is not yet valid. A crucial step is his implicit assumption of treating the light as a bundle of massless particles. However, the energy-stress tensor of massless particles is incompatible with an electromagnetic energy-stress tensor. Thus, it is necessary to show that the total energy of a light ray includes also non-electromagnetic energy. It turns out, the existence of intrinsic difference between the photonic and the electromagnetic energy tensors is independent of the coupling of gravity. Nevertheless, their difference is the energy-stress tensor of the gravitational wave component that is accompanying the electromagnetic wave component. Concurrently, it is concluded that Einstein's formula E = mc 2 necessarily implies that the photons include nonelectromagnetic energy and that the Einstein equation of 1915 must be rectified.

Abstract
There are two competing formulations of time in physics. Newton defended in the Principia the utilization of absolute time which, according to him "flows equably without relation to anything external." Leibniz, on the other hand, was against this concept and proposed relative time to replace it: "As for my opinion, I have said more than once, that I hold space to be something merely relative, as time is; that I hold it to be an order of coexistences, as time is an order of successions." Leibniz's ideas were accepted and developed by Ernst Mach in his book The Science of Mechanics . Mach proposed to replace Newton's absolute time by the angle of rotation of the planets relative to the frame of fixed stars. In this work we consider the implementation of relational time and its consequences for physics. We concentrate our analysis in a single phenomenon, namely, the flattening of the Earth due to its diurnal rotation. We consider the figure of the Earth in Newtonian mechanics. We point out some philosophical problems with this classical formulation. We then present the flattening of the Earth from the point of view of Relational Mechanics, which is a mathematical implementation of Mach's principle utilizing Weber's law for gravitation.

Presented at the 18th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference at College Park in July 2011, this four-page paper by André Assis of the State University of Campinas takes up the oldest dispute in the foundations of mechanics — whether time is absolute or relational — and works it through on a single concrete example: the flattening of the Earth by its diurnal rotation.

The hole theory
Space cells and holes
The theory needs one hypothesis: that space is built from indivisible space cells , elementary virtual volumes dV which appear and disappear continually. Leshan grounds this in the expectation, common to several approaches to quantum gravity, that there is a minimum measurable length.
When a cell vanishes, what is left is a "vacant place" that does not possess the properties of space-time . Since space-time's properties are duration and extension, a hole in it has neither: inside a hole, extension tends to zero and time dilation is infinite. From this Leshan draws the property the rest of the theory rests on — that holes contract distances and slow time , so that raising the concentration of holes in a region shifts that region's properties towards the hole's own.

Coriolis force is the sideways deflection experienced by a body moving within a rotating system — the apparent curving of winds and ocean currents on the spinning Earth being the standard example. It acts at right angles to the body's velocity and to the rotation axis, and in textbook mechanics it takes the form 2 m Ω × v , where m is the mass, Ω the angular velocity of the frame, and v the body's velocity within it. The expression was written down by the French engineer Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis in an 1835 paper on the energetics of rotating machinery such as water wheels, where he called it the compound centrifugal force .
Like centrifugal force , its companion, the Coriolis force is classed in modern mechanics as a fictitious or inertial force: a term that appears in the equations only when motion is described from a rotating frame, with no physical agent behind it. That classification is the point of dispute in the literature archived on this wiki, and this page follows the same division as the centrifugal-force article — the standard account first, then the objections raised by the researchers here.
The mainstream account
Newton's first law holds that a body free of net force moves in a straight line at constant speed. Seen from a frame rotating at angular velocity Ω , that straight-line motion appears curved, and the equations of motion acquire two extra terms to preserve the form of Newton's second law: a centrifugal term directed outward, proportional to Ω², and a Coriolis term, proportional to Ω and to the body's velocity, acting perpendicular to its motion.
On the orthodox reading these are bookkeeping devices, not forces. They have no agent and no reaction partner, and they vanish when the description is returned to an inertial frame. The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is a faint, extremely uniform bath of microwave radiation arriving from every direction in the sky, with a spectrum very close to that of a blackbody at about 2.725 K. In standard cosmology it is interpreted as relic radiation released when the expanding universe first became transparent to light, roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang .
It was found accidentally in 1964–65 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Holmdel, New Jersey, who could not eliminate a persistent excess antenna temperature of a few kelvin from their horn reflector at 7.35 cm. Their brief 1965 announcement in the Astrophysical Journal appeared alongside a companion paper by Robert Dicke, Jim Peebles, Peter Roll and David Wilkinson interpreting the signal cosmologically. Penzias and Wilson shared the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics. The COBE satellite's FIRAS instrument showed in 1990 that the spectrum matches a blackbody to remarkable precision, and COBE's DMR instrument detected in 1992 the temperature anisotropies — variations of order one part in 100,000 — whose statistics were later mapped in detail by WMAP and by Planck. Superimposed on this is a much larger dipole, at the millikelvin level, attributed to the motion of the solar system relative to the radiation field.
Within the standard model the CMB is the single most quantitatively powerful cosmological dataset: the angular power spectrum of its fluctuations is what fixes most of the parameters of the concordance model, including the Hubble constant and the density attributed to dark matter and dark energy .
A note on prediction
The CMB is usually presented as a successful prediction of the hot Big Bang, and Ralph Alpher, Robert Herman and George Gamow did estimate a present-day relic temperature of a few kelvin in the late 1940s. The cosmological constant , written Λ (lambda), is a term Einstein added to the field equations of general relativity in 1917 to permit a static universe, later discarded, and revived at the end of the twentieth century as the standard description of dark energy .
Einstein's original difficulty was that his field equations, applied to a uniform distribution of matter, gave no static solution: gravity would cause the whole to collapse. Λ supplied a uniform repulsion, tuned to balance the attraction exactly. The balance is unstable, as Arthur Eddington pointed out, and the motivation disappeared when the redshift –distance relation was published in 1929 (see Hubble Constant ). Einstein dropped the term; George Gamow later reported that Einstein had called it his greatest blunder, though the phrase survives only at second hand.
Λ returned in 1998, when two supernova survey teams reported that distant Type Ia supernovae are dimmer than a decelerating universe predicts, and concluded that cosmic expansion is accelerating. Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize. In the resulting concordance model — ΛCDM — the constant accounts for roughly 68 per cent of the total energy density, with cold dark matter and ordinary matter making up the rest.
The cosmological constant problem
Λ is mathematically equivalent to a uniform energy density of the vacuum with negative pressure, and this identification produces the largest quantitative failure in physics. Estimating the vacuum energy of quantum fields by summing zero-point contributions up to a natural cut-off gives a number exceeding the cosmologically inferred value by many tens of orders of magnitude — the figure of 120 orders is often quoted, and even the most conservative estimates leave a discrepancy of dozens of orders. Cosmology is the study of the universe as a whole — its structure, its history, and on the standard account its origin. It is the branch of physics in which the ratio of theory to observation is highest, and the branch this wiki disputes most comprehensively.
Category: Cosmology catalogues nearly 700 items. This page is a map of that literature; the arguments themselves are set out on the topic pages linked from it.
For Hermann Bondi's 1952 monograph of this name, see Cosmology (Bondi book) .
Cosmology or cosmogony?
A distinction drawn repeatedly in this literature is worth taking first, because it frames everything else. Cosmology is the study of the universe; cosmogony is the study of its origin. Glenn Borchardt argues that the two have been conflated, and that the second is not a legitimate scientific subject at all:
IUT denies that cosmogony, the study of the origin of the universe, is legitimate. The word "cosmogony" has not seen popular use in cosmology. To do so would imply that an alternative view was possible. … The creation of something from nothing is clearly a religious assumption, not a scientific one.
— Glenn Borchardt, "Infinite Universe Theory" (2007)
On that view the question is not which origin story is correct but whether an origin story is required. The alternative — an Eternal Universe , infinite in space and time — dissolves the problem rather than solving it, and is the position of a large part of the literature here.
The standard model and its critics
The mainstream account is the Big Bang : an expanding universe some 13.8 billion years old, beginning hot and dense, with structure growing under gravity from primordial fluctuations. Its principal supports are the redshift–distance relation, the cosmic microwave background, and the abundances of the light elements.

Cosmology is a monograph by the cosmologist Hermann Bondi , first published in 1952 by Cambridge University Press (reprinted 1960) in the Cambridge Monographs on Physics series.
Overview
Written soon after the term "Big Bang" was coined, the book aimed to establish cosmology as a distinct branch of physics . Bondi surveys the basic principles and the observational evidence, and reviews the cosmological theories of the day — Newtonian and general-relativistic cosmologies, the theories of Eddington, Dirac, and Jordan, Milne's kinematic relativity, and the steady-state theory (which Bondi himself co-created). For many years it was the standard introductory survey of the subject.
About the author
Sir Hermann Bondi (1919–2005) was an Austrian-British mathematician and cosmologist, best known as a co-author (with Thomas Gold and Fred Hoyle) of the steady-state theory of the universe. See also his Assumption and Myth in Physical Theory and the volume The Nature of Time , from a meeting he convened with Gold.

Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges acts along the line joining them, is proportional to the product of the charges, and falls off as the inverse square of their separation: F = k q ₁ q ₂⁄ r ². It is the foundation of electrostatics and, for most of the researchers catalogued on this wiki, the one piece of classical electrodynamics nobody wants to change.
The standard account
Charles-Augustin de Coulomb published the law in 1785, having measured the force with a torsion balance of his own design. Henry Cavendish had established the inverse-square dependence more precisely a decade earlier, by a null method — showing that no charge resides on the inner of two connected concentric spheres, which holds only if the exponent is exactly 2 — but did not publish, and the result became known only when Maxwell edited his papers a century later.
The null method remains the basis of the modern tests, and they are extraordinarily tight: modern experiments constrain any departure of the exponent from 2 to less than about one part in 10¹⁵. The same experiments are read as an upper bound on the photon rest mass, since a massive photon would give a Yukawa-type exponential cutoff rather than a pure inverse square.
In the standard formulation Coulomb's law is a special case, not an axiom: it is what Gauss's law — the first of Maxwell's equations — gives for a static point charge, and it is the low-velocity limit of the full electrodynamic interaction. The law as written applies to charges at rest; once charges move, the standard theory says that the electric force is supplemented by a magnetic one, and the whole is expressed by the Lorentz force law .
The inverse-square form has a structural consequence worth noting: it makes the electrostatic self-energy of a genuine point charge infinite. Classical electrodynamics has never resolved this, and it is renormalised away rather than answered in quantum electrodynamics.

Abstract
The cross antenna is a medium gain and circular polarization structure made of a conductor or strip line over a ground plane, following a cross contour of four or more branches. One end is feed by a generator and the other one is charged with a load impedance. This paper presents a theoretical and experimental analysis of an eight arms cross antenna, loaded with four different impedances. The theoretical study is made via the computational solution of Pocklington's equation applied to the structure; experimental results are obtained over an antenna of a 12 AWG wire over a ground plane, working in 3.2 GHz. We present radiation efficiency, gain, field pattern, and axial rate results.
Overview
This is an ordinary applied- electromagnetics engineering paper rather than a foundational one, and it should be read as such: it appeared in Apeiron but takes no position on any contested question in physics. The authors — J. Sosa-Pedroza, A. Lucas-Bravo and J. López-Bonilla of SEPI-ESIME-Zacatenco at the Instituto Politécnico Nacional in Mexico City — model and then build an eight-arm cross antenna operating at 3.2 GHz, and compare the computed radiation pattern against measurements taken in an anechoic chamber.
The motivation is that the cross structure is nearly unstudied. It belongs to the family of travelling-wave current-distribution antennas and was introduced by Antoine Roederer in an IEEE paper of 1990; the authors remark that "it seems that no other article has been written about the subject". Curtis E. "Curt" Renshaw (born 20 December 1957) is an American electrical engineer, defense contractor and independent relativity theorist. Over more than two decades he has developed a Galilean-Newtonian alternative to Einstein's special and general relativity, built on a "Radiation Continuum Model" of light that replaces Einstein's second postulate. His central claim is that once light is modelled correctly from first principles, the whole apparatus of time dilation, length contraction, relative simultaneity and velocity-dependent mass increase becomes unnecessary — and with the basis for special relativity removed, that of general relativity falls with it. He has argued this case in some thirty conference papers, in Galilean Electrodynamics , Apeiron , Physics Essays and the IEEE Electronic Systems Magazine , and at length in his book-length treatment Newton's Revenge: The Restoration of Space and Time .
Biography
Education
B.S. in Electrical Engineering — Georgia Institute of Technology, 1982
Second degree in physics — Georgia Institute of Technology, 2013
Master's-level work in electromagnetic theory — George Washington University and Georgia Institute of Technology
The electromagnetic theory is the background from which his later objections to relativity are drawn.
Engineering career
In 1982 Renshaw joined the Navy EHF Satcom Program (NESP) Office of the Space and Naval Warfare Systems Command, then NAVELEX, in Washington, D.C. NESP was the Navy component of the MILSTAR communications program and placed the first operational EHF satellite into service.
In 1985 he founded Tele-Consultants, Inc.

Daniel Jencka (born 1956) is an American composer and independent philosopher based in Albuquerque, New Mexico. Describing himself as a "philosopher-at-large," he is known for his work in the Philosophy of Science and on the nature of time and Consciousness , and in particular for his reappraisal of Aristotle's account of time as "the number of motion."
Biography
Jencka was born in 1956 in Detroit, Michigan. He began composing as a teenager and studied musical composition with the American composer Stanley Hollingsworth, who taught at Oakland University in Michigan. Jencka pursued undergraduate study of philosophy and music at Oakland University.
Alongside his musical activity he has worked in the renewable-energy industry in New Mexico, and he remains active as a composer and philosophical writer and presenter in the Albuquerque area.
Work
Jencka's philosophical work centers on the problem of time. He revisits Aristotle's classical thesis, set out in the Physics , that time is not a thing in itself but rather "the number of motion" with respect to before and after. Jencka argues that this roughly 2,300-year-old account retains its explanatory power and carries consequences that challenge assumptions held both in everyday thinking and in modern science.
He has presented this material publicly, including a talk titled "The Unicorn of Time and the Number of Motion," delivered in 2026 in Albuquerque as part of a series of "Many Worlds" presentations organized by The Larger Universe project. His broader interests extend to the philosophy of science and to questions concerning consciousness.

Dannel Roberts (also credited as Dannell Roberts ) is an independent theoretical physicist and inventor who has developed an alternative particle-based model of the atom that he calls the key ring atom . He is the author of Particle Mechanics: The Theory of Energy States , and presented his work in a sustained series of talks at the ExtraOrdinary Technology Conference between 2013 and 2017. He is not to be confused with the unrelated Jack Roberts documented elsewhere on this wiki.
Scientific contributions
The key ring atom
Roberts's work begins from a single universal particle that changes states, with each state having its own purpose and characteristics. From this he builds a mechanical, model-able picture of atomic structure — the key ring atom — which he uses in place of the conventional orbital picture to account for solids, liquids and gases, for chemical bonding, and for the properties of light. In his account of visible light, three particles with differing reflective and absorption properties are sufficient to explain the phenomenon. His book Particle Mechanics extends the same scheme to sound, electricity, magnetism, heat and cold, and introduces gravity "as a completely new concept."
Gravity shielding
Roberts's best-known claim, presented at the 2014 conference, is that gravitational shielding is achievable. He rejects the idea that gravity is a pulling force and argues instead that gravity is a particle that pushes — gravity particles stream toward and through an atom, so that interrupting the flow interrupts the effect. On his account the key ring atom makes it possible to show mechanically how that flow can be stopped; a device that did so he calls a "gravity cloaking device," which would suppress both gravity and inertia. Dark matter is the name given, in mainstream astrophysics, to a hypothetical form of matter that neither emits nor absorbs light and whose presence is inferred solely from its gravitational effects. It was introduced to close a gap in the accounts: galaxies and clusters of galaxies appear to move as though they contained far more mass than can be seen in stars, gas and dust. On the standard cosmological model dark matter accounts for roughly 85% of all matter, and together with dark energy for something like 95% of the total mass-energy of the universe — a figure which means that, on the orthodox account, the substance we can observe is a small residue of what is really there.
The literature collected on this wiki takes a very different view. Almost none of the researchers documented here accept dark matter as a substance. They regard it instead as an artefact — of a gravitational law misapplied, or of a gravitational law that is itself incomplete, or of forces other than gravity operating at galactic scale, or of a cosmology whose mass budget is wrong because its interpretation of redshift is wrong. What unites them is not a shared alternative but a shared diagnosis: that a discrepancy between prediction and observation was resolved by inventing the missing term rather than by re-examining the theory that generated it. As Tom Van Flandern put it, dark matter is the best known of the " ad hoc helper hypotheses" by which the standard model accommodates observations after the fact.
This article sets out the observational problem as the mainstream states it, then the distinct lines of objection found in the papers archived here, then the alternatives those researchers propose in its place.

Abstract
A review of the study of dark matter is given, starting with earliest studies and finishing with the establishment of the standard Cold Dark Matter paradigm in mid 1980-s. Particular attention is given to the collision of the classical and new paradigms concerning the matter content of the Universe. Also the amount of baryonic matter, dark matter and dark energy is discussed using modern estimates.
Overview
This is a historical review, written as a School lecture and circulated as astro-ph/0401341, in which Jaan Einasto traces the emergence of the Dark Matter concept from Ernst Öpik's 1915 estimate of the density of matter near the galactic plane to the acceptance of the Cold Dark Matter (CDM) model in the mid-1980s. Einasto is not a neutral chronicler: he was one of the principals. The 1974 Tartu paper of Einasto, Kaasik and Saar — which argued in Nature that all giant galaxies are surrounded by massive non-stellar "coronas" — is one of the two papers he identifies as having settled the question, the other being Ostriker, Peebles and Yahil (1974) from Princeton.
The review's organising claim is that dark matter was never "discovered" in a single observation. Einasto presents it explicitly as a Kuhnian paradigm shift: "as often in a paradigm shift, there is no single discovery, the new concept was developed step-by-step." He insists on separating two problems that are often conflated — local dark matter in the disk of our own Galaxy, and global dark matter around galaxies and clusters — and concludes that the first largely evaporated while the second did not. David de Hilster will be discussing whether or not Dark Matter is real or a fantasy. Much time and energy are spent by both dissidents and mainstream scientists trying to find this elusive "stuff". But David's question is: does it exist or are we looking for a ghost? Join him live this Saturday!
Summary
David de Hilster on why he thinks dark matter is unnecessary, built around a scripted video of his own and two papers from the society, with a panel discussion after. He was frank about his motive: he keeps seeing dissidents discussing dark matter when, on his reading, the work refuting it has already been done, and he wanted to get it off his chest.
The argument
The claim is that the anomaly is an artefact of treating galaxies as point masses. The Keplerian fall-off in stellar velocity is derived for a spherical, uniform gravitational field; a spiral galaxy is flat and full of arms, and its field is nothing of the kind. Overlaying the one on the other and finding a discrepancy does not establish an unseen mass.
His strongest exhibit was the reports of galaxies without dark matter, which struck him when he first saw them: the two in question are spherical. A spherical galaxy behaves as a point mass, so the point-mass calculation works and no anomaly appears — which he took to be the answer sitting in plain sight in the mainstream's own articles.

Das Universum funktioniert anders – Realität kontra Relativität ("The Universe Works Differently – Reality versus Relativity") is a 1998 German-language book by the engineer Eduard Krausz , published by Corona Verlag. In it Krausz sets out his Alternative Gravitation Theory and argues that the foundations of nuclear physics and astrophysics are far less secure than they are usually presented to be.
Krausz's central claim is that gravity is not a fixed property tied to an object's mass but the effect of a physical medium — an aether he pictures as a kind of pressure wave streaming out of space and pushing bodies toward one another and toward a planet. On this view a fluid flows around and through all bodies and particles in proportion to their mass. He contends that such a model explains nuclear- and astro-physical phenomena more consistently and more plausibly than mainstream physics, which he regards as fixated on particles. The book connects this theory to his 1991 "Gelsenkirchen experiment," which he presented as evidence for the partial shielding of gravity.
Written for a general readership, the book sits at the border between physics and the wider critical debate over the aether and relativity . Its argument is not accepted by mainstream physics.
Original German description
Realität kontra Relativität — Wesentliche Grundlagen der Kern- und Astrophysik sind weit davon entfernt, gesichertes Wissen zu sein. Deshalb lohnt es sich, den Entdeckungen des Autors und Forschers, Dipl.-Ing. Eduard Krausz, nachzugehen. Seine Alternative Gravitationstheorie kann kern- und astrophysikalische Phänomene durchgehend und wesentlich plausibler erklären als die herrschende Lehre, die ausschließlich auf Teilchen fixiert ist.

David Calder Hardy (born 15 April 1929) is a New Zealand photographer, milking-machine and pump engineer, and independent cosmological theorist. He is best known as the author of Genesis Continuous , a self-published model of an eternal, infinite universe that he advanced as an alternative to the big bang theory.
Biography
Hardy was born on 15 April 1929 at the Te Kuiti Hospital annex in the King Country region of New Zealand. An only child raised on a dairy farm, he described his formal schooling as limited, interrupted by illness and by farm work; he nonetheless recalled excelling in agriculture, practical science and elementary geometry at secondary school. When his father was injured in an accident, Hardy left school to run the family farm.
In 1946 he joined the Air Training Corps and was accepted into the Royal New Zealand Air Force, reporting to Wigram Air Force Base near Christchurch, but he was among a large portion of the intake released shortly afterward as servicemen returned from overseas following the Second World War. He later worked as a photographer, running his own photographic business, and as an engineer of milking machines and pumps. Among his engineering work, he designed a conversion kit giving a positive-displacement pump a variable flow rate, which was recorded in the patent journal.
Hardy married Ann Compton on 7 February 1955 at the registry office in Tauranga, New Zealand; the couple later divorced.

David Dameron is a researcher known for experimental and theoretical work on the Marinov Motor , a controversial electromagnetic device whose operation is claimed to be difficult to reconcile with the conventional Lorentz force law. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Work
Dameron published "Flux Leakage Tests for the Marinov Motor" in the journal Apeiron (Vol. 7, No. 3–4, 2000), reporting a series of tests intended to evaluate the effect of magnetic flux leakage on the motor's behaviour. He concludes that leakage may play a significant part in the observed effect but does not fully account for the motor's operation. A related study appeared in Physics Essays , extending the analysis to the electromotive aspects of the device and the question of a nonzero electric field arising from a direct current in a stationary conductor.
His work follows a line of investigation into the Marinov Motor pursued by researchers such as Thomas Phipps and J. P. Wesley, who argue that the device poses difficulties for standard electrodynamics. These positions lie outside the physics mainstream.

He is unusual among the scientists catalogued on this wiki in that the work was published in the mainstream literature : Astronomy & Astrophysics , General Relativity and Gravitation , Astrophysics and Space Science and The European Physical Journal D , together with chapters from Cambridge University Press, Kluwer and World Scientific. The ideas are heterodox; the venues were not.

Roscoe spent his academic career in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Sheffield , on Hounsfield Road, which was later absorbed into the School of Mathematics and Statistics; within it he belonged to the Particle Astrophysics and Gravitation research group, giving galaxy dynamics as his research interest. David H. Kelk (born 2 October 1972) is a Canadian computer scientist based in Oshawa, Ontario. His research interests are in computers, computer science, genetic algorithms, software engineering and, more specifically, search-based software engineering. He has also written on the sociology of scientific publishing and is a member of the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society .
Biography
Kelk is based in Oshawa, Ontario, Canada. He has been affiliated with the Faculty of Science at the University of Ontario Institute of Technology (UOIT) in Oshawa, where he pursued work in computer science and software engineering.
Work
Kelk's technical interests centre on computer science, software engineering and the application of genetic algorithms . He works in the area of search-based software engineering, a field that applies metaheuristic search techniques such as genetic algorithms to problems in software engineering.
In 2012, together with David Devine, Kelk authored the paper A Scienceographic Comparison of Physics Papers from the arXiv and viXra Archives . The study examined a selection of physics papers drawn from the arXiv and viXra preprint repositories, applying "scienceography" (the study of the writing of science) to compare how the two communities write and present their work. The authors reported that mainstream and fringe scientific papers could be distinguished from one another by conventional text-classification methods.
Kelk also has interests in physics and in role-playing games (RPGs).

David J. Nagel is an American physicist and engineer, Research Professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering of the School of Engineering and Applied Science at The George Washington University. He spent the greater part of his career at the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory , where he rose from research physicist to Superintendent of the Condensed Matter and Radiation Sciences Division, while serving concurrently as a naval officer, retiring as a Captain in the United States Naval Reserve.
He appears on this wiki as one of the most senior and conventionally credentialled figures associated with low energy nuclear reactions (LENR), a field he has followed as scientist, reviewer and manager since the day it began. His distinctive contribution is less experimental than assessive : a long series of status reviews, roadmaps and policy arguments setting out what the field has established, what it has not, and what governments, journals, societies and companies would have to do for it to progress. He prefers the expansion lattice-enabled nuclear reactions to the more usual "low energy", on the grounds that it puts the solid rather than the input energy at the centre of the phenomenon.

Known for Holographic model of consciousness and reality
David Jonsson is an author known for writing on a "holographic universe" interpretation of reality and consciousness. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Ideas
Jonsson is the author of the book Holographic Universe: Law of Attraction & Money (2013), in which he argues that the visible world is a hologram generated by the observer. In his framing, the "real object" is a person's inner thoughts, while the outer, visible world is a reconstructed interference pattern created by the mind. These ideas fall outside the scientific mainstream and are presented by the author in a self-help and metaphysical register rather than as peer-reviewed physics.
He is also associated with fringe "new energy" material on the electromagnetism of fluid flow and temperature gradients, distributed through online alternative-physics archives.

David L. Bergman (6 August 1938 – 3 June 2020) was an American electrical engineer and independent physicist, best known for the spinning charged ring model of the electron and as the founder and president of Common Sense Science, Inc. , the organization and publishing house through which a distinctive classical alternative to quantum mechanics was developed over three decades.
Bergman's central claim was that the elementary particles are not dimensionless points with unexplained intrinsic properties, but real physical objects with real geometry — specifically, charge distributed on a thin spinning ring. In a 1990 paper in Galilean Electrodynamics with J. Paul Wesley, he showed that such a ring, with only four free parameters, reproduces the electron's mass, charge, spin, and magnetic moment; is stable under electromagnetic forces alone with no ad hoc binding assumption; does not radiate; explains the gyromagnetic ratio of 2 rather than postulating it; and yields the anomalous magnetic moment to higher order in agreement with measurement.
With Charles W. Lucas, Jr. , Thomas G. Barnes and Glen C. Collins , Bergman built this into a broader program covering the proton, neutron, nuclear structure, inertia, gravitation and molecular structure, published in the quarterly journal Foundations of Science which he edited (the Common Sense Science quarterly, not the Springer journal of the same name). David Lackey (born 1969) is an independent researcher based in Merrimack, New Hampshire, United States, whose work addresses the structure and classification of fundamental particles and related questions in foundational physics.
Biography
David Lackey resides in Merrimack, New Hampshire. He conducts independent research in theoretical physics outside of the mainstream academic framework.
Work
Lackey's research centers on a proposed geometric relationship among the fundamental particles, in which quarks and leptons are treated within a single unifying scheme. His stated areas of interest include Pilot-Wave Theory as an interpretation of quantum mechanics, low-energy nuclear reactions ( LENR ), the value and origin of the Fine Structure Constant , and the broader goal of Unification in physics. He has presented a "geometric relation of fundamental particles" that seeks to display the relationships between quarks and leptons through a geometric arrangement.

David M. Bower is an independent researcher and critic of Einstein's special relativity who works within the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society community. He argues that the Lorentz–Poincaré (aether) version of relativity, with its preferred reference frame, is preferable to Einstein's version, and that space is absolute rather than purely relational. In recent years he has collaborated with Dennis P Allen on applying Allen's Neo-Newtonian mechanics to electromagnetism and to models of the elementary particles.
Biography
Little biographical detail about David M. Bower is publicly available; he publishes as an independent researcher without a listed institutional affiliation. His work has appeared as preprints on viXra since 2023, and he has presented in the CNPS online livestream series since October 2023, both alone and jointly with Dennis P. Allen.
Scientific contributions
The absolute nature of space
In A Simple Proof of the Absolute Nature of Space (2023), Bower offers what he describes as a logical extension and extrapolation of Newton's rotating-bucket argument. Where Newton used the curved surface of water in a spinning bucket to argue that rotation is absolute rather than merely relative, Bower extends the reasoning to argue that space possesses absolute properties with respect to translational motion as well as rotational motion. This conclusion places him in the classical, pre-Einsteinian tradition of absolute space, and underpins the rest of his critique of relativity.

Puchta) is an independent experimental researcher associated with Proton Spin Technology Inc. , known in the independent-inventor community for three linked lines of work: the Linear Magneto Effect , an anomaly he reports from driving electromagnetic energy against a crystalline structure; the amplification of gravity , which he approaches empirically through bench testers rather than through theory; and proton spin technology applied to hydrogen production and claimed low-energy fusion. He has presented this work publicly at the ExtraOrdinary Technology Conference over more than a decade, and his consistent position is that the phenomena should be judged from hardware running in front of an audience rather than from argument.
Biography
Public sources say little about Puchta's education or early career, and this article does not fill the gap with speculation. He describes the origin of his gravity work as accidental and industrial: in 1997, while working around Mercedes-Benz, he was examining very high voltage discharges through a xenon headlight transformer, and reports that "a slight modification lifted a salt shaker on a thin wire with 35W". By his account he circulated the device around the shop for a week and the others present agreed that he "made some sort of gravity defying device". He is associated with Proton Spin Technology Inc., which he describes as a research and development company working on hydrogen and fusion systems.

David Rosignoli (born 1972) is an American electrical engineer, a licensed professional engineer with more than fourteen years' practice as of 2011, and an experimentalist with an interest in anomalous and unconventional science and technology. He is Director of the Research Advisory Group for the Tesla Science Foundation, a member of the NTIC, and assistant organiser of the Tesla Conference.
Work
Rosignoli's contribution catalogued here is experimental rather than theoretical, which distinguishes it from most of this collection. Experimental Results in Measuring Atmospheric Electricity (2011), written with Michael R Treat and presented at the 18th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference, reports a measurement of the current drawable from the fair-weather atmospheric electric field. A metallised foil balloon lofted a 300-foot carbon-fibre tether, and a Keithley picoammeter isolated behind a remotely operated contactor recorded 0.8 μA at 275 feet — consistent with the roughly 1 μA that C. L. Stong had reported at 300 feet in Scientific American in 1974.
The paper is careful about method: the tether was kept off the ground on a varnished platform, the meter ran from a battery through an inverter, and readings were taken with the experimenters clear of the apparatus. Its practical findings — that an uninsulated carbon-fibre tether performs as well as the insulated wire earlier workers used, and that the splayed five-micron filaments of an uncoated tow make an efficient, very light collector — are of use to anyone repeating the measurement.

David S Walton is a British physicist, electronics engineer and teacher, known chiefly as a long-time collaborator of the British electronics engineer Ivor Catt . With Catt and Malcolm Davidson he formed the "Catt, Walton and Davidson" partnership, whose late-1970s articles and books challenged the conventional textbook treatment of Maxwell's displacement current and put forward a model of the capacitor as a transmission line.
Biography
Walton took his first degree in Physics at the University of Newcastle and remained there to carry out research in experimental atomic physics, leading to a PhD. His first teaching post was as a Lecturer in Physics at Trinity College Dublin, where he worked under the Nobel Prize winner E. T. S. Walton (no relation). At Trinity College he carried out research in electron time-of-flight spectroscopy and on anthracene scintillators.
He then left academic life to set up an electronics company, where he researched and published articles and a book on signal transmission and design issues in fast digital systems. This work led him on to the foundational concepts of electromagnetic theory. He subsequently worked for a multinational company and for a number of smaller companies, eventually running his own consultancy business in information technology; from 1999 to 2002 he was contracted to companies in Utrecht and Brussels to provide consultancy support for the management of their IT infrastructure.
In 2003 Walton made a complete career change and took up a physics teaching post at Emmanuel College, Gateshead, where he formally qualified as a teacher under the Graduate Teacher Programme. He taught at Emmanuel College for eight years before being appointed Head of Physics at Barnard Castle School in 2011.

David N. Talbott (born October 28, 1942) is an American self-taught comparative mythologist whose work offers a radical new vantage point on the origin of ancient cultural themes, myths and symbols. Working in the tradition of Immanuel Velikovsky , his research has been the primary catalyst behind the "Saturn Model" of recent planetary history, and is the subject of the feature documentary Remembering the End of the World . He is the author of The Saturn Myth and co-author (with Wallace Thornhill ) of Thunderbolts of the Gods and The Electric Universe . Talbott is the founder and director of The Thunderbolts Project .
Education
B.S. in education and political science — Portland State University
Talbott was raised in Oregon.
Scientific History
Talbott's interest in ancient catastrophe grew out of the controversy surrounding Immanuel Velikovsky , author of Worlds in Collision . In 1970, together with his brother Stephen L. Talbott as editor, he revived the student magazine Pensée . Late in 1971 the brothers decided to devote a feature issue to Velikovsky's ideas; the response was so great that it grew, between 1972 and 1974, into a landmark ten-issue series titled Immanuel Velikovsky Reconsidered , reaching a circulation of between 10,000 and 20,000 subscribers and bringing renewed scholarly attention to Velikovsky's work.
Beginning in 1971, and motivated in part by Velikovsky's then-unpublished manuscript In the Beginning , Talbott set out to test the Velikovskian thesis through the systematic comparison of the world's oldest myths, symbols and sacred images. Frederick David Tombe (born 1958) is a British independent researcher who writes on electromagnetism , the aether , and the foundations of Maxwell's equations. He is known for advocating the revival of the nineteenth-century luminiferous aether, which he models as a dense "electric sea" of rotating electron-positron dipoles, and for his "double helix theory of the magnetic field." His views on special relativity , the luminiferous aether and the reality of centrifugal force place his work outside the mainstream of modern physics.
He is among the most prolific contributors catalogued on this wiki: the list below runs to 122 papers written between 1984 and 2024, and he has continued to publish since.

Biography
Tombe has described how, early in his undergraduate studies, exposure to Einstein's special relativity alongside the concept of stellar aberration led him to become skeptical of relativity theory, and how his study of vector field theory in 1981 left him dissatisfied with the standard textbook treatment of Maxwell's displacement current.
In 1982 Tombe encountered the writings of anti-relativity authors including Professor Richard A. Waldron of the Ulster Polytechnic and, through him, the aether-drag work of Dr. Carl A. Zapffe of Baltimore, whom he visited in Minnesota shortly after graduating. Over the following years he corresponded with a worldwide network of aether and anti-relativity researchers, including Stanisław Kosowski in Warsaw and J. P. Wesley in West Germany.

Connell (born 1 November 1927) is an English physicist and former development engineer and systems analyst who, after retiring to Portugal, returned to physics and became a critic of both relativistic and gravitational theory. In a series of papers presented to the Natural Philosophy Alliance between 2009 and 2013 he argued that the changes to mass, length and frequency usually attributed to motion and to gravitation follow instead from the conservation of energy, and that gravity itself is electrostatic in origin rather than a property of mass.
Biography
Education

Connell worked as a development engineer on surveying instruments, on seismometers, and on the isotope gamma-ray analysis of light elements in slurry. He moved into computing, becoming chief programmer at Elizabeth Arden in 1968 and, by 1980, a senior analyst and consultant on critical-path analysis systems in New Jersey. He retired to Portugal in 1990 — "better weather" — and resumed his interest in physics in 2003, publishing articles on his own website from 2007 and conference papers from 2009. He continued to take part in the alliance's discussions into 2015.
Scientific positions
Connell's papers develop a single line of argument in which energy, rather than motion or gravitation, is the source of relativistic change.
Relativity from conservation of energy. He holds that neither speed nor a gravitational field has any mechanism for altering the mass of a body, but that raising or accelerating one requires energy, which by mass–energy equivalence appears as added mass in the body's own frame. David Wayne Allan (born September 25, 1936) is an American physicist and metrologist known for developing the Allan variance , a widely used statistical measure of frequency stability in clocks and oscillators. He spent his career in the Time and Frequency Division of the National Bureau of Standards (NBS, now the National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST) in Boulder, Colorado, and made significant contributions to precise timekeeping and to the GPS system. Ideas
Wilcock proposes that physical matter is formed by what he calls an "aether" or "Source Field" — an invisible, conscious, fluid-like source of universal energy. Drawing on the work of the Soviet astrophysicist Nikolai Kozyrev, he argues that rotation and its direction can produce anti-gravity and related effects, and that mainstream science has overlooked evidence for a conscious, energetic substrate underlying matter. These claims lie outside the accepted framework of modern physics and are not supported by the mainstream scientific community.
Wilcock develops these themes in books including The Source Field Investigations (2011) and The Synchronicity Key (2013), and through his website Divine Cosmos, where he publishes essays and lectures on "soul growth, ascension, and the evolution of consciousness." Miller occupies an unusual position in the literature collected on this wiki. He was not a dissident. He was as established as a physicist of his era could be: head of physics at the Case School of Applied Science for forty-three years, a member of the National Academy of Sciences, and president of the American Physical Society , in which capacity he delivered the 1926 address announcing his result. He worked with Edward Morley , co-author of the experiment his own work extended.
He matters here because his data did not go away . A large, careful, decades-long body of measurement, produced by a respected experimentalist using the most sensitive apparatus of its day, reported a small but systematic effect that the theory adopted in his lifetime says should not exist. That result was set aside rather than refuted — and much of the research documented on this wiki begins by going back to it. See Michelson–Morley experiment and Preferred frame .

Paul LaViolette, who has been researching pulsars for over 25 years, shows that while these pulsars have long been assumed to be spinning stars, the true nature of these radio sources has been grossly misunderstood.
In Decoding the Message of the Pulsars , LaViolette shows that pulsars are distributed in the sky in a nonrandom fashion, often marking key galactic locations, and that their signals are of intelligent origin. Using extensive scientific data to corroborate his theory, he presents evidence of unusual geometric alignments among pulsars and intriguing pulse-period relationships. Equally compelling is the message LaViolette contends is being sent by these extraterrestrial beacons: a warning about a past galactic core explosion disaster that could recur in the near future.

Deconstruction of Light Speeds in Moving Refractive Media was a live session presented by Joe Sorge on 9 May 2026 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
The independence of the Sagnac phase shift from refractive index can appear puzzling, particularly when compared with the Fizeau experiment where refractive index plays a central role. An intuitive basis for this difference is provided by decomposing the light-transit time in a moving dielectric into: vacuum transit, refractive delay, and motion-induced differential distance. Presented by Joe Sorge, hosted by Ian Cowan.
Summary
Joe Sorge , speaking from Las Vegas, presented work published in the European Journal of Physics . He attributed its acceptance to the journal's double-blind review — his earlier submissions, he said, were rejected by editors without being sent out. He described physics as a hobby taken up after a friend, studying Einstein at school, remarked that it was remarkable light always goes at the same speed for everybody; Sorge could not accept it and began reading.
The puzzle
The Sagnac fringe shift is independent of the refractive index of the medium, while the Fizeau experiment depends on refractive index centrally. The talk set out to explain the difference.
Fizeau in 1859 sent light around a circuit through flowing water, one beam with the current and one against. He expected the speed to be c / n plus or minus the water speed, and found instead c / n plus or minus v (1 − 1/ n 2 ) — Fresnel's partial drag coefficient, which fitted but which nobody was happy to explain. In 1907 Max von Laue accounted for it by relativistic velocity addition, taking the rest-frame speed as c / n . Dennis Letts obtained his undergraduate degree from Texas Technology University in mass communications in 1972 and studied advanced math and physics at the University of Texas at Austin. Letts began researching cold fusion in 1989 and started his experimental work in 1992 and has continued full time. Letts has performed approximately 6,000 experiments from 600 cells. His main research interest has been triggering methodology, beginning with radio frequency in 1992, which evolved to laser stimulation in 2003. Perhaps one of the most lasting contributions by Letts, so far, is a subtle, but highly important one: Letts invented the application of catalyst pellets for the recombination process in cold fusion cells, which recombines the hydrogen and oxygen evolved during cold fusion experiments. This innovation brought three benefits to the field. First, it reduced the cost for special recombination materials down from $1000 to $40. Second, it eliminated the need for the previous recombination material which may have clogged and been responsible for the accidental death of SRI International cold fusion researcher Andy Riley, and third, it allowed for more widespread use of closed cell calorimetry, being safer and more affordable.
Letts works in his personal laboratory in Austin, Texas, where he has enjoyed productive collaborations with Dennis Cravens, Ed Storms, and Scott Little for many years.

Abstract
In several recent papers we showed that choosing new sets of postulates, including classical (pre-Einstein) physics laws, within the main body of Einstein's special relativity theory (SRT) and applying the relativity principle, enables us to cancel the Lorentz transformation from the main body of SRT. In the present paper, and by following the same approach, we derive Einstein's equation E = mc 2 from classical physical laws such as the Lorentz force law and Newton's second law Einstein's equation is obtained without the usual approaches of thought experiment, conservation laws, considering collisions and also without the usual postulates of special relativity.
In this paper we also identify a fundamental conceptual flaw that has persisted for the past 100 years. The flaw is interpreting the formula E = mc 2 as the equivalence between inertial mass and any type of energy and in all contexts. It is shown in several recent papers that this is incorrect, that this is a misinterpretation. What Einstein considered to be a central consequence of special relativity is in fact derivable from (pre-Einstein) classical considerations. E = mc 2 becomes secondary, not fundamental, and whilst no doubt useful in certain circumstances, need not be valid in all generality.

Abstract
This report demonstrates that a changed model of the universe results when the assumption is made that permittivity reduces with time in an expanding universe. Age, expansion, and dark matter are all affected.
Overview
Dated 24 February 1999 and never published in a journal, this three-page report by Morton F Spears offers a single mechanism for three cosmological puzzles then in the news: a universe apparently younger than its oldest stars, an expansion that appeared to be accelerating, and the missing mass called dark matter . Spears states his aim as explaining them "without resorting to speculations or new theories… Only facts and physical laws are used", and writes deliberately for non-technical readers, with almost no algebra.
The argument is a chain of six numbered "Facts".
Permittivity falls as the universe expands
Matter of any kind placed between capacitor plates raises the measured capacitance above its vacuum value, so the effective permittivity of a volume of space rises with the amount of matter in it. Spears offers a "little bang" demonstration — insulated metal balls glued around an explosive charge, with capacitors along a radial path measuring permittivity as a ball passes — and then scales it up, imagining plates 10,000 light years square separated by 100 light years, enclosing the Earth. Long ago, when everything was closer together, such a measurement would have returned a larger capacitance. Hence "perceived permittivity in the space of our Universe is decreasing with time and distance from the big bang origin."

Abstract
The big bang theory postulates that the entire universe originated in a cosmic explosion about 15 billion years ago. Such an idea had no serious constituency until Edwin Hubble discovered the redshift of galaxy light in the 1920s, which seemed to imply an expanding universe. However, our ability to test cosmological theories has vastly improved with modern telescopes covering all wavelengths, some of them in orbit. Despite the widespread acceptance of the big bang theory as a working model for interpreting new findings, not a single important prediction of the theory has yet been confirmed, and substantial evidence has accumulated against it. Here, we examine the evidence for the most fundamental postulate of the big bang, the expansion of the universe. We conclude that the evidence does not support the theory; and that it is time to stop patching up the theory to keep it viable, and to consider fundamentally new working models for the origin and nature of the universe in better agreement with the observations.

Summary
Prompted by an email argument running within the society, Roger J Anderton narrowed his standing complaint to a single object: the Lorentz transformations, and the two ways of reading them. He set aside his own doubts about the mathematics for the occasion and accepted the equations as given, so that the question could be the interpretation alone.
His framing is that this is where the society and the mainstream talk past each other. Dissidents hold that the transformations should be read through Lorentz's theory rather than Einstein's; the mainstream dismisses the question as metaphysics and confines itself to whether the algebra fits the experiments. Since the two interpretations are agreed to be experimentally indistinguishable, there is no evidence that could settle it — which is exactly why nobody is listening.

Working from ChatGPT and checking against Gemini, he set them side by side. Lorentz: an ether exists, and with it a preferred frame; time and space are absolute; contraction and clock retardation are real physical effects of motion through the medium; only clocks at rest in the ether are truly synchronised; light travels at c relative to the ether. Einstein: no ether and no preferred frame; simultaneity is relative; space and time are unified into Minkowski's spacetime; the effects are kinematic relations between measurements in different frames with no underlying medium; light speed is invariant by postulate.

Abstract
Relying on the variational principle, it is proved that new contradictions emerge from an analysis of the Lagrangian density of the Klein-Gordon field: normalization problems arise and interaction with external electromagnetic fields cannot take place. By contrast, the Dirac equation is free of these problems. Other inconsistencies arise if the Klein-Gordon field is regarded as a classical field.
Overview
Eliahu Comay, of the School of Physics and Astronomy at Tel Aviv University, argues in this Apeiron paper that the Klein-Gordon (KG) equation — (□ + m 2 )φ = 0, sometimes called Schrödinger's relativistic wave equation — cannot be a fundamental equation of motion for a massive particle. His method is deliberately narrow: he accepts the variational principle and works out what it permits, and he explicitly excludes "corrections that rely on other physical arguments" as beyond the scope of the work. Everything is derived from the Lagrangian density and the Euler-Lagrange equation.
The conclusions are strong. Comay claims to prove that the KG field cannot represent probability density on dimensional and Lorentz-transformation grounds; that a KG particle cannot interact with an external electromagnetic field, and therefore cannot carry electric charge ; that the classical action of a free complex KG field vanishes rather than reducing to the classical particle action; that the mass parameter in the real KG Lagrangian does not behave like ordinary mass in Einstein's field equations; and that the Yukawa force derived from a scalar KG potential violates the orthogonality of 4-force and 4-velocity required by Special Relativity . In October 1987, whilst on a lazy holiday, I pondered on this question of the dinosaurs' gigantic size compared with present-day life. As a design engineer, I was particularly interested in calculations which showed that the bones of the larger dinosaurs were too weak to support their own body weight. Here was the essential paradox of the dinosaurs' large size. Their bones should buckle and crack. Yet the fossil bones in museums around the world showed that these giants had thrived in their own world of hundreds of millions of years ago. How can both of these statements be true?

A stronger gravity would tend to reduce the size of life whilst a weaker gravity would allow life to become larger. Dinosaurs may have become so huge because the earth's surface gravity was weaker than present.
The explanation is beautifully simple in its clarification of the dinosaurs' gigantic size. Using the concept of an increasing gravity allows a fascinating new world in which the gigantic animals of the past were forced to develop smaller sizes as gravity increased to the present day value. The Dinu Effect is the observation that two cylinders rotating under water attract or repel one another in exactly the pattern of two permanent magnets — attracting when spun in opposite directions and repelling when spun in the same direction — with no magnet, charge or field involved anywhere in the apparatus.
The effect is named after the Romanian physicist Ionel Dinu , who performed and filmed the underwater experiments from 2006 onward as part of a programme to show that electric, magnetic and gravitational forces are fluid-mechanical effects in a liquid aether . The name "Dinu Effect" was coined by David de Hilster in Principia Mathematica 2 , written with his father Robert de Hilster , where the effect is adopted as the experimental basis for the magnetic component of the Four Universal Motions .
Its importance to the researchers who use it is that it is a physical demonstration, not an argument . Magnetic-looking attraction and repulsion are produced in a bucket of water, in front of a camera, by rotation alone.
The experiment
The apparatus is deliberately simple. Two cylinders — in other runs, disks — are suspended in water and set rotating, and their subsequent motion is observed. The variable is the relative direction of rotation.
Opposite directions of rotation → the cylinders attract and move together.
Same direction of rotation → the cylinders repel and move apart.
This is the same rule that governs magnets, and it is the whole of the observation. Dinu has also run the experiment with rotating disks and has supported the physical work with computational fluid dynamics simulations.

Dmitry Yu Tsipenyuk is a Russian physicist associated with the Prokhorov General Physics Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists for his proposed generalization of special relativity known as the Extended Space Model.
Work
Together with collaborators (notably V. A. Andreev), Tsipenyuk proposes an Extended Space Model (ESM) that enlarges the (1+3)-dimensional Minkowski spacetime of special relativity to a (1+4)-dimensional space, adding the interval S as a fifth coordinate. In this framework he argues that scalar gravity and electromagnetism can be unified into a single field, that particle rest masses need not be constant, and that a photon can carry a nonzero variable mass. The model predicts that electromagnetic fields could, under certain conditions, be partially transformed into gravitational effects.
Tsipenyuk and colleagues have reported experiments intended to test this prediction, directing a beam of relativistic electrons (about 30 MeV) onto a tungsten target and measuring small deviations of a nearby rotating pendulum, with claimed forces at the microscopic upper bound of about 10 Template:Sup N. This unification programme and its experimental interpretation lie outside the accepted framework of general relativity and the Standard Model.

Abstract
The precession of the equinoxes was discovered in the second century BC by Hipparchus, and it was described as a slow revolution of the whole field of stars about the ecliptic poles. This could be explained if the Sun orbited some unseen object. The modern explanation was given by Newton as being the slow rotation of the Earth's polar axis about the ecliptic poles caused by gravitational forces from the Sun and Moon on the non-uniform mass distribution in the oblate Earth. In the first model, the Earth's celestial equator is fixed in space, and the celestial sphere appears to rotate. In the modern model, the celestial sphere is fixed, and the celestial equator rotates. These two models are indistinguishable by astronomical observations. This paper computes a range of possible solar orbits, depending only on the assumed mass of the unseen attractor, that were obtained by minimizing the squared error in the ecliptic longitude of Regulus as measured by Hipparchus circa 128 BC, Ptolemy in 138 AD, 11 observations by Arabic astronomers in the period of A.D. 830-975, the modern longitude of Regulus, and the modern precession rate. An intriguing possibility is that many transneptunian objects and long-period comets may orbit the same attractor that the Sun orbits. Pluto could have been captured by the Sun, if it had been deflected by Neptune. The goal of this line of research is to see if there is a particular attractor mass that will cause Pluto to have been captured by the Sun.

Domina Eberle Spencer (September 26, 1920 – May 2022) was an American mathematician, a longtime Professor of Mathematics at the University of Connecticut, and one of the most prolific figures in twentieth-century dissident physics. A child prodigy, she entered the Massachusetts Institute of Technology as a high-school student in a summer program and stayed to earn three degrees — an S.B. in Physics (1939), an S.M. in Mathematics (1940), and a Ph.D. in Mathematics (1942, at the age of 21) under the geometer Dirk Jan Struik. Over a career spanning more than seventy years she authored some 300 technical papers across mathematics, optics, illuminating engineering and the foundations of electrodynamics.
Spencer is best known for her decades-long scientific partnership with the MIT electrical engineer Parry Moon (1898–1988) — whom she later married — and for the New Gaussian Electrodynamics she developed in her later years, a reformulation of electromagnetic theory built on Ampère's original force law that dispenses with Einstein's special relativity . She co-founded the Natural Philosophy Alliance (NPA) in 1993 and served as its long-standing president. She died in May 2022 at the age of 101.
