Donald Roth is an independent United States researcher associated with the aether and "new energy" community, known for experiments that he interpreted as evidence that magnetic fields represent a flow of aether.
Biography
Roth is an independent investigator active in the alternative-energy and aether-theory community during the 1990s. He presented his experimental work to the Institute for New Energy at its First Aetheric Conference, held on July 19–20, 1997, and his results were subsequently reported in New Energy News (vol. 5, no. 4, August 1997).
Work
Roth's best-known experiment used a suspended magnetic torsion beam, essentially a bar magnet hung from a string and balanced at its center. When a strong magnet was placed on a nearby table with one pole directed toward the beam, the beam eventually settled toward the opposite pole after a series of oscillations. Roth reported that, after the arrangement had been maintained for about five days, the magnet could be moved a considerable distance away and the beam would still be attracted as though the magnet remained in place.
Roth interpreted this apparent "magnetic memory" as evidence that magnetism is a flow within the aether: once such a flow is established in a localized region of space, he argued, it can persist there even after the magnet that produced it is removed. These claims are outside mainstream physics, which describes the observations through conventional electromagnetic theory and does not recognize an aether medium.

Because the two share the same transformation law, they predict the same result for anything measurable in those coordinates, and the ether's preferred frame is hidden by the very contraction and clock-slowing that the theory posits.

Marett notes accurately that time dilation appears in Lorentz in 1899 and in Larmor in 1900, before Einstein, differing only in interpretation.

Trained at Harvard University in linguistics and Asian languages, he ranged widely across the ancient texts of Egypt, China, and India before turning to questions in the foundations of physics and consciousness.
Biography
White earned both a B.A. and a Ph.D. from Harvard University in the field of Oriental languages and civilizations, with a focus on linguistics and Asian languages, and spent a period studying at National Taiwan University. He went on to teach literature and Asian languages at Maharishi International University in Fairfield, Iowa, for many years. In his later life he lived in Taiwan, where his research and publishing were carried on through DeltaPoint Educational Technologies and the Sacred Scarab Institute. He died in Taiwan on March 21, 2021, at the age of 79.

Based in Vancouver, he developed an account of gravity and related phenomena founded on a revival of the aether of James Clerk Maxwell .

He served as a Justice of the Supreme Court of British Columbia from 1987 to 2007, and from 2008 to 2015 acted as counsel to Davis LLP in an advisory capacity.
Shaw was married to his wife Pat for 64 years and had two children. He died on March 24, 2025, in Vancouver at the age of 92.

Abstract
An abominable by-product of the modern relativity era is the widely circulated notion that a magnetic field is the relativistic component of the electric field. This idea arises out of applying the Lorentz transformation to Heaviside's versions of Maxwell's equations. The result yields both the Biot-Savart law and the Lorentz force along with the relativistic conversion factors. This article aims to demonstrate that the Lorentz transformation of the Maxwell/Heaviside equations, as regards producing the vxB component of the Lorentz force, is merely doing what a Galilean transformation would also do. It is restoring the convective component that was part of Maxwell's original fourth equation, and which Heaviside and Gibbs took away in 1884. This article also demonstrates that the Biot-Savart law is a solution to Maxwell's equations independently of the Lorentz transformation.

Edward Arthur Milne (14 February 1896 – 21 September 1950) was a British astrophysicist and mathematician, Rouse Ball Professor of Mathematics at Oxford from 1928, who built a complete cosmology out of the special theory of relativity and a symmetry postulate, without using general relativity or curved space at all. He named that postulate the cosmological principle .
Milne's first career was in stellar physics. He worked out the theory of radiative transfer in stellar atmospheres, the Milne–Eddington approximation for line formation, the theory of the outer layers of stars, and the escape of atoms from stellar surfaces. He disagreed sharply with Eddington over the internal constitution of stars, arguing for degenerate cores against Eddington's standard model. He was awarded the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1935 and was its President from 1943 to 1945.
Kinematic relativity
From 1932 Milne turned to cosmology. His starting point was that the general theory of relativity smuggles in far more structure than the evidence warrants, and that a cosmology should be deduced from as little as possible. He assumed only special relativity, a set of equivalent fundamental observers, and the requirement that the universe look the same to all of them — his cosmological principle.

Abstract
In the study of an Earth orbiting satellite, the terms of the series expansion of the Earth's gravitational potential can be expressed as functions of the eccentricity of the satellite. These functions are also known as eccentricity functions. The series expansion of these functions given by Kaula [2] appears to result in instabilities at high eccentricities. When calculating the eccentricity functions, researchers resort to numerical integration techniques instead. The approach followed in this contribution bypasses the problem of instability at high eccentricities by using a Hansen coefficient definition. As a test, we first calculate analytical expressions for various known eccentricity functions and then we proceed with the calculation of the eccentricity functions associated with degree and order 20, 30, 40, 50 sectorial harmonic coefficient expansion of the gravitational potential. Our calculation demonstrates the efficiency of Hansen coefficient approach that differs from that given by Kaula. It is efficient, fast, and can easily be performed with the help of a personal computer, with no instabilities at higher eccentricities.
Overview
Ioannis Haranas, Omiros Ragos and Michael Harney address a computational problem in satellite geodesy: how to evaluate the eccentricity functions that appear in the spherical harmonic expansion of a planet's gravitational potential, without the numerical instabilities that afflict the standard series.

Edmund Storms obtained a Ph.D. in radiochemistry from Washington University (St. Louis) and is retired from the Los Alamos National Laboratory after thirty-four years of service. His work there involved basic research in the field of high temperature chemistry as applied to materials used in nuclear power and propulsion reactors, including studies of the "cold fusion" effect. Over seventy reviewed publications and monographs resulted from this work as well as several books, all describing an assortment of material properties. He presently lives in Santa Fe where he is investigating the "cold fusion" effect in his own laboratory. These studies have resulted in sixteen presentations to various conferences including the ACS and APS. In addition, twenty-one papers have been published including three complete scientific reviews of the field, one published in 1991, another in 1996 and the latest one in 1998. A critical evaluation of the Pons-Fleichmann Effect was published in 2000. In May 1993, he was invited to testify before a congressional committee about the "cold fusion" effect. In 1998, Wired magazine honored him as one of 25 people who are making significant contributions to new ideas.
Work on cold fusion
Storms is among the small number of researchers with an established mainstream career in nuclear science who continued working on the cold fusion claim after most laboratories abandoned it in the early 1990s. His approach has been that of a materials chemist rather than a physicist: he has argued consistently that the phenomenon's notorious irreproducibility is not evidence against it but the central clue to its nature, and that the reaction cannot occur in ordinary metal but only at some rare structure formed by chance during preparation — a condition he named the nuclear-active-environment , or NAE.

Eduard Krausz is a German diploma engineer (Dipl.-Ing.) and independent researcher based in Groß-Umstadt, known for an alternative theory of gravity in which gravitation is the effect of a physical medium rather than a property of mass. He set out his ideas in the 1998 book Das Universum funktioniert anders - Realität kontra Relativität .
Scientific work
Krausz rejects the standard account in which gravity is an unchanging quantity fixed by an object's mass. In his Alternative Gravitation Theory he treats gravity instead as the action of an aether — a medium he pictures as a pressure wave issuing from space that pushes bodies toward a planet and toward one another. On his account a fluid flows around and permeates all bodies and particles in proportion to their mass, and he holds that this picture accounts for nuclear- and astro-physical phenomena more consistently than mainstream physics, which he regards as too narrowly fixed on particles.
In 1991, at the Fachhochschule Gelsenkirchen, Krausz carried out an experiment — since known as the Gelsenkirchen experiment — which he presented as evidence that gravity can be partially shielded. The experiment was reported in the German magazine Raum & Zeit and was later the subject of an independent replication attempt. His work has circulated in the German-language critical-physics and alternative-science communities rather than in the mainstream literature, and his conclusions are not accepted by mainstream physics.

Edward Henry Dowdye, Jr. (13 November 1943 – 31 December 2020) was an American laser optics physicist, retired from NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, and the author of the Extinction Shift Principle — a purely classical emission theory offered as an alternative to both special and general relativity.
Dowdye was unusual in this literature on two counts. First, his objection to general relativity was observational rather than philosophical : he argued that light bending near the Sun occurs only at the thin plasma rim and not in the vacuum beyond it, which is what refraction predicts and not what gravitation predicts, and he pursued this claim through the published deflection and timing data. Second, he was by his own description the only working emission theorist of his generation — the tradition having lapsed since Walter Ritz (1878–1909) — and his version was distinctive in applying to gravitation as well as electromagnetism, where earlier emission theories addressed light alone.
He was one of the featured scientists in the feature-length documentary Einstein Wrong - The Miracle Year (2013), in which he appears alongside Patricia Anne de Hilster , Robert de Hilster and David de Hilster .

Edward Williams Morley (29 January 1838 – 24 February 1923) was an American chemist whose name is attached to the most argued-over experiment in modern physics, but whose own reputation in his lifetime rested on something else: he was the most exact analytical chemist of his generation.
Life and chemical work
Morley was born in Newark, New Jersey, the son of a Congregational minister, and was taught at home before entering Williams College. He trained for the ministry at Andover Theological Seminary and was ordained, but was unable to secure a pulpit; in 1869 he took a professorship of chemistry and natural history at Western Reserve College in Hudson, Ohio, moving with the college to Cleveland in 1882. He remained there until his retirement in 1906.
His major chemical work was the determination of the atomic weight of oxygen relative to hydrogen, published in 1895 after more than a decade of work in which he prepared both gases to a purity nobody had previously achieved and weighed the water formed by their combination. The result stood as the standard value for years and is still cited as a model of precision measurement. He also carried out careful studies of the oxygen content of the atmosphere, and served as president of the American Chemical Society in 1899. He was awarded the Davy Medal of the Royal Society in 1907 and the Elliott Cresson Medal in 1912.

Edwin Eugene Klingman is an American physicist and author known for his work on a self-interacting gravitomagnetic "C-field" and for a long series of essays submitted to the Foundational Questions Institute (FQXi). He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Background
Klingman earned a PhD in physics and worked as a research physicist in atomic and molecular physics. His doctoral work was later published as The Automatic Theory of Physics , which describes how a robot might derive a theory of physics from pattern recognition and entropy.
Ideas
Klingman argues for a gravitomagnetic field, which he calls the "C-field," treated as a continuous field filling space everywhere. He proposes that the C-field associated with massive rotating black holes offers a simpler account of the light-years-long astrophysical jets than magnetic-field explanations. In his FQXi essays he also questions foundational assumptions of quantum mechanics, including aspects of Bell's theorem, and explores the nature of time, information and consciousness. These positions lie outside the accepted mainstream of physics.

Edwin Powell Hubble (November 20, 1889 – September 28, 1953) was an American astronomer who established that the spiral nebulae are galaxies far beyond the Milky Way, and who discovered in 1929 the linear relation between a galaxy's redshift and its distance now known as Hubble's law .
His name is attached to the expanding universe, and his relation is universally cited as its observational proof. This is one of the more striking ironies in the history of cosmology, because Hubble himself never accepted that interpretation , warned repeatedly against it, and in later life inclined toward a static, endless universe in which redshift arises from some unrecognised principle of nature. His caution is regularly invoked by the researchers catalogued on this wiki.
Early life and education
Hubble was born in Marshfield, Missouri, in 1889. He studied mathematics and astronomy at the University of Chicago and then went to Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, where he read law at his father's urging. He passed the bar and practised briefly in Louisville, Kentucky, before abandoning law for astronomy — returning to Chicago for his doctorate and joining the staff of Mount Wilson Observatory.

Because the period–luminosity relation of Cepheids allows their distance to be calculated, he could show that Andromeda lies far outside the Milky Way. Efficiency is a four-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It is the fourth part of the ten-part handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and it follows immediately on " Conservation Laws ".
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
Efficiency is the ratio of useful output to total input, and the reason it earns four pages here — more than the conservation laws themselves — is that the ratio is much easier to get wrong than it looks. An over-unity claim is a claim that this number exceeds one. Most of the ways it can exceed one have nothing to do with new physics.
Efficiency is not coefficient of performance
The commonest confusion in the whole subject is between efficiency and coefficient of performance . A domestic heat pump delivers three or four joules of heat into a house for every joule of electricity it consumes, and its COP is therefore 3 or 4. This is not a violation of anything: the extra energy is not created but moved , pumped from the cold outside air into the warm inside, and the electricity pays only for the pumping. A device whose output is of a different kind from its input — heat moved versus work supplied — can have a ratio above one all day long.
Several claimed over-unity devices are of exactly this character, drawing on an unmeasured ambient reservoir. Force is generally understood as cause of an action and result of an action is often quantified as work-done or as energy-transferred. All these terms are very vague and have no clear meanings or definite mechanisms of action. Force is considered as the primary entity and work or energy is considered as the result of action of force. The concept, put forward in the ?Hypothesis on MATTER , depicts force, work and energy as terms with clear meanings. Abstract
The conviction that relativistic simultaneity has a conventional nature is shared by many authors, but it will be shown that simultaneity exists in the physical reality and therefore cannot be conventional. If the coefficient - we call it e 1 - of the space variable x in the Lorentz, or other, transformation of time had a conventional nature it should be possible to modify it without touching the empirical predictions of the theory: this expectation can be called Reichenbach-Jammer conjecture ("RJ conjecture"). Given that Einstein's principle of relativity leads necessarily to the Lorentz transformations, and thus also to a fixed nonzero value of e 1 , the modification would imply a reformulation of the relativistic idea itself. With respect to the idealized expectation, based on the RJ conjecture, the concrete development of physics produces some exciting novelties. Several phenomena, in particular those taking place in accelerating frames (Sagnac effect, and all that), converge in a strong indication of e 1 = 0. This implies absolute simultaneity and a new type of space and time transformations, which we call "inertial". We give eight proofs of absolute simultaneity, deduced from essentially independent normally accepted premises.

This is Selleri's summary statement of a programme he pursued from the mid-1990s until his death. This is the first instalment of Eduard Bardas' Proto-Theorie (published on his site prototheo.de). It is written in German, as a continuous essay rather than as a formal paper: there are no equations, no tables and no numerical predictions. When Einstein Equivalence Principle is taught to physics students - it seems an easy concept to understand and intuitively must be right. But there are a lot of problems with the idea when one looks more deeply.
Summary
Roger J Anderton 's session on the equivalence principle, hosted by Ian J Cowan with Franklin Hu assisting. He described it at the outset as a rough outline of a subject too big for one session and one he is still not sure about in places.
The argument
His starting point is the standard route: two postulates give special relativity, the equivalence principle added to them gives general relativity. So whatever is wrong with special relativity is inherited, and Einstein 's own version of the principle — that in free fall the effect of gravity is abolished and general relativity reduces to special relativity — builds on it directly.
His specific objection is that the principle deals only with attraction. He traced the contactless force from Newton's apple to Roger Boscovich, who reasoned that a force acting without contact cannot be attractive only, since particles sometimes repel, and drew the curve on which the force flips sign with distance. We are familiar with the attractive part of that curve and unfamiliar with the rest. Applied to a collapsing star, the reversal stops the collapse before a singularity forms — a "breathing" black hole rather than a singular one — and Anderton noted a paper observing that Einstein's 1905 notion of observer covariance had a precursor in Boscovich's eighteenth-century essay on space and time, which the mainstream ignores.

Abstract
The theoretical foundation of LIGO's design is based on the equation of motion derived by Thorne. His formula, motivated by Einstein's theory of measurement, shows that the gravitational wave-induced displacement of a mass with respect to an object is proportional to the distance from the object. Abstract
Einstein postulated in his 1905 article that light speed is isotropic in all inertial frames in order to derive the Lorentz Transformations. But the light speed postulate is logically wrong for the following reason: suppose, a short light pulse is emitted from a source mounted, say, in the origin of the coordinate system K, which is at rest. A coordinate system K' is moving at v in the x -direction. At the moment, when the origins of both K and K' are coinciding, one spherical wave front is lounged at the origin of K. This means that there will be one spherical wave-front expanding around the origin of K, because the origin of K' moves away at v . But the Lorentz Transformations transform this pulse (lounged in K) into a wave-front spherically expanding in K', although there cannot be such a spherically expanding wave-front around the origin of K'. How could there be one, as only one spherically expanding wave-front was generated around the origin of K, where the emitter is mounted! K' moves away at v , without carrying with it a spherically expanding wave front at the origin of K'. But the Lorentz transformation equations are predicting that! This cannot be correct! It is logically impossible!

Einstein's Lost Key: How We Overlooked the Best Idea of the 20th Century is a 2015 popular-science book by the German physicist and science writer Alexander Unzicker . Published on 28 November 2015 by CreateSpace Independent Publishing Platform in a 236-page paperback edition (ISBN 978-1519473431; ISBN-10 1519473435), it argues that Albert Einstein's early, and later abandoned, treatment of gravitation as a spatially variable speed of light was the more physical of the two routes Einstein took toward a theory of gravity, and that its premature abandonment cost twentieth-century physics its best idea. An updated and revised edition appeared in 2022, and the book is also available as a Kindle e-book and as an Audible audiobook.
The book appeared in the centenary year of the completion of the general theory of relativity and is the popular counterpart to Unzicker's own technical work on Mach's principle and variable-speed-of-light gravitation. It followed his two earlier critiques of contemporary theoretical physics, Bankrupting Physics (with Sheilla Jones) and The Higgs Fake , both of which drew sharp reactions from the physics community.
Synopsis
One hundred years after the completion of the general theory of relativity, conferences, meetings and celebrations took place all around the world — yet, Unzicker argues, a decisive consideration on the subject by Einstein himself had completely fallen into oblivion. Already in 1911, Unzicker writes, Einstein held the key to an even greater discovery in his hands: a theory concerning the variable speed of light that would have explained the origin of gravity by referring it to the distant masses in the universe.

When nuclear physicists separate quarks, a strong force of attraction develops between them and the greater the separation the greater the force pulling them back together. The gluons that bind quarks behave like elastic strings. Stars in the Milky Way Galaxy appear to rotate far too fast for the stars to remain in orbit; however, their rotation can be explained if gravitons are elastic strings that gain greater potential energy when they act across great distances. Gravitons, like gluons, have the characteristics of elastic strings. This same finding explains why electrons remain in orbit about the nucleus of the atom even though their velocities appear far too fast for them to stay in orbit. Protons and electrons behave as though they are connected by elastic strings. This also explains rubber bands and steel springs that gain potential energy when stretched. Elastic strings can be used to explain all the forces of nature and a myriad of other conundrums of science.
Overview
Kelland David Terry proposes that every force in nature is transmitted by physical strings possessing what he calls perfect elasticity and perfect cohesion — a framework he names VES theory, for Virtual Elastic String. His starting observation is that quark confinement already looks like this: separate two quarks and the attraction between them grows rather than falling off, exactly as a stretched rubber band pulls harder the further it is drawn. Gluons, he concludes, behave like elastic strings.

Entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with a system's macroscopic state, and equivalently a measure of the energy in a system that is unavailable to do work.
The standard account
The concept arose from the study of heat engines. Rudolf Clausius introduced the term in 1865, defining the change in entropy of a system as the heat exchanged reversibly divided by the absolute temperature, and stating the second law of Thermodynamics in the form that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Ludwig Boltzmann then gave the statistical interpretation, S = k log W , where W counts the microstates compatible with the observed macrostate; the constant k now carries his name and, since the 2019 revision of the SI, has the exact defined value 1.380649 × 10 −23 J/K. Shannon's 1948 measure of information has the same mathematical form, and the connection between the two is more than formal.
Two consequences drive most of the argument about entropy. The first is the arrow of time : the microscopic laws of physics are very nearly time-symmetric, yet entropy increase picks out a direction. The usual account traces this not to the dynamics but to the initial condition — the universe began in a state of extraordinarily low entropy, and everything since has been relaxation from it. Why it did so is an acknowledged open problem, not a settled one. The second is the heat death argument, made by Helmholtz, Kelvin and Clausius in the mid-nineteenth century: if the universe is a finite isolated system, its entropy must rise to a maximum, after which no further work can be extracted.
On this wiki
The heat-death extrapolation is where researchers here concentrate their objection, and the objection is usually about the isolated system premise rather than about thermodynamics itself.

It is one of three claims listed on the site's Cosmology page as consequences of the theory, alongside "gravity is a particle" and "mass increases from gravity over time".
Overview
The note opens by quoting the second law as stated in a textbook — "The entropy of the universe never decreases: during any process, the entropy either remains constant or else increases", from Franklin Miller's College Physics , 5th edition, p. 372 — and rejects it: "This is not true for AD. Why decay lowers entropy
The mechanism is the one that runs through the whole theory. Eppur Si Muove (Italian for "and yet it moves," the phrase traditionally attributed to Galileo) is a book by the Bulgarian dissident physicist Stefan Marinov (1931–1997), first published in 1977 and reissued in a fourth edition in 2008. It gathers Marinov's experimental and theoretical case against Albert Einstein's special theory of relativity , centred on his claim to have measured the absolute velocity of the Earth through the aether by detecting a direction-dependence in the one-way speed of light .
The book
The core of Eppur Si Muove is Marinov's account of the experiments he devised to detect the Earth's motion relative to absolute space. Chief among them is his "coupled-shutters" (later "coupled-mirrors") method, in which two rotating shutters or mirrors mounted on a common shaft are used to compare the time of flight of light travelling in opposite directions along the same axis. Marinov reported that this arrangement revealed an anisotropy in the observed one-way velocity of light, from which he calculated an absolute velocity of the Earth of roughly 360 km/s in a definite direction — a result he presented as a direct measurement of motion through the aether and as a refutation of the relativistic postulate that the one-way speed of light is the same in every frame.
Alongside the experiments, the book sets out Marinov's own "absolute space–time" theory: a reworking of relativistic mechanics and electrodynamics in which the world-invariant constancy of the two-way velocity of light is retained, but absolute simultaneity and a preferred rest frame — the aether — are restored. The fourth edition carries a preface by the Soviet physicist Andrei D. Sakharov and a detailed description of the apparatus, together with Marinov's replies to his critics.

Abstract
The paper presents the correspondence between physical quantities used in electrodynamics on the one hand and on the other those applied in elasticity and hydrodynamics having taken into account the SI units of physical quantities and assumed an analogy between mass and electric charge. Due to such correspondence almost every equation of electrodynamics is accompanied by an equation used in theory of elastic waves or hydrodynamics. Consistency of the analogy is clear and evidenced in the four tables (P waves, S waves, irrotational direct currents and rotational currents). Some changes concerning the form or the understanding of several equations are proposed. It has been shown that the Coulomb gauge and the first Helmholtz equation used in hydrodynamics have exactly the same physical meaning. Lorentz gauge with its sign changed is recognized as corresponding to one of the relations between stress and strain used in the theory of pressure elastic waves. The formula for the energy volume density of electromagnetic waves was modified in order to obtain the consistency with the corresponding formula for elastic S waves. Then the formula for the volume density of elastic force corresponding to that of the Lorentz force is proposed. The analogy between the Ohm's law for non-rotational direct electric current and the Hagen and Poiseuille's law for non-rotational flows is drawn.

The equivalence principle is the statement that the mass which resists acceleration (inertial mass) and the mass which responds to gravity (gravitational mass) are the same thing, so that all bodies fall alike in a gravitational field and a uniformly accelerated laboratory cannot be distinguished locally from one at rest in a gravitational field.
The standard account
The observation that bodies of different weight fall at the same rate goes back to Galileo, and Newton tested it with pendulums of different composition in the Principia . The empirical statement — that the ratio of gravitational to inertial mass is the same for all substances — is called the weak equivalence principle or the universality of free fall. It was tested to high precision by Loránd Eötvös with a torsion balance from 1889 onwards, and the Eötvös–Pekár–Fekete experiments published in 1922 remain a reference point in the literature. Modern torsion-balance work and lunar laser ranging constrain the Eötvös parameter to roughly one part in 10 13 , and the French MICROSCOPE satellite mission (2016–2018, final analysis 2022) tightened this to about one part in 10 15 for titanium and platinum test masses. No violation has been detected.
Einstein took a further step in 1907, in what he later called the happiest thought of his life: he proposed that a freely falling observer feels no gravity at all, and that all local physics — not just falling bodies — is the same in a freely falling frame as in an inertial frame far from any mass. This stronger statement, usually called the Einstein equivalence principle , adds local Lorentz invariance and local position invariance to the universality of free fall, and it is the foundation on which General Relativity is built: gravity is geometrised precisely because it can be locally transformed away. Eric Sheldon (born 24 October 1930) is a British-American physicist, Professor Emeritus of Physics and Applied Physics and Honors Director Emeritus at the University of Massachusetts Lowell. Trained as a physical chemist and theoretical nuclear physicist, he is the co-author with Pierre Marmier of the widely used multi-volume textbook Physics of Nuclei and Particles , and in later years turned to questions in relativity and cosmology — most notably a re-examination of the relativistic twin paradox that questioned how the standard textbook treatment is presented and taught.

Sheldon was born in Pilsen, Bohemia, and was educated in England, at Pinner Park Elementary School and Harrow County School in London. He read physics at the University of London, taking a B.Sc. (General) in physics, chemistry and mathematics followed by a B.Sc. (Special) in physics with honours in 1952, and a Ph.D. in 1955. He afterwards studied and worked at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH Zurich) and the University of Zurich, and was later awarded the higher doctorate of D.Sc. by London.

R. Bruce , he argued that the sudden and violent events astronomers observe — stellar flares, jets, the behaviour of novae and quasars — are lightning on a cosmic scale, produced by the same physics as a lightning stroke in the Earth's atmosphere.
His paper "Lightning in Astronomy" appeared in Nature in December 1974. He was a Fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society and a council member of the Society for Interdisciplinary Studies, and his work is part of the tradition now labelled the electric universe , though his own claim was a good deal narrower than that label suggests.

Crew was born in Stoke-on-Trent and trained as an electrical engineer. He joined British Petroleum in London and travelled widely installing switchgear in power stations. He was a Fellow of the Institution of Electrical Engineers, and in retirement he developed a fire protection system for cables used in industrial plants and underground railways.
Passionately interested in all aspects of science, and especially astronomy, he became a Fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society and a council member of the Society for Interdisciplinary Studies (SIS). A prolific writer with a wide circle of correspondents, in his later years he was in contact with the Hungarian scientist László Körtvélyessy on the electrical aspects of the Sun, and the two published together in 2002. Erik Cabuy is a Belgian biologist and cancer researcher based in Strombeek-Bever, Belgium. He holds a PhD in biomedicine and works on telomere biology, cellular aging, the DNA-damage response and the origins and treatment of cancer.
Biography
Cabuy earned a doctorate in biomedicine and carried out research on telomere maintenance and radiosensitivity while associated with the Brunel Institute of Cancer Genetics and Pharmacogenomics at Brunel University in the United Kingdom. He has since been based in Strombeek-Bever, Belgium, where his work has been linked to Reliable Cancer Therapies, a non-profit organization providing information on evidence-based cancer therapies and funding the development of promising treatments. He is also the founder of Recorpus, a medical-technology venture focused on the developmental origin of cancer and new strategies for its treatment.
Work
Cabuy's research has centered on telomeres, the protective structures at the ends of chromosomes, and their role in cellular aging and genome stability. In a study published in Radiation Research in 2005, he and colleagues examined telomere maintenance in eleven primary fibroblast cell lines carrying genetic defects that confer sensitivity to ionizing radiation, including cells from patients with ataxia telangiectasia, Nijmegen breakage syndrome, Fanconi anemia, and defects in Artemis, DNA ligase I and DNA ligase IV. Using Southern blot, flow-FISH and quantitative FISH measurements, the work reported accelerated telomere shortening and telomere abnormalities in most of the radiosensitive cell lines compared with cells from normal individuals.
His later work addresses the developmental origin of cancer and proposes alternative approaches to cancer treatment through the Recorpus initiative

Ernest Joachim Sternglass (24 September 1923, Berlin – 12 February 2015, Ithaca, New York) was a German-born American physicist, inventor and author, Professor Emeritus of Radiological Physics at the University of Pittsburgh. He is known on this wiki above all for his relativistic electron-positron pair model of matter and cosmology — a scheme in which every particle, and ultimately the universe itself, is built from tightly bound, near-light-speed electron-positron pairs, with no recourse to quarks — and, in the wider world, for his long and deliberately controversial campaign on the health effects of low-level radiation from bomb fallout and nuclear power plants. He spent most of his career arguing positions that the physics and health-physics establishments rejected, and he never retracted them.
Biography
Sternglass was born in Berlin in 1923 and emigrated with his family to the United States in 1938, fleeing Nazi Germany.
After wartime and postwar service he worked at the U.S. Naval Ordnance Laboratory, where his experimental work on secondary electron emission began. As a young researcher he corresponded with, and in 1947 visited, Albert Einstein at Princeton to discuss that work and his broader theoretical ambitions. Einstein famously advised him against a purely academic theoretical career, urging him instead to "keep a cobbler's job" — to earn his living by practical work so that his thinking would remain free and honest. Ernst Mach (18 February 1838 – 19 February 1916) was an Austrian physicist and philosopher of science whose criticism of Newton's absolute space and absolute time is one of the deepest and longest-running threads in the literature collected on this wiki.
Mach held chairs at Graz, Prague and finally Vienna, where his professorship was in the history and theory of the inductive sciences. As an experimentalist he is remembered for the photographic study of supersonic projectiles — he and Peter Salcher published images of the shock cone in 1887, and the ratio of a body's speed to the speed of sound in the medium was later named the Mach number in his honour. He also did extensive work on the physiology of sensation, including the visual contrast effect known as Mach bands.
His lasting influence, however, is philosophical. In Die Mechanik in ihrer Entwicklung, historisch-kritisch dargestellt (1883, translated as The Science of Mechanics ) Mach argued that physics should confine itself to relations among observable quantities, and that Newton's absolute space and absolute time were metaphysical additions doing no empirical work. His most famous target was Newton's rotating-bucket argument. In Relativity the Newtonian notions of absolute motion, absolute time, and absolute reference frame have been replaced with relative motion, relativistic time, and inertial reference frames in motion. Erwin Rudolf Josef Alexander Schrödinger (12 August 1887 – 4 January 1961) was an Austrian theoretical physicist who created wave mechanics in 1926 and shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Dirac . He is unusual among the founders of quantum theory in that he spent the rest of his life objecting to what the theory was taken to mean.
In a series of four papers in Annalen der Physik during 1926, Schrödinger took de Broglie 's matter waves seriously and wrote down the wave equation that carries his name, deriving the hydrogen spectrum from it as an eigenvalue problem. In the same year he proved that his wave mechanics and Heisenberg 's matrix mechanics are mathematically equivalent. He succeeded Planck at Berlin in 1927, left Germany in 1933 in protest at the Nazi regime, and after a period at Oxford and a dangerous year in Graz settled at the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies from 1940 to 1956.
His 1944 book What Is Life? argued that the hereditary material must be an aperiodic crystal carrying a code-script, and is credited by Crick, Watson and Wilkins among others with drawing them into molecular biology. He also worked on unified field theory alongside Einstein , and wrote extensively on philosophy, including Nature and the Greeks , Mind and Matter and My View of the World — the last drawing openly on Vedanta.

Escape from Einstein is a 1992 book by Ronald R. Hatch setting out an ether gauge theory as a replacement for special and general relativity . It is the first and only book-length statement of the programme Hatch pursued for the rest of his life, later refined under the name Modified Lorentz Ether Theory (MLET).
What gives the book its standing in this literature is who wrote it. Hatch was not an outsider to the subject he criticised: he was one of the principal algorithm designers of the Global Positioning System, inventor of the carrier-smoothing technique universally called the Hatch filter , and later President of the Institute of Navigation. His argument is that the operational reality of GPS — a system he helped build — tells against Einstein rather than for him.
The book's own summary of what distinguishes the theory: a return to absolute simultaneity while allowing clocks to run at different rates; the replacement of the Lorentz transformations by gauge transformations (scaled Galilean transformations) ; a unification of the electromagnetic and gravitational forces; an account of the source of inertia ; and a physical mechanism underlying the equivalence principle. "Rather than curved space, the ether gauge theory postulates an elastic ether ."
Publication
Kneat Kompany appears to have been Hatch's own imprint: the ISBN prefix carries only this one title, and the company's address in Wilmington, California is Hatch's own. He cited the book himself simply as "Kneat, Wilmington, CA". It ran to a single 1992 hardcover edition with no reprint. Library and dealer records give the extent as 242 pages, though some listings — including this page previously — give 232.

An elastic ether, and matter made of waves
Hatch's ether is a McCullagh-type elastic solid , possessing shear elasticity (needed to carry transverse light)

This article is about the cosmological view. For the 2003 book by Karim Amen Khaidarov , see Eternal Universe (book) .
The eternal universe is the view that the cosmos has no beginning and no end in time — that there was no moment of creation, no first instant, and no singular origin from which everything else follows. It is a claim about time rather than about extent : a universe may be held to be eternal whether or not it is also held to be spatially infinite, and the two questions are argued separately here and at Infinity .
Among the researchers documented on this wiki the eternal universe is close to a default position. It is the one thing that most critics of the Big Bang hold in common, and it is held by people who agree on very little else — aether theorists and plasma physicists, tired-light advocates and quasi-steady-state cosmologists, philosophers attacking the notion of a first moment and astronomers reporting that distant objects look too old for the standard timeline. What follows reports their arguments and attributes them; it does not assert that the universe is eternal. A substantial minority of contributors here, including several creation-science authors, argue the opposite.
The claim and its history
For most of the history of natural philosophy an eternal cosmos was the assumption rather than the thesis. Aristotle held the world to be everlasting, without generation or destruction, and the medieval dispute over whether the universe had a temporal beginning was fought largely between that inheritance and the doctrine of creation. Newton's universe had no age; the nineteenth-century picture of an unbounded space filled with stars carried no origin date with it.

Eternal Universe is a 2003 work by the Kazakh researcher Karim Amen Khaidarov , written at Borovoye and issued through his Bourabai Research institution. Its subject is narrow and its target is precise: it re-analyses the supernova data that in 1998 was taken to show an accelerating universe — the observation from which dark energy was inferred — and argues that the acceleration disappears when the same measurements are processed without relativistic adjustments and against an absorbing ether .
The conclusion the title announces is that the universe is neither expanding nor accelerating, has no beginning, and requires neither a big bang nor dark energy to account for what is observed.
The work is dedicated to the memory of the author's daughter, Anastasia.
The argument
In December 1998 S. Perlmutter and colleagues of the Supernova Cosmology Project published "Measurements of Ω and Λ from 42 high-redshift supernovae", drawing on the Calán/Tololo Supernova Survey. Distant type Ia supernovae appeared fainter than expected, and the standard reading of that shortfall was an accelerating expansion. Khaidarov opens by observing that this conclusion sits badly with the framework it was meant to serve: it disagrees with each of the three variants of the Einstein–Friedmann model.
His alternative takes the same supernova data and drops the relativistic corrections, substituting a classical premise: that space is filled with a universally present substance, the ether, which carries electromagnetic waves and continuously damps them — exactly as waves fade in any ordinary isotropic medium, whether solid, liquid or gas.

Evan L. Ragland is an independent researcher known for proposing an alternative model of atomic and nuclear structure. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Ideas
Ragland presented an abstract, "The Alternate Atomic Model", at the American Physical Society March Meeting in 2008. In it he described a model, which he says he introduced in 1992, in which concentric electron and nucleon fields spin together about an empty central region, offered as an alternative to the standard picture of the nucleus. His related writings connect this model to claims about the nuclear strong force and to experiments on the Fleischmann–Pons ("cold fusion") effect. These proposals lie outside mainstream nuclear and atomic physics.

Abstract
One can ask how it was possible for Lorentz's simple and elegant theory of gravity to be passed over and for Einstein's wacky theory of gravity to be accepted. We examine a bit of this puzzle by looking at two papers published in 1905 and 1906 that specifically address Lorentz' theory. The first paper by R. Gans examines the theoretical implications for a number of issues including the relationship between inertial and gravitational mass. The second paper by F. Wacker (a student of Gans) explores, among other things, the advance of the perihelion of Mercury after including a term for a mass increase with velocity through the ether. We look specifically for criticisms which might demonstrate fatal flaws in Lorentz' theory.

"Existence or Nothing" is an article by Glenn Borchardt published on 8 September 2025 on The Scientific Worldview .
Asked how the fact of existence supports the assumption that the universe is infinite, Borchardt answers that an infinite universe can produce an infinite number of things but cannot produce nothing — nor can it produce the opposite limit, perfectly solid matter. Every real portion of the universe has both properties: all space contains what appears to be matter, and all matter contains what appears to be space.

title: Natural Philosophy Wiki
content_preview: The expanding universe is the standard interpretation of the observed redshift of distant galaxies: that the galaxies are not moving apart through a fixed space
search_text:
The expanding universe is the standard interpretation of the observed redshift of distant galaxies: that the galaxies are not moving apart through a fixed space, but that the space between them is itself increasing in scale, so that light in transit is stretched in proportion to the growth of the scale factor while it travels.
The picture assembled quickly. Vesto Slipher measured large radial velocities for spiral nebulae between 1912 and 1917; Alexander Friedmann found expanding and contracting solutions of Einstein's field equations in 1922; Georges Lemaître connected the solutions to the observations in 1927 and proposed a "primeval atom" origin; and Edwin Hubble published the linear redshift–distance relation in 1929 (see Hubble Constant ). Extrapolated backwards, an expanding universe implies a hot dense beginning — the Big Bang — and with it a finite age, currently quoted as about 13.8 billion years.
Four observations are usually presented as the evidential core: the redshift–distance relation itself; the Cosmic Microwave Background and its near-perfect blackbody spectrum; the abundances of the light elements, in particular the roughly one-quarter helium fraction by mass, which big-bang nucleosynthesis calculates from a single parameter; and the apparent time dilation of distant Type Ia supernova light curves, which stretch in proportion to (1 + z ) as expansion predicts. To these is usually added the Tolman surface-brightness test, in which the surface brightness of galaxies should dim with redshift far more steeply in an expanding universe than in a static one.
Genuine open problems remain inside the model — the Hubble tension , the unexplained magnitude of the cosmological constant , and the surprising maturity of the earliest galaxies observed by JWST, which has forced revisions to models of early structure formation though not to the expansion framework itself.

Abstract
One of the most profound statements the late Professor Sam Warren Carey (Emeritus Professor of Geology from the University of Tasmania) said to me when I first started researching Expansion Tectonics was: If 50 million believe in a fallacy it is still a fallacy. The point he was making was that the validity of any theory does not depend upon the number of people believing it; hence, an accepted theory may still be fundamentally wrong regardless of how many people believe it is correct. The Plate Tectonic interpretation of global data, for instance, is based on the fundamental premise that the Earths radius has remained constant, or near constant, throughout history. As will be outlined in this paper, this contrasts with an Expansion Tectonic interpretation of the same global data which is based on the fundamental premise that the Earths radius has been steadily increasing throughout Earth history.
Overview
James Maxlow presents here a summary of his modelling programme in Expansion Tectonics , the tradition running from Mantovani (1889, 1909) through Lindemann, Hilgenberg, Vogel and Koziar to Samuel Warren Carey , whose remark about fifty million believers and a fallacy opens the paper. Maxlow's central methodological claim is disarmingly simple and worth stating precisely: the geological, geographical and geophysical data used to support Plate Tectonics and Expansion Tectonics are identical . What separates the two accounts is one premise — whether Earth radius has been constant. Remove it, he argues, and the same data reconstruct better.

Abstract
The primary assumption of the Big Bang model is that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic, and hence the density of the universe is constant everywhere. A secondary assumption is that the expansion of the Universe has no fixed center. Both assumptions are contradicted by voluminous experimental evidence. Independent analyses place the center of the universe at about a hundred fifty million light years from the Milky Way. General graphical analysis of the Sloan Survey indicates that the spatial density of galaxies, taken as a surrogate measure of the density of matter in the universe, drops from this center in an approximate 1-over-r-squared pattern. Furthermore, analysis of the Deep Galactic Pencil Surveys indicates that a radial ~450 million light year periodic variation is superimposed on this pattern. The same pattern exists for Quasars and other artifacts.

Abstract
Considering that photons travel at the velocity of light c in the fundamental frame, we expect logically that these photons travel at velocity c-v (or c+v) with respect to a frame moving at velocity v. We know that the observed velocity is measured as c. However, that logical consequence has never been explained. Using Newton's physics and conventional logic, we explain how the velocity of light APPEARS constant in the two way measurement of the velocity of light, while it is c-v (and c+v) in the Sagnac effect. We answer the question: "With respect to what does light move?" This paper gives a physical explanation how the velocity of light is really (c-v) with respect to the observer, even if the observer's tools always measure a velocity represented by the number c. We explain how this problem is crucial in the Global Positioning System (GPS) and in clocks synchronization. The Lorentz' transformations become quite useless. This apparent constant velocity of light is the most fascinating illusion in science.
Overview
Paul Marmet, a spectroscopist at the National Research Council of Canada and later at the University of Ottawa, wrote this ten-page paper in May 2000 as a condensation of the argument of his 1997 book Einstein's Theory of Relativity versus Classical Mechanics . Marmet's answer is that light moves at c with respect to a single absolute frame, that it therefore really does travel at c ± v relative to a moving observer, and that the apparently invariant value every experiment returns is an artefact of the clock synchronization procedure used to obtain it. "This apparent constant velocity of light is the most fascinating illusion in science."

Abstract
This document is an extended presentation of the formalism introduced in a paper called "The Organizational Structure of Physics" (The OSP) , presented at the 18th annual conference of the Natural Philosophy Alliance. One of the direct consequences of the proposed engineering framework is the possibility to generalize the equations describing the interactions of physical quantities. Basic elements of the formalism are presented as a reminder, followed by the application of the proposed concepts to the formalization of Planck values definition as well as a generalization of Maxwell's equations.
Overview
Laurent Hollo's 52-page document is an extended presentation of a formalism he introduced at the 18th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference under the title The Organizational Structure of Physics (OSP). He describes it as "an engineering framework" and is explicit that "this is still a work in progress".
The proposal is a systematic organisation of physical quantities rather than a new physical theory. Quantities are placed in a space-time matrix and grouped into standard domains — gravitic, electric, magnetic and thermic — each with the same internal structure, comprising Conduction, Radiation, Static and Dynamic groups. Across every domain the same roles recur: a potential (the cause), a rigidity promoting the establishment of a flux, a resistance opposing it, a current (the effect), and a charge that stresses the medium. An energetic domain — potential energy, kinetic energy, force, power, momentum, action — is then derivable from any standard domain rather than only from the gravitic one.
Two applications occupy the last quarter of the document.
The generalisation of Planck values rests on the observation that Planck-scale energetic quantities should come out the same regardless of which domain they are computed from.

The Extinction Shift Principle is a purely classical emission theory developed by Edward Henry Dowdye, Jr. (1943–2020), a laser optics physicist retired from NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. It proposes that the phenomena attributed to special and general relativity can be derived instead from the principles of optics, using Galilean transformations of velocities in Euclidean space geometry — with no spacetime curvature, no length contraction and no time dilation.
Dowdye presents it as a revival of a lapsed tradition. Emission theories — in which light is emitted at speed c relative to its source rather than relative to an absolute frame — were pursued in the early twentieth century, most notably by Walter Ritz (1878–1909), and largely abandoned after his death. Dowdye described himself as the only emission theorist still working in his lifetime, and his version differs from the earlier ones in an important respect: where Ritz and his contemporaries applied emission ideas to electromagnetism , the Extinction Shift Principle applies them to gravitation as well , and so challenges general relativity and special relativity together.
The principle
The name refers to the extinction of the original light signal and its re-emission by the intervening medium — the classical optical process by which light entering a medium is absorbed and re-radiated by the particles of that medium, taking on the velocity characteristics of the new source. In Dowdye's treatment this process, rather than the geometry of spacetime, accounts for the observed behaviour of light near massive bodies.

A thought-provoking insight into the evolution of cosmology for undergraduate students and general readers, this book shows that the mystery of the origin of the universe is far from being solved. Cosmology has advanced over time through observational evidence as well as a lot of speculation. In this historical approach, the authors argue that the speculative element has become a dominant part of modern cosmology. They show how assumptions have been made and portrayed as confirmed facts. This unique book gives not only a critical assessment of the big bang theory, but presents a host of anomalous observations, and puts forward an alternative, controversial theory on the origin of the universe. A non-mathematical account, it contains analogies from everyday life so that readers can understand the concepts easily and follow the arguments presented.

Faheem Murtaza (born 1970) is a Pakistani lawyer and independent researcher on the unification of the fundamental interactions, based in Abbottabad, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He holds a Master of Science in mathematics and an LL.B., and practises law; as of 2011 he had been working on unification for some eighteen years.
Work
Murtaza presented two papers to Natural Philosophy Alliance conferences, Quantum Gravity at the sixteenth meeting in 2009 and The Quantum Law of Gravity at the eighteenth in 2011, the latter published in the Proceedings of the NPA .
Both pursue a single programme: a proposed relation between a particle's momentum, its gravitational acceleration and a mass differential, from which he argues that Newtonian gravity, general-relativistic effects and quantum behaviour all follow as special cases. The central move is to identify an "induced charge" carried by any orbiting body in proportion to its angular momentum, q = K mvr/M with K = c/√(kG), so that gravitational attraction becomes a magnetic force between induced charges and gravity and electromagnetism are unified. Subsidiary results include a proportionality between gravitational acceleration and magnetic flux density, a formula giving orbital inclination from the mass ratio of a planet to its primary, a relation gt = c between gravity and time, and an identification of the Planck time with the ratio of a particle's radius times a mass differential to its momentum.
The 2011 paper is notable for a publication accident rather than its content: the Proceedings version appeared with the reviewer's queries and the unfilled section headings of the submission template still embedded in the running text.

Farzan Amini is an Iranian engineer and new-energy researcher known for proposing that low-energy nuclear reactions (LENR, or "cold fusion") occur in hydroelectric machinery and in a range of natural systems. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Work
Amini has been described as a mechanical manager for the Farab Corporation in Iran, a builder of hydroelectric dams. He argues that jet-plasma and cavitation processes in high-flow hydro machinery can trigger cold-fusion-type reactions, and has extended this "vorticity-fusion" idea to phenomena such as the air–sea interface and global warming, the rheology of blood ("tribonucleation fusion"), volcanoes and wildfires. His writing has appeared in the fringe-science journal Infinite Energy , including an analysis interpreting the 2009 Sayano-Shushenskaya hydroelectric station accident in Russia in terms of low-energy nuclear reactions.
These claims fall outside the scientific mainstream, which does not recognize low-energy nuclear reactions as an established phenomenon.

Continuation of Faster than light (FTL) signals from 29 June; dealing with some issues raised.
Summary
A continuation of the session a fortnight earlier, Roger J Anderton taking up four points that had been raised against it. He hosted himself; the talk had been moved to an unfamiliar time and the green room was almost empty.
The mathematical charge
The centrepiece is an argument he had passed over quickly the first time, taken from a paper of Ralph Baierlein's on two myths about special relativity: that the Lorentz transformations do not reduce to the Galilean ones as v / c tends to zero, contrary to what students are taught.
The demonstration is short. Setting γ to 1, the time transformation becomes t ′ = t − vx / c 2 . If x were a constant, vx would go to zero with v — but x is a variable, and can be made large as v is made small, so the product need not vanish. The limit is therefore t ′ = t − vx / c 2 , not t ′ = t . Anderton put up a set of published lecture notes stating the false claim in terms, and drew the conclusion he wanted: a great deal of the mathematics taught to students of relativity is wrong, and the physicists then interpret experiments through it.

Answering the objection that only Harold W Milnes claims to send information faster than c , Anderton showed a segment of the documentary The Time Lords on Günter Nimtz, who splits a microwave signal, sends half through air and half at a barrier, and finds the tunnelled portion arriving first — at 4.7 times c over about 14 centimetres, since reported at some 300 times. Abstract
Some 20 years ago there was considerable research done comparing the gravity felt by a test mass in deep wells, deep mines, deep in an ice pack, and on high towers. The data from this research argued that gravity below the Earth's surface began to deviate from Newtonian while gravity above the Earth's surface showed no deviation. A non-singular gravitational force shows this behaviour. Here we calculate the gravitational force on a test mass outside a sphere with uniform density and the force on a test mass inside a hollow spherical shell. the result of these calculations show that the non-singular force predicts that a test mass below the Earth's surface should be less than the Newtonian gravity while a test mass above the Earth's surface should correspond to the Newtonian prediction.
Overview
"Fifth" Force is a five-page paper by Pharis E Williams , dated 26 January 2013 and presented at the 20th Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference that July.
Its subject is the fifth-force episode of the 1980s, when measurements down mineshafts and up towers appeared to show gravity departing from Newton's law over intermediate distances. Williams frames the choice sharply: "either Newton's Law of gravity needs to have a correction or an independent fifth force is needed", and notes the precedent — when proton–proton scattering departed from Coulomb's law, physics chose a new force "and [has] had the fun of searching for a method of unifying electromagnetism and the strong force ever since."
His alternative is a non-singular force law:
F = −(GmM/r²)(1 − λ/r) e −λ/r
which is finite at the origin and reduces to Newton's when λ → 0.

Author(s) Erasmo Recami , Vilson Tonin-Zanchin
Keywords gravitational laws, general relativity , new effects, cosmological constant
Published 1989
Pages 215-220
Abstract
In the recent literature, a few claims appeared about possible deviations from the ordinary gravitational laws (both at the terrestrial and at the galactic level). The experimental evidence does not seem to be conclusive; nor is it clear if new forces are showing up, or if we have to accept actual deviations from Newton or Einstein gravitation (in the latter case, the validity of the very Equivalence Principle might be on the stage). In such a situation, the attempts by various authors at explaining the "new effects" just on the basis of the ordinary theory of General Relativity (for instance, in terms of quantum gravity) can be regarded as logically questionable. In this pedagogically oriented paper, we approach the problem within the classical realm, by exploring whether the possible new effects can be accounted for through minimal modifications of the standard formulation of General Relativity: in particular, through exploitation and extension of the role of the cosmological constant.
Presented at
Foundations of Mathematics & Physics in the 20th Century: The Rejection of Intuition (1 January 1989)

title: Fine Structure Constant
content_preview: The fine structure constant , written α, is the dimensionless number that measures the strength of the electromagnetic interaction between elementary charged pa
search_text:
The fine structure constant , written α, is the dimensionless number that measures the strength of the electromagnetic interaction between elementary charged particles. Its value is close to 1/137.036, and because it is a pure number — independent of any choice of units — it is often taken to be the single most fundamental quantity in physics.
The standard account
Arnold Sommerfeld introduced the constant in 1916 while extending the Bohr atomic model to elliptical orbits, in order to account for the fine structure — the small splitting of the spectral lines of hydrogen. In SI form it is written α = e²/(4πε₀ħc), combining the elementary charge, the permittivity of free space, the reduced Planck constant and the speed of light . The units cancel. The current recommended value is α ≈ 1/137.035999, known to better than a part in 10 9 , making it one of the most precisely determined numbers in science; it is measured independently through the electron 's anomalous magnetic moment, through atom-recoil experiments with caesium and rubidium, and through the quantum Hall effect.
α turns up wherever charge and light meet. It sets the ratio of the electron's velocity in the first Bohr orbit to the speed of light, the ratio of the Compton wavelength to the Bohr radius, and the size of each successive order in the perturbation expansion of Quantum Electrodynamics — which is why QED calculations converge so usefully.
What no accepted theory supplies is a reason for the number. Nothing in the Standard Model predicts 137.036 rather than any other value; α is put in by hand, and in quantum field theory it is not even a constant but a running coupling that grows at higher energies (reaching roughly 1/127 at the mass of the Z boson). Feynman called it "one of the greatest damn mysteries of physics: a magic number that comes to us with no understanding by man." No. of pages 10

Abstract
The Michelson-Morley experiment for examining light-speed constancy in paths moving linearly is second-order in speed, so it has never been conducted with paths moving relative to Earth. The Sagnac experiment is a first-order experiment, but it does not address motion that is linear, since its path motion is caused by rotation. The design of an interferometric experiment that is not only sensitive to linear motion, but also first-order in speed, needs two features: 1) optical paths in uniform translational motion, and 2) paths for light return without cancellation of possible effects. Two arrangements with these features are here presented: a conveyor-like arrangement, and a shearing parallelogram arrangement. Both can be implemented with fiber-optic technology. If the entire optical loop is fiber, the light-speed constancy in a moving path of the fiber is examined; if the fiber loop is broken to leave a gap of vacuum (or air), the light-speed constancy in a moving path of vacuum (or air) is examined. According to the same analysis as that for a fiber-optic gyro, translational motion in these arrangements will lead to an increase of optical path length and an increase of the travel time difference, a result falsifying the principle of the light-speed constancy.
Overview
Ruyong Wang's paper is an experiment-design proposal rather than a theoretical argument. Its premise is that the two classic optical tests of light-speed constancy each have exactly one of the two properties a decisive test needs, and neither has both. Journal The Toth-Maatian Review

Abstract
Attention is called to the remarkable fact that, relative to the observer, Maxwell's equations allow field-source motions but not field-sink motions. These equations thus implicitly refer to a "preferred observer." On correcting this unwarranted suppresssion of instrumental degrees of freedom, we obtain generalized equations for electromagnetism that (at first order in detector velocity) prove to be Galilean invariant. The extra parameters needed to describe filed-detector motions enter the wave equation and spoil the spherical symmetry of radiation propagation, so our previous "acausal" hypothesis of radiation convection by the absorber, in conjunction with physical non-occurrence of the Lorentz contraction, - receives independent confirmation. Higher-order correction to Maxwell's equations are also discussed. Experimental testing of the radiation convection hypothesis becomes imperative and should be feasible in view of the first-order nature of the effect. Convection is defined as something that occurs at the locus of each detector - a 'pulling along of the wave by the detectors.

Flavio Tabanelli is an Italian researcher from Mirandola, in the province of Modena, known on this wiki for a single paper of 1999: a historical analysis of nearly fifty years of interferometry arguing that the results of Michelson , Morley and Miller form one continuous body of non-null data .
Almost nothing is recorded about him beyond the paper and his location. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists . What follows is drawn from the paper itself.
Coherence and continuity
Tabanelli's Coherence and Continuity of the Non-Null Experimental Results by Michelson, Morley and Miller (1999) examines the interferometer observations from 1877 to 1924 — a span beginning a decade before the celebrated 1887 experiment and running through Morley and Miller's later work.
His conclusion separates two things that are usually run together:
A detailed historical analysis of interferometer observations (1877-1924) shows that early experimental procedures were faulty but that observed fringe shifts were real, albeit much smaller than expected.
— Flavio Tabanelli, Coherence and Continuity of the Non-Null Experimental Results (1999)
That is a more careful position than either side of the usual dispute takes. He does not claim the early experiments were well executed — he grants that the procedures were faulty. What he denies is that faulty procedure explains away the readings: the fringe shifts were real , and they were small — much smaller than a stationary ether would require, but not zero.

Forrest Bishop (born 25 July 1955) is an American engineer and independent researcher based in Seattle, Washington. He is the founder and chairman of the Institute of Atomic-Scale Engineering, and is best known outside dissident-physics circles for the Bishop Ring , a rotating space-habitat design he proposed in 1997.
Space habitats and nanotechnology
Bishop's work in the 1990s belonged to the molecular-nanotechnology community that formed around Eric Drexler's proposals, and he presented at the Fifth Foresight Conference on Molecular Nanotechnology. He developed a "Universal Assembler" concept as part of extended work on the nanofactory idea, and his illustrations are held in the Foresight Institute's nanomedicine art gallery.
The Bishop Ring is his most widely cited contribution and carries his name in the space-settlement literature. It departs from the Stanford torus and the O'Neill cylinder designs of the 1970s by assuming carbon-nanotube construction rather than steel, which allows a far larger structure: roughly 1,000 km in radius and 500 km wide, rotating to give one gravity at the rim and enclosing some three million square kilometres of habitable surface — an area comparable to India. At that scale the habitat needs no roof. Atmosphere is retained by rotation alone, behind retaining walls about 200 km high, leaving the ring open to space along its axis.

"Frames Derivation" is one of the two derivations by which Ricardo L Carezani obtains the equations of Autodynamics . It is the shorter and, in Carezani's words, "more classical" of the pair; the other is the Galilean Simplification . Both are published by the Society for the Advancement of Autodynamics at autodynamics.org.
Overview
The derivation has two halves. The first is a critique: Carezani walks through the standard relativistic derivation of velocity addition and of force, and argues that two steps in it are unmotivated. The second is constructive: he discards the second coordinate system altogether and derives, from a single frame, what he calls the Simplified Lorentz equations — the transformation that carries the rest of Autodynamics.
Throughout, β = v / c , m 0 is the rest mass and c the speed of light .
The argument
The objection to the relativistic derivation
Carezani starts from the Lorentz transformation applied to a point P at rest in frame F , with F moving at velocity v relative to the observer's frame F ′ . Differentiating and dividing d x ′ by d t ′ gives the velocity-addition expression
v ′ = v x + v 1 + v x v c 2
His first objection is that this expression "has 3 velocities even though it must only have 2". The velocity v x , he writes, "appears spontaneously through the mathematical operation of the derivative" and "has no physical meaning. There is no energy to move point P (originally at rest in frame F ) with respect to the F coordinate system." He takes this to be why, in his view, the relativistic velocity sum fails to conserve energy and momentum when applied to a dynamic phenomenon.

Francesco Piantelli is an Italian physicist, a retired professor of biophysics at the University of Siena, known for his experimental work on nickel-hydrogen low-energy nuclear reactions (LENR), commonly described as "cold fusion." He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Work
Beginning in the early 1990s, Piantelli investigated anomalous heat production in systems of nickel and hydrogen. Working at times in collaboration with Sergio Focardi, he reported experiments in which nickel samples exposed to hydrogen produced excess heat, including a widely recounted 1993 run in which an apparatus reached temperatures said to have exceeded 1400 °C before being stabilised. He attributed key results to the preparation of the nickel surface at the nano-scale.
Piantelli's nickel-hydrogen approach is often cited as a precursor to later devices, and he pursued patents on his reactor concept. His claims of anomalous heat fall within the field of cold fusion / LENR, which remains outside the accepted scientific mainstream and is not recognised by most of the physics community. Alongside this work, his career centred on biophysics and biomedical research.

Francis L. Tanzella is a chemist and experimental researcher known for his long-running work on cold fusion and low energy nuclear reactions (LENR). He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Career
Tanzella holds a Ph.D. in chemistry from the University of California, Berkeley, and carried out post-doctoral work in electrochemistry. He joined SRI International in Menlo Park, California, in 1986, where he became a program manager and principal investigator in the institute's energy research program. There he worked closely with Michael McKubre in a group that investigated claims of anomalous heat and nuclear effects in palladium–deuterium electrochemical cells following the 1989 Fleischmann–Pons announcement.
Work
At SRI, Tanzella participated in calorimetric experiments that reported excess heat and attempted to correlate it with the production of helium in deuterium-loaded palladium systems. He has authored and co-authored numerous conference and journal contributions in the LENR / condensed matter nuclear science (CMNS) field, including collaborations with physicist Peter Hagelstein, and has summarised "the state of the science based on measurements made at SRI." After leaving SRI he continued as an independent consultant, carrying out third-party evaluation of commercial LENR devices.
Cold fusion and LENR remain outside the accepted scientific mainstream, which has not reproduced the claimed effects to general satisfaction; Tanzella is among the researchers who continue to argue that the experimental anomalies are real and warrant further study.

Francis X. Roarty (also credited as Fran Roarty) is an engineer and independent researcher known for his writings on hydrino theory and low-energy nuclear reactions ("new energy"). He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Ideas
Roarty writes in support of Randell Mills' claim that hydrogen can occupy states below the conventional ground state (so-called "hydrinos"), producing more energy than ordinary chemistry allows. In a 2009 essay he argued that experiments at Rowan University had independently confirmed excess heat consistent with Mills' Black Light Process. Roarty proposes an interpretation in which such sub-ground-state behaviour arises inside Casimir-like cavities, where he suggests time-dilation and Lorentz-contraction effects scale hydrogen atoms toward a new force balance. He has argued that the dispute over whether hydrinos are physical reflects a relativity-like frame difference in which "both sides are correct." These interpretations lie outside the accepted physics of atomic hydrogen and are not endorsed by mainstream science. In an accompanying biographical note he describes himself as a systems engineer whose background includes engineering physics, electronics, avionics, and R&D prototyping.
