Overview
This is Section 11 — headed "Illegal Statics" — of an unpublished book Yuri N. Keilman wrote in 2000. The wiki abstract is his own note on it: "Electron, Proton, Neutron solutions were obtained in violation of my 'Extended Electrodynamics'. In 2008 was published a much better version of the theory."
The section opens candidly: "Sometimes we want to jump over the troubles." His Extended Electrodynamics imposes a boundary condition at the interface with vacuum, requiring both μ² and its derivative across the boundary to vanish. He proposes to violate it, and identifies two ways.
A soft violation keeps μ² continuous but lets its derivative jump, so the governing equation fails at a single surface with a finite left-hand side — a defect confined to a set of measure zero, which does not affect volume integrals. A hard violation lets μ² itself jump, so the derivative becomes infinite and the equation's left-hand side is infinite rather than zero. He chooses the hard violation, on the grounds that "it is the same order like the use of a point charge but even better because the integral of energy will not turn infinite." The advantage claimed is decisive: "we will get a static model for any particle with any charge, spin, mass, and magnetic moment."
He then rewrites Gauss's theorem for a vector with a jump across an internal surface, finds that the resulting surface terms are proportional to certain scalars that often vanish or integrate to zero by symmetry, and computes the global quantities.

If that is right, then every experiment whose logic rests on a transverse effect is silent about the ether, and Persson holds that three of the four canonical tests are of exactly that kind.

Immanuel Velikovsky (Russian: Иммануил Великовский ; Vitebsk, 10 June 1895 – Princeton, 17 November 1979) was a Russian-born American independent scholar, physician and psychoanalyst, best known as the author of a series of controversial books reinterpreting the events of ancient history — above all the 1950 bestseller Worlds in Collision . Drawing on comparative mythology and ancient literary sources (including the Bible), Velikovsky argued that the Earth suffered catastrophic near-collisions with other planets — principally Venus and Mars — within human memory, and that electromagnetic forces play a far greater role in celestial mechanics than mainstream astronomy allows.
His ideas were vigorously rejected by the academic establishment, yet his books sold widely and inspired a generation of catastrophist and dissident researchers. The dispute over his work and the campaign to suppress it became known as "the Velikovsky affair." His emphasis on planetary catastrophe and cosmic electricity later became a foundational influence on the Electric Universe movement and on the work of researchers such as David Talbott and Wallace Thornhill .

Velikovsky was born in Vitebsk, in the Russian Empire (now Belarus), into a Jewish family. A gifted student, he traveled widely in his youth and studied at Montpellier in France and in Palestine before enrolling in medicine. search_text:
Inertia is the resistance of a body to any change in its state of motion. It is the content of Newton's first law — a body continues at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a force acts on it — and it is quantified by inertial mass through the second law, F = ma .
Newton set out the law in the Principia (1687) against a background of absolute space, and the difficulty has been there ever since: acceleration relative to what ? Newton's rotating-bucket argument treated the answer as absolute space itself. Ernst Mach rejected that in the 1880s and argued that the inertia of a body is determined by its relation to all the other matter in the universe — the water in the bucket knows it is rotating because the fixed stars are there. Einstein named this Mach's principle in 1918 and took it as one of the motivations for general relativity, but the theory as built realises it only partially: it does predict frame dragging by rotating matter, an effect measured by Gravity Probe B and by satellite laser ranging, but it does not derive local inertial frames from the distant mass distribution, and Einstein himself came to regard the principle as not fully implemented.
The equality of inertial and gravitational mass is one of the best-tested facts in physics, confirmed to about one part in 10 15 . What no accepted theory provides is a mechanism : neither general relativity nor the Standard Model says what physically resists acceleration, or why. This is an acknowledged gap and not a manufactured one.

Filling that gap is one of the most active themes in the literature collected here, and the proposed answers divide sharply into local and cosmic explanations.

They present the historical development of the concept of "inertia", various kinds of the body inertia manifestation and practical use of inertia in operating mechanisms. The notions of inertia and inertness are introduced. Some authors use the inertia and inertness notions designating one and the same body property by them. By inertia is most often meant the attempt of the body to preserve its state invariable in relation to the inertial (motionless) reference system. The most advanced formulation of the inertia properties is given in [5]: "Every body offers resistance in attempting to put it in motion or to change the modulus or direction of its movement". This expression is, in essence, Newton's first law...
Overview
Felix F Gorbatsevich's essay is an attempt to clear up what he regards as a persistent terminological confusion at the base of mechanics, and then to use the cleaned-up vocabulary to argue for an ether medium. His claim is that two distinct properties have been run together under one word. Inertness is a body's resistance to having its state changed — a property of mass, present whether the body moves or not, and in his view simply a synonym for mass. Inertia is a property of motion: it is the kinetic energy a body carries relative to another body, and it exists only relative to that other body and manifests only in collision. Once these are separated, he argues, several long-standing puzzles dissolve.

The energy required to accomplish this must be contained within the body (for limited movement or acceleration), or the body may generate the required energy by harnessing energy that may be present in the aether, whether it is electrical, magnetic, nuclear, gravitational, acoustic, or zero point energy for unlimited movement or duration of acceleration. Any form of energy present in the vicinity of the body may be said to exist in the aether occupied by the body unless the energy is shielded from entering into that space. A brief account of the NASA Breakthrough Propulsion Physics Project is also given.

Infinite Universe Theory ( IUT ) is the cosmology developed by Glenn Borchardt as the alternative to the Big Bang. It is the cosmological application of neomechanics and of Borchardt's Ten Assumptions of Science , and it holds that the universe is infinite and eternal in both the microscopic and macroscopic directions, has no origin, no edge and no age, and is therefore not a proper subject for cosmogony at all.
The name belongs to both a theory and a book: Borchardt first set the position out in a 2007 paper for the Proceedings of the Natural Philosophy Alliance , and expanded it into the book Infinite Universe Theory in 2017.
The central argument
Borchardt's case does not begin with data but with an assumption, and with the claim that the opposing assumption is equally unprovable and usually unnoticed. Big Bang cosmology presumes a finite universe with an origin; IUT assumes infinity. Neither can be proven. His contention is that physics adopted finity without ever registering that a choice had been made, and that "fundamental assumptions exist as unconscious presuppositions before they are brought into the light of day."
Once infinity is assumed, an origin becomes incoherent — in his phrasing, "it is not possible for the universe not to exist everywhere for all time" — and the assumptions of inseparability and conservation forbid matter or motion coming into being from nothing. Cosmogony, the study of the origin of the universe, is thus not a difficult science but an illegitimate one, having no object.

Infinity is the concept of the unlimited — of a magnitude, a number, a duration or an extension that has no end. In mathematics it is a working object, handled by rules laid down since Cantor and reproduced in every calculus and set-theory course. In physics it is something else: a quantity that has no meter reading, that no experiment returns, and that appears in the equations of the accepted theories in two very different roles. It appears as an idealisation, harmless and convenient — the infinite straight wire, the infinitely massive source, the limit taken as a variable grows without bound. And it appears as a result, where a theory that was supposed to describe something finite produces a divergence instead: the point-mass singularity of general relativity, the moment of the Big Bang , the infinite self-energy of the electron, the infinite energy density of the zero-point field.
Among the researchers documented on this wiki, infinity is contested ground in both directions at once. Many of them hold that physics has wrongly refused an infinity that is real — the infinite extent and infinite age of the universe — while simultaneously tolerating infinities that are not real, the divergences that arise inside its own equations and are then removed by hand. Others take the opposite view on one or both counts, arguing for a finite closed space, or for a lower limit to divisibility below which no infinity of the small exists. What unites the collection is that infinity is not treated here as a technicality. It is treated as the assumption that decides what kind of universe is being described, usually before any observation has been consulted.
Potential and actual infinity
The distinction that runs under most of these disputes is the classical one between potential and actual infinity. Inflationary Effects on the Formation of Galaxies is a two-page note by Mitch Emery of Maumee, Ohio, published in Proceedings of the NPA volume 5, number 1 (2008), pages 48–49. It develops the framework of his earlier paper New Physics Based on Force-Free Circular Motion , and its stated purpose is to explain how galaxies formed and "why the bars of a spiral galaxy exist."
The underlying idea is that circular motion can be inertial rather than forced. Emery is careful to distinguish this from ordinary circular motion under a force, and works through the case of a ball on a string at some length: there the tension holds the momentum at right angles and drags the ball round, so that "it is only force that upholds Newton's First Law of Motion."

Interacting galaxies ( colliding galaxies ) are galaxies whose gravitational fields result in a disturbance of one another. An example of a minor interaction is a satellite galaxy 's disturbing the primary galaxy's spiral arms . An example of a major interaction is a galactic collision, which may lead to a galaxy merger .
Satellite interaction
A giant galaxy interacting with its satellites is common. A satellite's gravity could attract one of the primary's spiral arms , or the secondary satellite's path could coincide with the position of the primary satellite's and so would dive into the primary galaxy (the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy into the Milky Way being an example of the latter). That can possibly trigger a small amount of star formation . Such orphaned clusters of stars were sometimes referred to as "blue blobs" before they were recognized as stars. [ 1 ]

Abstract
In the conventional view electric charge and gravitational mass are objective, intrinsic properties of macroscopic objects and fundamental particles. Forces and interactions are consequences of such particle properties. Intrinsic redshift is the hypothesis that a significant part of the redshift observed in some astronomical objects — particularly quasars — is not caused by cosmological expansion or by motion away from the observer, but is instead a property intrinsic to the object itself. If true, redshift would cease to be a reliable measure of distance, and the distance scale on which modern cosmology and the Big Bang model rest would require fundamental revision.
The hypothesis is most closely associated with the astronomer Halton C Arp , whose observations of apparently connected objects with wildly differing redshifts formed its principal evidence, and with William Tifft , who reported that galaxy redshifts fall into preferred, quantized values. It remains firmly rejected by mainstream astronomy, but is a central topic in the critical-thinkers literature catalogued on this wiki.
The standard interpretation of redshift
In conventional astronomy an object's redshift is understood as the sum of three effects: the cosmological redshift produced by the expansion of space, the Doppler shift due to the object's own motion, and a usually small gravitational redshift. Because the cosmological term dominates at large distances, redshift is used directly as a distance indicator through Hubble's law — the foundation of the extragalactic distance scale. On this view there is no additional, object-specific component, and a high redshift necessarily means a great distance.

Title Investigation of Frame-Dragging-Like Signals from Spinning Superconductors using Laser Gyroscopes
Author(s) Martin Tajmar
Keywords Frame-Dragging, Gravitomagnetism, London Moment
Published 2008
Volume AIP CP969
Abstract
The search for frame dragging around massive rotating objects such as the Earth is an important test for general relativity and is actively pursued with the LAGEOS and Gravity Probe-B satellites. Within the classical framework, frame dragging is independent of the state (normal or coherent) of the test mass. This was recently challenged by proposing that a large frame-dragging field could be responsible for a reported anomaly of the Cooperpair mass found in Niobium superconductors. In 2003, a test program was initiated at the Austrian Research Centers to investigate this conjecture using sensitive accelerometers and fiber optic gyroscopes in the close vicinity of fast spinning rings at cryogenic temperatures. This paper will discuss the measurements recently obtained with the fiber optic gyroscopes. They show, that the angular velocity applied to the superconductor can indeed be seen on the sensors below a critical temperature. The signal amplitude is about 8 orders of magnitude below the values applied to the ring for the case of clockwise rotation only. Counter-clockwise rotation responses were at least an order of magnitude weaker. The critical temperature for Al and Nb was 16 K and for YBCO around 32 K, which does not coincide with the material's superconducting temperature. The origin and the signature of the observed signals so far is not clear. Our measurements and analysis suggest that the signal cannot be explained by mechanical influence or by carefully monitored magnetic fields surrounding the sensors.

Ionel Dinu (born 1 June 1972) is a Romanian physicist, physics teacher and experimentalist, best known for his underwater experiments with rotating disks and cylinders , which demonstrate a purely mechanical model for magnetic attraction and repulsion.
Dinu's programme is to show that the forces normally attributed to fields acting across empty space are in fact fluid-mechanical effects in a liquid aether : that electrostatic and gravitational attraction correspond to Bjerknes forces , and that magnetic attraction and repulsion occur between vortices . His experiments are offered as the demonstration that action apparently at a distance is in every case transmitted through the intervening liquid.
His rotating-cylinder result was adopted by Robert de Hilster and David de Hilster as the experimental basis for the magnetic component of the Four Universal Motions , where it is named the "Dinu effect" — a name coined by David de Hilster in Principia Mathematica 2 .
The underwater experiments
The experiments are simple enough to be shown on video and are the reason Dinu is cited elsewhere on this wiki. Cylinders (and in other runs, disks) are set rotating while submerged in water, and their mutual behaviour is observed.
The result is that rotating cylinders in water attract or repel one another in the same pattern as permanent magnets :
Opposite directions of rotation → attraction. The flows between the two cylinders reinforce one another and the cylinders move together.
Same direction of rotation → repulsion. The opposing flows between them create a disturbance that forces the cylinders apart.

Forum, V71, N6, pp. 705-716 (June 1924). A Professor of Celestial Mechanics maintains thay Einstein's theory of relativity has not been proved, unless we accept on faith the special pleadings and assumptions of his followers. He calls attention to the wide divergence between stellar positions predicted by Einstein and the actual positions observed at the time of eclipses, and he argues that Newton's conclusions can be equally well vindicated if Newtonians permit themselves similar liberties in explaining away embarrassing facts.
Overview
This is the first half of a two-part debate staged by The Forum in 1924 under the running head "Is Einstein Wrong? — A Debate". Poor's contribution is subtitled "The Errors of Einstein"; the reply, "The Triumphs of Relativity" by Archibald Henderson, was promised for the July issue and is not part of this document. Poor was Professor of Celestial Mechanics at Columbia and wrote as a working orbit-computer rather than as a theorist, and the piece is addressed to the general reader: it contains no equations, only two star-displacement diagrams from the 1922 eclipse and a photograph of the 1923 eclipse taken at Yerbaniz, Mexico.
Poor's target is not the mathematics of General Relativity as such but the claim that the theory has been observationally verified . He argues that the two celebrated astronomical tests — the anomalous perihelion motion of Mercury and the deflection of starlight at a solar eclipse — do not do the work claimed for them. On his account the Mercury result is an artefact of applying a formula written in relativistic ("proper") time to observations reckoned in ordinary astronomical time, and the eclipse result is a number extracted by a reduction procedure that already assumes the effect it reports. Abstract
Due to their conviction that the laws of nature must be identical in any inertial frame, the physicists of the beginning of the twentieth century were led to extend the relativity of Galileo to the electromagnetism of Maxwell, but this seemed to imply the abondonment of universal time and absolute simultaneity. In a previous paper* we have criticised, from a logical viewpoint , the criteria intended to demonstrate the relativity of simultaneity and we have proposed replacing them by other criteria. According to these, the relativity of simulteneity was called into question.
We propose here a rigorous experimental method intended to verify the simultaneity of two events. By means of this device, we demonstrate that one can define an absolute simultaneity. The method also permits an exact synchronization of clocks. We then demonstrate that the relativity of time of Einstein's theory must be discarded. On the other hand, the relativity principle appears as an approximation only, valid for bodies moving at low speeds relative to one another.
On the contrary, the slowing of the clocks moving with respect to the ether can be maintained. But this does not mean that Lorentz's theory can be retained without change.

Sir Isaac Newton (25 December 1642 – 20 March 1727, Old Style) was an English natural philosopher and mathematician, author of Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687), and the founder of the mechanical description of nature that governed physics for two centuries.
For many of the researchers collected on this wiki, Newton is not a historical figure who was later superseded but the correct starting point . Among them is an identifiable group who make a strong claim — that the universe is Newtonian at every scale — which puts them directly at odds with the physics of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.
That is not the position of the wiki as a whole. The critical tradition documented here is varied, and Newtonian mechanics is one strand within it rather than a consensus.
This page gives his life briefly and then documents that tradition. The standard biography is exhaustively covered elsewhere; what follows concentrates on what is contested.
Life and work in brief
Newton was born prematurely at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, three months after his father's death. He entered Trinity College, Cambridge in 1661, and it was during the plague years of 1665–67, when the university closed and he returned home, that he laid the foundations of the calculus, of his theory of colour, and of his thinking on gravitation — the period later mythologised through the falling apple.
He became Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge in 1669

Ivor Catt (19 December 1935 – 21 June 2025) was a British electronics engineer known both for pioneering work on high-speed digital logic and wafer-scale integration and, more controversially, for a heterodox account of electromagnetism built on the ideas of Oliver Heaviside. He took a B.A. in engineering at Trinity College, Cambridge, published influential work on crosstalk and interconnection delay in digital systems, and patented the wafer-scale integration technique commercialised in the late 1980s by the British company Anamartic. From the late 1970s onwards he argued, chiefly in the pages of Wireless World and its successor Electronics World , that the textbook treatment of electric current, charge and displacement current is incoherent, and he spent four decades pressing the physics establishment for an answer to what became known as the Catt Question.
Biography
Catt was born on 19 December 1935 in Devon, England, and spent part of his childhood on an RAF airbase in Singapore, leaving with his mother and sister shortly before the Japanese invasion of 1942. He did National Service in Germany, won a State Scholarship in mathematics, and then read engineering at Trinity College, Cambridge, taking his B.A. degree.
He married Freda Mansfield in 1959; the couple had one son. He lived for many years in St Albans, Hertfordshire, from where he ran his own publishing imprints and, from the 1990s, an extensive personal website archiving his writings and his correspondence with academic physicists. Catt died on 21 June 2025 at Watford General Hospital, aged 89.

search_text:
J. Burton
Residence France
Known for Natural philosopher
There are many scientific theories out there. Some of them are mainstream, others are completely out of mainstream. Whatever their appeal however, how are we to know that a given scientific point of view is better or more accurate than another? Every theory has flaws after all, so how can we be sure that we're on the right track? Is there really a "right track"? Hasn't modern science taught us through its so-called "axiomatic method" that all knowledge is by necessity partial and fragmentary? Aren't we then forever subordinated to an arbitrary choice of postulates that will give us arbitrary theories and arbitrary knowledge? Is that what modernity brought us: knowledge as a matter of taste or "elegance" ? Or else, are we missing something?
It is in that context that I'd like to bring in a new understanding of the nature of reality, which explains its structure regardless of the particular postulates that will be used to build on a given scientific theory. I called this endeavor "Absolute Metaphysics", after Kurt Gödel's concept of a process of "clarification of meaning" expressed in his never publicly delivered 1961 lecture "The modern Development Of The Foundations Of Mathematics In The Light Of Philosophy".

The geophysicist J. Marvin Herndon is the proponent of a radical theory about Earth's core and its relationship to Earth's magnetic field, the shield that protects our planet's animal and plant life from the sun's radiation. According to Herndon, at the center of Earth there is a naturally occurring nuclear‑fission reactor, five miles in diameter, that provides the energy needed to generate and sustain the geomagnetic field. Described as a maverick by Guy Gugliotta in the Washington Post (March 24, 2003), Herndon has encountered resistance to his theory in the geophysics community, but some believe that his concept may prove to be one of the most important contributions to geophysics in the history of the field. "This is on a scale of {the theory of} plate tectonics, which took 50 years to accept," Hatten S. Yoder Jr., the director emeritus of the Geophysical Laboratory of the Carnegie Institution of Washington, in Washington, D.C., told Lidia Wasowicz for United Press International (March 27, 2003, on‑line). "I think Herndon's got something just as big, just as important." Herndon, an independent researcher, is the president of the Transdyne Corp., a scientific research and management company in San Diego, California.

Fields Electromagnetism , experimental energy devices
Jack Scholze (born March 6, 1958) is an American independent experimenter based in Honolulu, Hawaii, who builds and tests electromagnetic devices in the amateur "free energy" tradition. He documents his work on a personal YouTube channel, where he presents pulse motors, motor-generators, battery chargers, and energy-capture apparatus wound with unconventional coil geometries.
Biography
Scholze lives in Honolulu, Hawaii, and pursues his experimental work outside of the mainstream academic and industrial physics community. He shares his experiments publicly through online video, positioning himself within a wider community of hobbyists and dissident researchers who investigate claims of over-unity and vortex-based energy.
Work
Scholze's experiments center on direct-current and alternating-current pulse motors, motor-generators, battery chargers, and other energy-capture devices. Much of his work explores exotic inductors and inductor winding geometries, including Rodin coils, Starship coils, conical coils, and designs he associates with names such as Powell Abha, Matthews, and Hendershot coils. Many of these coils are toroidal or donut-shaped and carry several separate windings.
His interest in the geometry of inductors draws on "vortex math" ideas popularized by Marko Rodin, in which winding patterns are arranged according to numerical sequences said to concentrate or channel electromagnetic effects. Scholze presents his devices as investigations into whether such geometries can capture or amplify energy, a premise that lies outside established electromagnetic theory. His contributions consist chiefly of self-published demonstrations and build logs rather than peer-reviewed publications.

Jacques Moret-Bailly is a French physicist and retired professor at the Université de Bourgogne in Dijon, France. Originally a specialist in molecular spectroscopy, he is known in dissident cosmology for proposing the CREIL effect (Coherent Raman Effect on Incoherent Light) as a non-Doppler, non-expansion explanation of astronomical redshifts. (He is also listed on this wiki under the spelling "Moret-Bailey".)
Biography
Moret-Bailly spent his career at the Université de Bourgogne (University of Burgundy) in Dijon, where he worked as a professor of physics before retiring. His early research was in molecular spectroscopy. In later work he turned to theoretical optics and its application to astrophysics and cosmology, publishing a long series of papers from the early 2000s onward.
Scientific work
Molecular spectroscopy
Moret-Bailly's original field was molecular spectroscopy, the study of how molecules absorb and emit light. This background in the interaction of light with matter informed his later work on light propagation through low-density gases.
CREIL and alternative redshift
Moret-Bailly is best known for the Coherent Raman Effect on Incoherent Light (CREIL), which he introduced around 2003 as an alternative account of cosmological redshift. He argues that when ordinary (incoherent) light propagates through a very low-pressure gas of excited atomic hydrogen, a coherent Raman-type interaction shifts the light's frequencies toward the red without blurring images or scrambling the order of spectral lines. Because the shift is smooth and image-preserving, he claims it can be mistaken for a Doppler shift or for cosmological expansion.

Scientific career
Fields Physics , Electromagnetism , History of science
James Arathoon is a researcher and speaker in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society (CNPS) online seminar series, where he has given talks on the foundations of electromagnetism, the interpretation of the Michelson-Morley experiment, the nature of charge and mass, the fine-structure constant, and the history of science and medicine. His work is critical of Special Relativity and of the conceptual foundations that mainstream physics takes for granted, and he draws on the older critical electromagnetic tradition, particularly the writings of the Irish physicist and mathematician Alfred O'Rahilly.
Biography
Little biographical detail about Arathoon is available in public sources. A 1991 undergraduate thesis submitted for a B.Sc. in Geophysical Sciences at the University of Lancaster, Atmospheric Electricity Investigations: Measurement of Atmospheric Conductivity , reporting measurements made with a Gerdien condenser at a weather station near the university, was self-archived under his name on the Internet Archive in 2023. He has presented regularly in the CNPS livestream seminar series since 2023, hosted by Ian Cowan.
Scientific contributions
Incompatibilities with Special Relativity
Arathoon argues that Special Relativity is not compatible with the ordinary theory of measurement and with dimensional analysis. On this view the relativistic treatment of length and time is not simply a novel but self-consistent account of measurement; rather, it conflicts with the requirements that any coherent system of physical units and dimensions must satisfy. James DeMeo is an American researcher in geography and atmospheric science, and Director of the Orgone Biophysical Research Lab in Ashland, Oregon, which he founded in 1978.
He matters most on this wiki for a single sustained piece of work: the recovery and defence of Dayton C Miller 's ether-drift experiments . DeMeo went back to Miller's original records and to the 1955 reanalysis that dismissed them, and produced the most detailed case in print that the dismissal was wrong. Much of what is now argued about Miller on this wiki rests on what DeMeo found there.
His wider research programme — cross-cultural work on the origins of warfare, and laboratory work on Wilhelm Reich's findings — is more controversial and is described below.

Studied Earth, atmospheric and environmental/social sciences at Florida International University
PhD, University of Kansas , 1986 — where he undertook graduate-level research explicitly testing Wilhelm Reich 's claims
Career

He founded the Orgone Biophysical Research Lab in 1978, and in 1994 established the Greenspring Center , a high-altitude research facility in the Siskiyou Mountains near Ashland, Oregon.

James J. Keene is an American scientist, Director of the Binary Mechanics Lab, which he founded in 1999, and originator of Binary Mechanics — a theoretical framework that treats space, time and energy as fully quantized ("binary") rather than continuous, and that seeks to derive fundamental physical constants from first principles. Keene has served as Editor of the Journal of Binary Mechanics since 2010. Working outside the academic physics mainstream as an independent researcher, he argues that the continuous mathematics underlying legacy quantum mechanics and the Standard Model describes events at points in space and time that do not physically exist, and he is a frequent presenter in the CNPS online seminar series.

He has published original research in peer-reviewed journals in quantum physics, neuroscience, behavioral science and computer science, including some thirteen papers in physiology and biophysics.
Since 1999 he has been Director of the Binary Mechanics Lab, which his profiles list as based in Portsmouth, Commonwealth of Dominica, West Indies. He is also a software developer: he is the author of the HotBasic compiler, an extended-BASIC compiler producing console, CGI, GUI, DLL and OBJ applications for Windows and Linux, in development since the early 2000s. James R. Hofmann is an American historian of science, Professor of Liberal Studies at California State University, Fullerton . He is the author of André-Marie Ampère: Enlightenment and Electrodynamics (Cambridge University Press, 1995), for a long time the only full-length biography of Ampère in English and still the standard one.
He appears on this wiki because Ampère's force law between current elements is among the most argued-over subjects here, and Hofmann is the historian most often relied on for the circumstances in which that law was produced.
André-Marie Ampère: Enlightenment and Electrodynamics
Published in the Cambridge Science Biographies series edited by David Knight, the book sets Ampère's scientific work against the whole of his life: a man with no formal schooling who read his way through his father's library, whose father was guillotined in the Terror, and who held simultaneously to the scientific optimism of the Enlightenment and to a Catholic faith he found difficult. Hofmann treats the mathematics, the chemistry and the electrodynamics together rather than extracting the physics from the life, and gives close attention to how Ampère actually reasoned from experiment to force law.
"The providential timing of scientific discovery" (2026)
Hofmann returned to the subject for the 250th anniversary of Ampère's birth, in "The providential timing of scientific discovery: André-Marie Ampère in 1820", Comptes Rendus — Mécanique 354 , 671–678 (2026), doi:10.5802/crmeca.374 .

James Noel Robb (March 7, 1942 – August 5, 2023) was an American farmer, U.S. Army radar technician, amateur radio operator, and independent researcher from Danville, Kansas. He pursued self-directed investigations in Electromagnetism , Vortex Theory , biophotonics , and Bioenergy , and held the amateur radio callsign KD0CBW .
Biography
Robb was born on March 7, 1942, in Stillwater, Oklahoma, to Noel Neville Robb and Pauline Louise (Hallman) Robb. From an early age he was drawn to science and technology, becoming an avid reader of Popular Mechanics and an enthusiastic builder of science-fair projects.
Drafted into the United States Army the day before his 25th birthday, Robb trained at the U.S. Army Signal School and served in Vietnam for 19 months and 27 days as a specialist in radar technology (military occupational specialty 26D20, GCA Radar R&M). He was honorably discharged on March 5, 1973 with the rank of Specialist.
Returning to Kansas, Robb farmed the family land near Danville, working as a pioneer farmer from 1968 to 2023. He was also a licensed amateur radio operator under the callsign KD0CBW.
Robb died on August 5, 2023, near Danville while storm spotting and checking his rain gauges. A memorial service was held on August 19, 2023 at Pleasant Valley Mennonite Church in Harper, Kansas, with inurnment at Fairview Cemetery, Danville.

He is a long-time advocate of the Electric Universe concept and a contributor to the Structured Atom Model (SAM) developed by Edo Kaal , and he frequently presents these ideas to conferences and interest groups.

James Sorensen is an electrical and software engineer who develops feature-rich websites using Drupal . He has had a strong interest in science from an early age, but came to regard mainstream cosmology, astronomy, and physics as having gone down what he calls a "mathematical rabbit hole," questioning concepts such as quarks and black holes as logically inconsistent. He pursued a career in computer programming, which he considered more logical, until 2010, when he encountered the Electric Universe idea and it rekindled his interest in science.
Sorensen is a skilled communicator who enjoys speaking to groups about recent developments in complex scientific theories, and who aims to make difficult material understandable for an audience that is scientifically curious but not necessarily steeped in the sciences. He regards the Electric Universe approach as one that returns science to the hands of researchers and engineers.

Sorensen advocates the Electric Universe concept, which holds that electricity and plasma play a far more fundamental role in nature than conventional science acknowledges. Jan Olof Jonson (born 11 January 1962) is a Swedish electrical engineer whose work argues that the whole of electromagnetism can be derived from Coulomb's law alone, once retardation and the special theory of relativity are applied consistently, and that Maxwell's field theory is therefore unnecessary.
Education
MSEE, Royal Institute of Technology (KTH), Stockholm, 1982
Work
Jonson has contributed to Natural Philosophy Alliance and CNPS conferences continuously since 2000, and the programme running through that body of work is a single one. His starting point is the standard observation that the magnetic force between currents is the electrostatic force seen from a moving frame — the derivation familiar from Purcell's textbook — and his claim is that if this is carried through rigorously, with the propagation delay of the interaction taken into account element by element, Coulomb's law by itself accounts for the forces between conductors, for electromagnetic induction and for radiation, with no independent magnetic field required.
The recurring test case is Ampère's bridge , a rectangular circuit divided into two halves that repel one another. This experiment sits at the centre of a two-hundred-year-old dispute over whether the force between current elements takes Ampère's original form, which includes a longitudinal component, or the Grassmann form underlying the modern Lorentz force . Jaroslav Grigorievich Klyushin (also transliterated Yaroslav Klyushin ; born April 1940 in Leningrad , Soviet Union) is a Russian physicist and mathematician based in St. Petersburg. He heads the Chair of Applied Mathematics at the St. Petersburg State University of Civil Aviation and serves as editor of Galilean Electrodynamics East (GED-East). He is known for his work on a generalization of Maxwell's equations and for a unified treatment of electrodynamics and gravitation that he terms "gravidynamics."
Biography
According to his own account, Klyushin was born in Leningrad in April 1940 into a family of the city's intelligentsia; his father worked as an engineer and later as a professor at the Radiotechnical Institute in Taganrog, and his mother was a singer at the Leningrad Opera. During the Second World War he was evacuated as a child and raised largely by his grandmother in the Ural region and later in Taganrog.
In 1957 he entered the Institute of International Relations in Moscow, studying in the Oriental Faculty. In 1962 he was arrested by the KGB in connection with student discussions he had organized on the democratization of the Soviet system. He subsequently turned to mathematics and physics, settling in St. Petersburg, where he became a professor of applied mathematics at the University of Civil Aviation.
Scientific contributions
Klyushin's principal research concerns a reformulation and extension of classical electromagnetic theory. Jean-Pierre Vigier (16 January 1920 – 4 May 2004) was a French theoretical physicist, assistant to Louis de Broglie for fourteen years, and the leading twentieth-century exponent of the causal stochastic interpretation of quantum mechanics — the position that quantum processes, though genuinely stochastic, remain causal , in the tradition of de Broglie and David Bohm .
He is one of the most substantial figures catalogued on this wiki. He published more than two hundred papers, sat on the editorial board of Physics Letters A , and was known in the French press as l'hérétique de la physique and l'éternel résistant — the second a reference to his wartime service in the French Resistance as much as to his standing in physics.
For this wiki his most directly relevant contribution is a specific one: the argument that a small but non-zero photon mass makes the small ether drift measured by Michelson and by Miller not an embarrassment to relativity but a consequence of it.

Vigier earned his Ph.D. in Mathematics from the University of Geneva in 1946 and served briefly as a member of the French Atomic Commission alongside Frédéric Joliot-Curie. In 1948 he was appointed assistant to Louis de Broglie (Nobel Prize 1929, for the discovery of the wave nature of particles), a position he held until de Broglie's retirement in 1962, although their collaboration continued for another ten years.

Jean-Claude Pecker (10 May 1923 – 20 February 2020) was a French astrophysicist, author and rationalist. He was Professor at the Collège de France from 1964 to 1988 and Director of the Institut d'Astrophysique from 1972 to 1979, and served as General Secretary of the International Astronomical Union from 1967 to 1970 and as Secretary of the International Academy of Humanism. He wrote several books and hundreds of papers on astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, human rights, pseudoscience, science and society, and the history of astronomy.
His principal research was in solar physics and stellar atmospheres — the textbook Astrophysique Générale , written with Évry Schatzman, was a standard reference for a generation — and it is from that established position that he engaged, from the 1980s onward, with objections to the standard cosmological model.
Cosmological work
Pecker's contribution to the non-standard cosmology literature centres on the redshift . With Jean-Pierre Vigier he developed a tired-light mechanism in which the redshift arises from an interaction between photons carrying a small non-zero rest mass and the matter lying between source and observer, an account set out in " A Possible Tired-Light Mechanism " (1988). He also worked with Toivo Jaakkola on spatial fluctuations in the Hubble constant, and set out his objections to the standard model directly in " Some Critiques of the Big Bang Cosmology " (1997).

Jeffrey P. Baugher ("Jeff Baugher") is an American researcher working on the foundations of General Relativity , the cosmological constant problem and dark energy. He argues that the "worst theoretical prediction in the history of physics" — the roughly 120-order-of-magnitude mismatch between the observed cosmological constant and the vacuum energy density predicted by quantum field theory — is not a physical puzzle at all but the symptom of a notational and geometrical mistake buried in the way physics represents energy density and the constituents of a line. He calls his alternative framework Integral Geometry .
Biography
Baugher was affiliated with the Department of Electrical Engineering at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio, at the time of his 2013 paper in Progress in Physics . Earlier he co-authored engineering work with Ronald A. Coutu on micromechanical structures with stable linear positive and negative stiffness, published in the Society for Experimental Mechanics conference series ( MEMS and Nanotechnology , Volume 4, 2011). On this wiki he has been described as a PhD student with an interest in the history of field theory, developing a counter-argument to parallelism and differential geometry which he calls Integral Geometry .
He has published most of his physics work as preprints on viXra and has presented it to the CNPS livestream seminar series.

Jeff Yee (born 12 October 1972) is an American technology executive and independent theoretical physicist, known as the originator of Energy Wave Theory (EWT), a classical wave model in which particles are standing waves in an aether and the fundamental forces arise from wave interference.
Yee came to physics from outside it. A mechanical engineer by training and a wireless-industry executive by career, he began researching particle physics in 2007 while writing a time-travel novel, and by 2014 was publishing mathematical models of the wave structure of matter. His stated aim is reductive: that the energies of all particles and the strengths of three of the four forces follow from four constants of the medium plus one property of the electron.
He credits his intuition for the theory to an unlikely source — growing up surfing in Hawaii, where he says he came to understand ocean waves and their energy long before he applied the idea to matter.
Career
Jeff Yee is a technology executive, with various roles in the wireless industry at AT&T, Treemo Labs, Antenna Software, Moovweb and ZTE. Jeff brings product and entrepreneurial experience to theoretical physics, as a contributor to Energy Wave Theory . As an author, Jeff provides an overview of the subatomic world and its relationship to energy, in the The Particles of the Universe series on Amazon. As he states in the first book in the series, a better understanding of the subatomic realm should lead to new and innovative products. In the second book in the series, many of the issues within the quantum domain of physics is simplified and united into classical physics.

Kooistra experimented with suspended magnets and freely rotating rings, and reports that the surprising results have a conventional explanation , at least to first order, and that Marinov critically misunderstood his own device .

He is a prolific writer on the subject, having released several hundred short papers through open preprint repositories. His ideas fall outside mainstream astronomy and have not been published in peer-reviewed scientific journals or adopted by professional astronomers.
Biography

Beginning around 2012, he began publishing a series of papers outlining what he calls stellar metamorphosis, circulating his work largely through preprint archives such as viXra , the General Science Journal, and personal websites and video channels rather than through established academic journals. He is affiliated with the Natural Philosophy Alliance community of independent researchers, under which he describes his work as that of a "Scientific Revolutionary." Over the following decade he authored hundreds of short papers applying his framework to specific stars, exoplanets, and Solar System bodies.
Scientific contributions
Wolynski's central proposal is the General Theory of Stellar Metamorphosis, which holds that stars and planets are not fundamentally different kinds of objects but rather the same object observed at different stages of a single evolutionary sequence. Jesse Babcock (born 1915) is an American self-taught theorist associated with the Natural Philosophy community. He is known for an unorthodox cosmological framework he calls the "true suction" theory, which he developed to explain the origin of matter, energy and Gravity outside the framework of mainstream physics.
Biography
Babcock reports having only an eighth-grade formal education, a fact he presents as central to his outlook, arguing that it left him unencumbered by conventional scientific training. By his own account he became interested in perpetual motion as a child before 1923, and at around the age of fifteen concluded that a working perpetual-motion device could not be built until "the secret of the universe" was understood. He states that experiments imagining spring-and-spoke wheel mechanisms convinced him that any purely mechanical arrangement will always balance out, ruling out perpetual motion in practice.
Babcock dates the origin of his theory to 1953. He recounts hearing a radio report that high-frequency sound waves from jet engines were damaging the lungs of ground crews, which led him to reconsider the idea that sound is "nothing." Reflecting on empty space, he concluded that space must be endless and that it is the only source from which anything could arise.
Work
Babcock's central claim is that space itself possesses a dynamic characteristic he terms "true suction," from which all matter and energy originate. In his view "true suction" is not an object or substance but a property of space, and everything that exists ultimately derives from space and this characteristic.

Aether Physics Model
The Aether Physics Model treats the aether not as empty space but as a quantum structure — a lattice of "aether units," each conceived as a quantum of rotating magnetic field — from which the properties of subatomic particles and the forces between them are said to be derived. On this basis Bourassa and Thomson offer a "unified force theory," an account of dark matter, and what they describe as a means of quantifying consciousness, presenting the model as a mathematically self-consistent alternative to the Standard Model rather than a modification of it.
Bourassa set out the foundations of the approach with Thomson in the papers " A New Foundation for Physics " (2006) and " Electron Binding Energies in the Aether Physics Model " (2007), and the two developed it at length in their book Secrets of the Aether . Bourassa has described his interest in the aether as a lifelong project begun in his teens, and points to hoped-for applications in energy and other technologies. The Aether Physics Model is not accepted by mainstream physics.
His background is in technical industry, where he worked in design and in computer-aided design (CAD) management and training before turning to aether research through the institute.

Jim Johnson (born 22 December 1942) is an American writer and editor based in Olympia, Washington, and the managing editor of The Essential Guide to the Electric Universe , the introductory resource hosted on the Thunderbolts Project website.
Work
The Essential Guide grew out of a request made in 2009 by David Talbott to Bob Johnson, for a summary that would give newcomers enough grounding in plasma behaviour to follow Electric Universe arguments without finding them far-fetched. Jim Johnson took on the task of building that summary into a structured online resource, organised to move from familiar material — stellar distances, the aurorae, planetary magnetospheres — through the history of electromagnetic science to a more technical treatment of plasma, with appendices, a glossary and links to video material.
He presented the project at the 18th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference in 2011, in a paper whose interest lies less in its physics than in its frankness about the state of the field it serves. Johnson describes the Electric Universe as a "paradigm" rather than a theory, on the grounds that its ideas "are less than full-blown theory and are still in a very qualitative state of patterns and examples", and that "underlying mathematics is not yet the EU's long suit". He defends that status as a legitimate stage of enquiry by appeal to the qualitative-physics literature in artificial intelligence, particularly Johan de Kleer's work on causal reasoning about circuits, and argues that the task ahead is to deepen the model with quantitative work rather than to defend it as complete.

John B. Miller is an American physicist and astronomer associated with Western Michigan University in Kalamazoo, Michigan. With his collaborator Thomas E Miller he developed the de Sitter redshift interpretation of the redshifts of quasars and galaxies — an account in which cosmological redshift is a gravitational effect of de Sitter spacetime rather than evidence of an expanding universe.
Scientific work
Miller's work addresses one of the puzzles that has long fuelled non-standard views of redshift : quasars at very high redshift appear almost as bright as objects at intermediate redshift, which is difficult to reconcile with the expansion interpretation, in which more distant (higher-redshift) objects should generally appear fainter.
In his 1994 paper " Are Quasars Manifesting a de Sitter Redshift? " Miller proposed that quasar redshifts are a de Sitter redshift — a gravitational redshift arising in de Sitter spacetime, whose asymptotic character causes the redshift to rise very steeply with distance. On this interpretation an object's observed redshift is not a simple measure of recession velocity or distance, and the near-constant apparent brightness of quasars across a wide range of redshifts becomes expected rather than anomalous.
With Thomas E Miller he later extended the analysis to large modern surveys, arguing that under a de Sitter-space interpretation the intrinsic brightness of objects is roughly the same at all redshifts — for instance, that some 95% of Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxies and quasars fall within a magnitude range of only about 2.8. The John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society ( CNPS ) is a worldwide society of critical thinkers — professors, PhDs, scientists, engineers and interested lay people — who openly question mainstream physics and cosmology and who develop and present alternative theories, philosophies and models. Taking "natural philosophy" in its older and broadest sense, the society covers physics, cosmology, mathematics and the philosophy and history of science, and provides an open forum for serious scientific work that falls outside the accepted paradigm. It is the organization that owns and maintains the Natural Philosophy Wiki on which this article appears, together with the associated World Science Database.
The society describes itself as "a world-wide think-tank of critical thinkers... who openly criticize mainstream physics and cosmology and who propose alternative theory, philosophy, and models." Its members — many of whom have worked together for more than two decades — apply critical thinking to identify what they see as flaws and failures in mainstream science, and to propose new directions in natural philosophy.
Namesake
The society is named in honour of Dr. John E. Chappell Jr. (1933–2002), a historian of science and earth scientist widely regarded as the modern father of the organized "dissident science" movement. Chappell founded the Natural Philosophy Alliance , the CNPS's predecessor, and devoted much of his life to promoting open, scholarly debate of alternatives to accepted physics — motivated in large part by his conviction that Einstein's theory of relativity was mistaken. John Gideon Hartnett (born 24 March 1952) is an Australian physicist known in two very different capacities: as an experimentalist who helped build some of the most stable clocks in the world , and as a cosmologist who argues that the universe requires neither dark matter nor dark energy — and who rejects the Big Bang outright.
Like Pierre-Marie Robitaille , Hartnett is a case of dissent issuing from technical accomplishment rather than from outside the discipline. His work on ultra-stable cryogenic oscillators is mainstream precision metrology of a high order, commercialised and sold to national standards laboratories. His cosmology is not accepted at all.
Education and career
Hartnett was born in Manjimup, Western Australia. He took both his B.Sc. (Hons I) and his PhD with distinction at the School of Physics, University of Western Australia, and in 2005 became an ARC QEII Post-Doctoral Research Fellow. He worked for many years in the Frequency Standards and Metrology research group at UWA, latterly as a research professor, and subsequently at the University of Adelaide. He has published more than eighty papers in refereed journals and holds two patents.
Frequency standards and metrology
Hartnett's experimental speciality is the cryogenic sapphire oscillator — a frequency standard in which a pure sapphire resonator, cooled with liquid helium, supports an exceptionally stable microwave "whispering gallery" mode. John M. Hunter is a British researcher in cosmology and gravitation who proposes that the observed expansion of the universe is better understood as a global rescaling of all lengths and physical constants, and that dark energy is an artefact of misreading the relationship between redshift and scale factor.
Work
The rescaling symmetry principle
Hunter's central proposal, set out in " The Rescaling Symmetry Principle " (2008), is that every length in the universe and every physical constant changes continuously and simultaneously, at a rate governed by the number of length dimensions in the quantity concerned: d Q / Q = aH d t , with H half the Hubble constant. Lengths and the speed of light carry a = 1, Planck's constant 2, the gravitational constant 3, the permittivity of free space −3, while masses, the fine structure constant and the Hubble constant are unchanged.
Because everything changes together, he argues, no local experiment can detect the change — timing light over a fixed distance, or lunar laser ranging for a drift in G , must both return null results. The cosmological redshift, on this account, arises from the changing value of Planck's constant rather than from expanding space.
He reports that the resulting magnitude–redshift relation matches the Type Ia supernova data without invoking dark energy, and that a matter density of one quarter critical follows naturally, with an equation of state parameter of −1.
Later statements
His own summary of the position, given in the World Science Database record below, is that "dark energy is an illusion created due to the misunderstanding of the relationship between redshift and scale-factor", and that the model reproduces the WMAP5 value of Ω m = 0.249. He has continued to develop the argument in preprints posted to viXra.

John J. Durie is an author known within the dissident-science community for his paper on the telescopic aberration of light, a phenomenon central to long-running disputes over the aether and Einstein's special relativity . He is listed in Jean de Climont's Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Biography
Little verifiable biographical information about John J. Durie is available. He is documented primarily through his 1983 paper on stellar aberration and through his inclusion in de Climont's Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists . His work was circulated within critical-physics circles; the archived copy of his paper was contributed by the dissident physicist Thomas E. Phipps Jr.
Scientific work
Durie's known contribution is his paper "On the Telescopic Aberration of Light," published in the Toth-Maatian Review in January 1983. The paper addresses the aberration of starlight first reported by James Bradley in 1728, in which the observed direction of a star shifts with the Earth's orbital motion. This effect has long been treated as a test discriminating between an aether -based account of light propagation and the relativistic explanation. Durie's analysis engages the classic questions of stellar aberration and ether drag, placing his work among dissident treatments that revisit whether telescopic aberration truly favors special relativity over an aether model.

John Linus O'Sullivan (born 1938) is an Irish-American independent researcher in cosmology and the foundations of physics. Born in Tralee, Ireland, he took up the study of cosmology after retiring from a career in business, and developed a wave-based model in which the electromagnetic field is held to have a duality — much as light has a wave–particle duality — which he presents as a new way of thinking about the structure of the universe. His ideas are his own and are not part of mainstream physics.
Biography
O'Sullivan was born in 1938 in Tralee, County Kerry, Ireland, and has lived in the United States since 1960, settling in Fairfield, Connecticut. After a career in the business world he turned in his retirement to the study of cosmology and physics, working as an independent researcher and publishing his conclusions through the Natural Philosophy community.
Cosmological model
O'Sullivan's central idea is that the electromagnetic field is dual in nature, paralleling the wave–particle duality of the photon. From this starting point he builds an account in which space and matter arise from standing-wave energy: mass, light and gravity are treated as different aspects of the same underlying electromagnetic waves rather than as separate ingredients.
In his 2013 paper " Space and Time " he set out the relationship between space and time in these terms, and in " Electromagnetic Wave Energy and Time " (2015) he developed the theme further, distinguishing a finite energy that carries time — mass-energy linked to light and gravity through "open-ended standing waves" — from an infinite energy that has no time, and arguing that time exists only as the transfer of finite energy. John O'Malley Bockris, an Australian electrochemist, coined the term "hydrogen economy" in the 1970s. Bockris' hydrogen economy describes a system in which hydrogen would be used to transport energy from renewable sources over large distances and store it in large amounts. In 1962, Bockris first proposed a plan to supply US cities with solar-derived energy via hydrogen. In 1971, he published the first article on hydrogen in a referred journal. Bockris published Energy: The Solar-Hydrogen Alternative in 1975, one of the first detailed description of what a solar-hydrogen economy would look like.
Mainstream career
Bockris (1923–2013) was one of the significant figures of twentieth-century electrochemistry, and the great majority of his work is entirely conventional. Born in Johannesburg and raised in England, he took his doctorate at Imperial College London, where he ran a research group in the late 1940s — Martin Fleischmann was among the graduate students who joined its discussions. He moved to the University of Pennsylvania in 1953, then to the Flinders University of South Australia, and to Texas A&M in 1978, where he held a Distinguished Professorship until his retirement in 1997.
His textbook Modern Electrochemistry , written with A. K. N. Reddy and first published in 1970, became one of the discipline's standard works and remains in print. He published several hundred papers across five decades on electrode kinetics, the structure of the electrical double layer, electrocatalysis, corrosion and fuel cells, and supervised a very large number of doctoral students.

John W. McAlister is an American consulting engineer based in Delray Beach, Florida, who has built table-top mechanical experiments intended to test the equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass.
Work
McAlister's first paper, " A Mechanical Test of the Equivalence Principle " (1992), reported an anomalous energy loss in a magnetically suspended body revolving inside a spinning centrifuge, the centrifuge providing a pseudo-gravitational field.
Its successor, " A Special-Case Test of Newton's Second Law of Motion " (2010), was designed to reproduce the effect in a simpler configuration whose retarding forces could be enumerated. A half-kilogram weight falls on a wire over a pulley, drawing a carriage of 1.0 to 4.5 kg along a marble runway on three roller bearings; a microsecond timer records the fall. From thousands of runs over six months he reports an "inertial force index" — the factor by which the carriage's inertia must be increased for the force balance to close — of between 1.030 and 1.118, and concludes that gravitational and inertial mass should not be treated as equal.
The paper's chief merit is that it publishes the full grid of results across eight carriage masses and four drop lengths rather than a single figure, which is what makes the systematics visible: the discrepancy grows as the carriage gets lighter and as the drop gets longer, neither of which a modification of Newton's second law could produce.
He presented the 2010 work at the 17th Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference .

Since the late 1990s he has argued for a physical ether , against special relativity , and for an account of gravity in which matter absorbs a small fraction of the ether particles passing through it, producing an inward drift he calls the ether-wind .

Persson's papers return to a small set of connected claims, developed and restated across many short pieces.
An ether that is neither autonomous nor entrained. His distinctive move is to reject the terms of the usual debate. The ether itself is not dragged, but two of its properties are — gravity and the ether-wind — and these "follow a celestial body like shadows". The ether consists of non-colliding particles moving at c , which he describes as "not a gas but a special state of aggregation".

José Francisco García Juliá is a Spanish independent researcher based in Valencia who works on alternative interpretations of the cosmological redshift . He is known for proposing non-expansion, " tired light " mechanisms in which light loses energy through interaction with other electromagnetic radiation, offering an account of the redshift of distant galaxies that does not require an expanding universe.
Biography
García Juliá works independently in Valencia. Since 2007 he has published a long series of short papers — more than fifty — chiefly on the electronic preprint archive viXra , together with work in the alternative-cosmology journal Apeiron: Studies in Infinite Nature . He presented at the 17th Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference in 2010.
No institutional affiliation appears on his papers, which give only a Valencia address.
Work
Redshift
García Juliá's central claim concerns the origin of the redshift observed in the light of distant galaxies. In place of the standard reading, on which the redshift measures the expansion of the universe, he argues for a tired light mechanism: photons lose energy gradually in transit through an exponential decay E ( t ) = E (0)e − t /τ , so that the Hubble constant is reinterpreted as the inverse of an energy-loss time constant rather than as a rate of expansion.
The distinctive feature of his treatment is that one mechanism is made to cover two phenomena. Light crossing intergalactic space interacts with the microwave background and acquires the cosmological redshift; light generated inside a quasar interacts with that object's much denser radio-wave field and acquires an intrinsic redshift on the way out. A filled shell of eight electrons in the Lucas packing model: two great circles of four toroidal ring electrons each, their magnetic axes alternating around each circle. Figure 5 from "A Physical Model for Atoms and Nuclei — Part 1" (2002).
Joseph C. Lucas is an American physicist and independent researcher, and the author — with his father Charles W. Lucas, Jr. — of the physical geometrical packing model of the atom and nucleus that forms the atomic-structure component of the Common Sense Science programme.
His contribution is a specific and unusually concrete one. Taking Bergman 's toroidal ring electron as given, Lucas asked what happens when such objects — real, finite-sized rings of circulating charge, each carrying a magnetic dipole — are packed around a nucleus. Using combinatorial geometry constrained by results he obtained from physical experiments with ring magnets , he derived the sizes of the successive electron shells as 2, 8, 18 and 32 — the shell structure actually exhibited by the Periodic Table — together with an argument for why the table has exactly seven periods and no shell of 50. The same packing analysis was then applied to protons and neutrons, yielding the nuclear magic numbers and an account of nuclide spin.
He introduced the model in Galilean Electrodynamics in 1996, and it was reprinted and extended in the Common Sense Science quarterly Foundations of Science between 2002 and 2003.
Biography
Joseph C. Lucas is the son of Dr. Charles William Lucas, Jr. , the physicist known for the universal electrodynamic force law and a co-founder of Common Sense Science ; the two collaborated on all of Joseph's principal papers. He lives in Temple Hills, Maryland.

Józef Kajfosz (born 11 February 1933) is a Polish–Czech physicist who spent his professional career in experimental nuclear physics before turning, as an independent researcher, to questions concerning particle composition , special relativity , and the foundations of physics.
Education
Graduated from Brno University , 1956
PhD, Institute of Nuclear Physics , Řež, 1968
Biography
Kajfosz was born in 1933 in Czechoslovakia. After graduating from Brno University he joined the Institute of Nuclear Physics in Řež, near Prague, where he remained until 1972. In 1972 he moved to the Institute of Nuclear Physics in Cracow, Poland, working there until 1993. He subsequently settled in Cracow.
Scientific contributions
During his time at Řež, Kajfosz carried out research in nuclear spectroscopy, studying beta and gamma radiation using the neutron beam of a nuclear reactor. After moving to Cracow he worked on the application of nuclear methods across various branches of science, in particular Particle-Induced X-ray Emission (PIXE) analysis using the proton beam of a cyclotron. He is a coauthor of more than 100 published scientific papers. Together with W. Kwiatek he developed a widely cited method for the non-polynomial approximation of the background in X-ray spectra, a technique used in the fitting and analysis of PIXE data.
Outside his professional field, Kajfosz has pursued an independent interest in particle composition and the foundations of physics. Describing himself as neither a theorist nor a particle expert, and treating the subject as a hobby, he has proposed an alternative model of particle composition and interactions and has published a series of papers offering critical remarks on special relativity, the principle of relativity, and the role of the ether.

Title Just Which Equivalence Principle Do You Believe In?
Author(s) James Carter
Keywords Equivalence Principle
Published 1998
Abstract
The Pound-Rebka experiment is often presented as an experimental proof of the Equivalence Principle. However, careful examination of this experiment reveals five different ways that its results can be interpreted. While all are compatible with the Equivalence Principle. each offers a distinct view of both gravity and the nature of the photons being measured. As a result, the Equivalence Principle has a different meaning and definition fur each interpretation. After each of these five possibilities has been presented, the listeners will be asked the following questions for discussion. Does anyone have a different explanation of this experiment? Which Equivalence Principle do you believe in? Since only one of these explanations can be correct, does anyone know of an experimental method by which one of these could be shown to be superior over the others and thus established as the true reality?

He describes himself as an amateur, and his papers are unpublished pieces circulated through the Natural Philosophy Alliance rather than journal articles.
His work is more coherent than the three separate titles below suggest: they are three applications of one idea.

Top-down instead of bottom-up

search_text:
The Kennedy–Thorndike experiment was an interferometer test carried out by Roy J. Kennedy and Edward M. Thorndike and published in 1932, designed to detect a dependence of the speed of light on the velocity of the apparatus rather than on its orientation . It is the companion to the Michelson–Morley experiment , and the two together are what actually pin down the Lorentz transformation — a point that is easy to miss, and that a good deal of the argument catalogued on this wiki turns on.
What it did, and why the difference matters
The 1887 Michelson–Morley apparatus had two arms of equal length and was rotated. A rotation test asks whether light takes different times along different directions. If the arms are equal, an isotropic slowing of clocks in the moving frame cancels out of the comparison, so the experiment is sensitive to length contraction but blind to time dilation.
Kennedy and Thorndike therefore built an interferometer with arms of deliberately unequal length — differing by about 16 cm, the largest difference their light source's coherence would tolerate — and did not rotate it. Instead they left it fixed and photographed the fringe pattern over months, letting the Earth's rotation and its orbital motion change the instrument's velocity. Under the Lorentz–FitzGerald contraction hypothesis alone , with no time dilation, an unequal-arm interferometer's fringe pattern should shift as the speed of the apparatus changes. The apparatus was mounted in vacuum in a temperature-controlled bath, since with unequal arms a fraction of a degree of drift would swamp the effect. They found no shift attributable to the Earth's motion.
The logical structure was made explicit by H. P. Robertson in 1949 and refined by Mansouri and Sexl in 1977. Three classes of experiment are needed:
Michelson–Morley constrains the dependence of light speed on the direction of travel — length contraction.

Title Kepler's Second Law and Conservation of Angular Momentum
Author(s) Pari Spolter
Keywords kepler, gravity, planets
Published 2011
Abstract
Kepler's second law is calculated for 18 planets and asteroids. It is shown that equal areas are swept in equal intervals of time only near the perihelion (P) and the aphelion (A). A highly significant relation between the ratio of the area swept at the average of P and A to the area swept at semimajor (S) in the same interval of time and the eccentricity is presented. The equation is ratio = a⋅eb+c with a = −0.617, b = 2, and c = 1.00. The correlation coefficient is 0.9975. The ratio is equal to (1 - e^2)^1/2 , which is equal to sin θ, where θ is the smaller angle between the two vectors v and r. Angular momentum is a vector perpendicular to the plane formed by v and r and is conserved, indicating that there is no torque in the direction vertical to the plane of the orbits.

Mohammad Shafiq Khan challenges the mainstream and presents a critique of relativity. Hosted by Roger Anderton.
Summary
Roger J Anderton took up the open challenge to Einstein's relativity posted online by Mohammad Shafiq Khan , an independent researcher with a master's in physics, and ran it past ChatGPT. Khan's central charge is that Einstein's 1905 paper rests on trickery: Voigt's transformation was a mathematical possibility, Lorentz altered it by introducing the gamma factor, and the result is a manipulation rather than a physical argument — so that nature was made subservient to mathematics, and relativity, the big bang and spacetime all descend from it. His papers appeared in the Indian Journal of Science and Technology in 2012 and as an open letter to physicists, and, as Anderton noted, were ignored regardless of having been published.
Right from a certain point of view
Asked flatly whether Khan is right, the assistant said no. Asked whether Khan is right from a certain point of view, it said yes — and that second answer was the talk. Anderton framed it, as he had before, with Obi-Wan Kenobi's "what I told you was true, from a certain point of view", offering it not as a defence of relative truth but as a diagnosis of what relativity has done to the idea of truth.
The concession, once drawn out, was fairly substantial. "This booklet is a compilation exploring the history of kinetic gravitational theories in the very prolific period spanning the 18th and 19th Centuries. Natural philosophers before, during and after Isaac Newton attempted to determine the cause of gravitation without resorting to the mystical notion of "action-at-a-distance". Historians of science often state incorrectly that Newton's Principia (1687) leads to the idea that gravitational force can act across empty space without any medium between bodies. Yet, Newton's rejection of action-at-a-distance was clearly stated in his letter to Richard Bentley in 1693... Isaac Newton, to his credit, did not reject the idea of a medium, but neither did he discuss it in the Principia (first edition).
"Other philosophers did develop completely novel theories of how gravity acts by endowing a universal medium (aether) in space with certain properties. Generally, kinetic gravity theories fall into one of two classes: those in which the aether acts as waves or those in which this medium acts as corpuscles or particles. (I would not rule out a third as-yet undefined class, however)
"The main purpose of this booklet is an exact reprint of " Kinetic Theories of Gravitation " by William B. Taylor as it first appeared in Annual Report of the Board of Regents, Smithsonian Institution, V31 , pp. 205-282..." - From the Introduction
Ford's reprint includes some additional material and comments. See http://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Kinetic_Theories_of_Gravitation for full text of the original.

Kipley A. Farr , known as Kip Farr, is an American author and independent researcher in Weber County, Utah, who writes on cosmology and its relationship to religion. His book Cosmology and Religion (1994) sets the scientific and the Christian theological account of the origin and nature of the universe alongside one another. In the World Science Database, from which this wiki's membership records are drawn, Farr gives his research interest as the Electric Universe — the alternative cosmology holding that electric currents and plasma, rather than gravity acting alone, are the dominant organizing forces in the cosmos.

Farr lives in the Ogden area of northern Utah. His World Science Database record places him at North Ogden; other listings give the neighboring town of Farr West. He holds no university or institutional post, and his work belongs to the tradition of independent inquiry this wiki documents: writing outside the professional academy on questions that sit between physical cosmology, theology and the origin of the universe.
Farr is recorded in the database as a supporter member rather than as a presenting researcher, and as attending the 19th Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference , held 25–28 July 2012 at the Albuquerque Marriott Pyramid North in Albuquerque, New Mexico — one of the largest of the NPA 's annual meetings, with 125 papers and some 220 recorded participants.
