Kjell Prytz is a Swedish physicist at Mälardalen University in Västerås, and the author of Electrodynamics: The Field-Free Approach (Springer, 2015) — an undergraduate textbook that builds electromagnetism from the direct interaction of charges rather than from fields, and treats Weber 's force law as a working tool rather than a historical curiosity.
He is an unusual figure in this catalogue in one respect: the heterodoxy is not at the margin of his career but inside a peer-reviewed Springer textbook series, and it sits alongside a substantial record in mainstream experimental particle physics.
Career and mainstream work
Prytz has been a senior lecturer and docent in physics since 1996, first at the University of Gävle — the affiliation recorded on this wiki — and latterly at Mälardalen University, where he works in the School of Education, Culture and Communication. He remains active, publishing in the American Journal of Physics as recently as 2026.
His earlier career was in high-energy physics, on the NMC muon experiment at CERN and on ZEUS at HERA, together with work on the ATLAS first-level calorimeter trigger. He is best known in that field for a single-author theoretical paper: "Approximate determination of the gluon density at low x from the F 2 scaling violations" ( Physics Letters B 311, 1993), which gives what is now generally called the Prytz approximation and has been cited on the order of a hundred times. He extended it to next-to-leading order the following year and returned to it in later papers.
He has since moved substantially into physics education research, and more recently into forestry and climate questions.

Lambda CDM Cosmology overview and Roundtable Discussion was a live session presented by Harry Hamlin Ricker on 21 September 2024 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
The Standard Cosmology known as Lambda CDM Cosmology will be presented and discussed in a roundtable format, where participants are invited to join in the discussions.
Summary
This was a survey rather than an argument: Harry Ricker set out what the standard cosmological model actually says, in the belief that one cannot criticise a theory whose vocabulary one does not share. He ran it as a roundtable, pausing after each section for comment, and much of the value is in the interruptions.
What the model is
Lambda-CDM — the concordance model, in Sabine Hossenfelder's phrase — is big-bang cosmology with two additions. Lambda is the cosmological constant, associated with the vacuum or dark energy, introduced to account for the expansion accelerating; CDM is cold dark matter, undetectable except through its gravitational effect on luminous matter. It assumes general relativity and an expanding metric space, a direction and universal scale for time, and the cosmological principle.
Ricker flagged his own difficulties as he went. What is meant by metric space is never made clear — to him it is an abstraction, an empty void, and what exactly is expanding is unexplained. He traced the model's shape through the diagrams: an initial flash, inflation by a factor of some 10 27 , a long coasting period during which galaxies form, and a late acceleration attributed to dark energy. When Larry was 22, he made several visits to the 1937 Worlds Fair at Treasure Island with his brother Sid. There, Larry saw a closed television transmission for the first time. Larry also saw an automobile motor rotate under a strobe light which made a spinning object appear to stand still. Larry was also interested in farm stock and the other amusements of the day.

Laurent Hollo (born 7 August 1967) is a French-Canadian computer security analyst living in Carignan, Quebec, whose papers to the Natural Philosophy Alliance between 2010 and 2012 propose a standardised taxonomy of physical quantities based on their dimensions in space and time.
Work
Hollo's project is organisational rather than revisionary, and he is explicit that his formalism is "fully compatible with current knowledge". His starting observation is that the equations of different branches of physics share a recurring shape which the separate notational conventions of each branch conceal — so that the same role is played by quantities with unrelated symbols, while one name may cover quantities playing different roles.
His scheme arranges every physical quantity on a matrix whose axes count powers of length and of time, so that neighbouring cells differ by one factor of a metre or a second. Quantities are then sorted into four domains — gravitic, thermic, electric and magnetic — alongside two special ones for space-time and for energy; into four groups according to whether they carry, promote or oppose the transfer of energy; and into generic roles — charge, current, flux, potential, field, resistivity, permittivity and so on — defined without reference to any particular domain.
The organising axiom is a single generalised form of Ohm's law: Effect = Cause / Opposition . Because roles are defined generically, the scheme implies quantities that are unfamiliar or unnamed in one domain but standard in another, such as a gravitic permittivity or a current of heat; Hollo notes that most of these already exist under other names. Abstract
Urbain Le Verrier became famous by discovering Neptune from its effect on the orbit of Uranus. He turned his attention to Mercury, publishing a preliminary paper in 1841 and a definitive paper in 1859 on the Theory of Mercury. He discovered an unexplained shift in the perihelion of Mercury, which he attributed to the presence of a small unknown planet he called Vulcan, which was never found. The results were corrected in 1895 by Simon Newcomb, who increased the anomalous shift by about 10% but offered no new explanation for it. Albert Einstein, at the end of his 1916 paper on General Relativity, derived a specific solution for the perihelion shift which exactly matched the discrepancy. Dating from the 1947 Clemence review paper, that explanation and precise value have remained to the present time, being completely accepted by theoretical physicists as absolutely true. The highly technical 1859 Le Verrier paper was written in French, and astronomers and theorists have gone on from the study of the Solar System to the study of the Universe. The partial translation given here throws light on Le Verrier's analysis and thought processes, and points out that the masses he used for Earth and Mercury are quite different from present day values, possibly leading to a different fit to the old data. A 1924 paper by a professor of Celestial Mechanics critiques both the Einstein and the Le Verrier analyses, and a 1993 paper gives a different and better fit to some of Le Verrier's data. Nonetheless, the effect of errors in planet masses seems to give new condition equations that do not change the perihelion discrepancy by a large amount. Lee Smolin (born June 6, 1955) is an American theoretical physicist and a founding faculty member of the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics in Waterloo, Ontario. He is an adjunct professor of physics at the University of Waterloo and a member of the graduate faculty of the philosophy department at the University of Toronto. Smolin is a mainstream physicist best known for his work on quantum gravity and for his widely-read books criticising the dominance of String Theory in fundamental physics and calling for a greater diversity of approaches — a theme that has made his work frequently cited in dissident-physics circles.

Abstract
In electromagnetism, Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced electric current is such as to oppose the change that causes it. Lenz's law would therefore appear to be closely related to the law of conservation of energy, apart from the fact that it operates in conjunction with non-conservative forces. It will now be shown that Lenz's law is a manifestation of the ongoing transfusion of aether between the positron sources and the electron sinks of the luminiferous medium. Energy in the form of pressurized aether is drawn up from the luminiferous medium by a pumping mechanism which sometimes resembles an Archimedes' screw. This pumping mechanism will involve the simultaneous sinking of already existing pressurized aether.
Overview
Lenz's Law is a five-page paper by David Tombe dated 15 December 2008 and published in the General Science Journal . It is one of several by the same author in this catalogue, and it shares its constituent model with them; see also The Double Helix and the Compound Centrifugal Force , Radiation Pressure and Einstein's Mass-Energy Equivalence Formula , The Centrifugal Force Argument and Newton's Cradle and the Transmission Line .
The paper contains no equations. Its argument is that Lenz's law — that an induced current opposes the change producing it — is "a manifestation of the ongoing transfusion of aether between the positron sources and the electron sinks of the luminiferous medium."

Fields Chemical engineering
Leslie C. Case (September 11, 1930 – July 15, 2010) was an American chemical engineer, inventor, and independent researcher who, in the later part of his career, became known within the Cold Fusion community for a gas-phase process he called "catalytic fusion."
Biography
Case was born in Tulsa, Oklahoma, on September 11, 1930. He spent his career as a chemical engineer and inventor, holding patents in the field of polymer chemistry; his work on polyether polyols was the subject of the reported patent-office case Case v. CPC International, Inc. (U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, 1984). Case had a broad range of interests over his life, including gemstone cutting, the recovery of shale oil, the growing of grapes and production of wine in Australia, and alternative energy. He died at his home in Newfields, New Hampshire, on July 15, 2010, at the age of 79.
Education
Several degrees, including a Doctorate of Science — Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Work
In his later years Case turned to low-energy nuclear reaction research, which he preferred to describe as "catalytic fusion" rather than "cold fusion." His approach used a sealed container holding a precious-metal catalyst supported on activated carbon together with deuterium gas. In demonstrations he loaded activated carbon, including coconut-shell carbon, with roughly 0.1 to 0.5 percent by weight of a precious metal, reporting that palladium at about 0.4 percent worked best. When the sealed cell was pressurized with deuterium (on the order of a few atmospheres) and heated to roughly 200 °C, Case reported excess heat and the accumulation of helium-4, which he interpreted as a signature of deuterium-deuterium fusion.

Title Let's Keep It Simple
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) Arnold G Gulko
Keywords hydrogen atom, fine structure constant, electron structure , quantum mechanics , energy shell
Published 2008
No. of pages 11
Abstract
We exist in a particulate nature in which there are only two particles which possess significant mass at rest and long term independent stability. These are the electron and the proton. So when we consider our particulate nature from the perspective of the independently stable particles which abound around us, the nuclear zoo of particles in that nature can be simplified by focusing on only these two.
Overview
Arnold Gulko's paper is a compact statement of a programme he developed at length in The Vortex Theory, Revised (2006) and in Infinite Energy magazine. Its strategy is reduction: of all the particles catalogued by physics, only two have both significant rest mass and long-term independent stability, the electron and the proton ; the simplest association of those two is the hydrogen atom ; and so the whole of the particulate world can be tested against one question, whether we understand hydrogen. Gulko's answer is that we do not, and that the failure is not a gap but a foundational error.
The error, on his account, is the assumption that the electron is a structureless point. He argues that the electron must instead be a physically extended, two-sided object whose size is set by its energy content, and that the size of the hydrogen atom, the fine structure constant and the Rydberg energy all follow from that size once one supposes the two particles are held apart by a "double energy shell" of energy circulating between them. Where the mainstream sees a mathematically successful theory whose interpretive difficulties are secondary, Gulko sees calculations built on assumptions he considers demonstrably wrong: "when incorrect assumptions enable correct calculation we have chaos instead of science". I have decided to go public with my work and my claims this time. I am doing this for two reasons. (1) I now have a patent on file (filed Oct 19, 1997) for the process, and (2) The results to date have been less than expected. I could use some feedback.
Overview
This is a short open letter (dated 22 November 1997, published in New Energy News in January 1998) in which Frank J Znidarsic describes an experiment and asks the cold fusion community for feedback and prior art. It is candid to an unusual degree — Znidarsic states plainly that "the results to date have been less than expected" and, at the end, that "the latest tests showed no anomalous energy."
Its interest is chiefly historical . The empirical relationship Znidarsic reports here in rough form is the seed of the theoretical programme he pursued for the next two decades — his claim of a fixed " velocity of the transitional quantum state " underlying cold fusion, antigravity and force unification, developed in his later papers such as " The Control of the Natural Forces " and " Elementary Anti-Gravity ".

Znidarsic's premise is that cold-fusion electrodes behave as room-temperature superconductors , and that the fusion process is driven by the mechanical vibration of a superconducting structure at a characteristic frequency. He notes that CETI's active beads, about 1,000 ångströms thick, and Talbot and Scott Chubb 's fine-grained palladium, are structures of a particular small size, and proposes that the operating frequency is set by that size.

The Letts-Cravens experiment is described by M. Srinivasan in his Report on the ICCF-10 (accomplished in August-2003). At the end of the experiment's description, Srinivasan says: "Several theoreticians are presently trying to model the possible mechanism of coupling between the laser and the deuterium loaded lattice". However, what sort of models can be tried? As it is known, according to Quantum Mechanics cold fusion cannot exist. Therefore, for the explanation of the results obtained in several cold fusion experiments, it is necessary to introduce new principles missing in Quantum Mechanics. However, only new principles are not enough for the enterprise. Actually cold fusion needs a new model of neutron, a new nuclear model, and a new hydrogen model of atom. New principles are proposed in the author's Quantum Ring Theory, as for instance the spin-fusion, the accordion-effect, the contraction of the ether, etc. The main models proposed are the following:
a new model of neutron n=p+e, where the electron is tied to a quark up of the proton through the spinfusion phenomenon,
a New Nuclear Model of Hexagonal Floors, where the accordion-effect is responsible by several nuclear properties, as for example the changing of the nuclei distortions, measured by the nuclear electric quadrupole moment.
a new hydrogen atom, where the contraction of the ether works into the electrosphere. Here we analyze how these models, working by new principles, can help us understand the results obtained in the Letts-Cravens experiment.

Keywords light, photon, wave–particle duality, luminic motion, aether, propagation, aberration, Particle Model
Light is the most contested phenomenon in physics. Everyone agrees on what light does — it propagates in straight lines, refracts, diffracts, interferes, polarises, carries energy in discrete amounts, and travels at a definite and very large speed. What no one has satisfactorily explained is what light is , and what — if anything — it travels in .
This article is about the nature and propagation of light . Two closely related questions are treated at length elsewhere on this wiki and are only summarised here: the constant c and whether it is invariant is the subject of Speed of Light , and the quantum of light is the subject of Photon .
The literature collected on this wiki contains some 260 papers bearing on light. They do not agree with one another. They include corpuscular models in which light is literally made of particles, wave models in which it is a disturbance of a real medium, models in which it is neither and models in which it is both, entrained-aether accounts of its propagation, ballistic and emission theories, and detailed proposals about how light interacts with gravity and with matter. What unites them is a refusal of the standard answer that light is "both a wave and a particle" and that the question stops there. The researchers documented here treat that formula as a contradiction given a name rather than an explanation, and the persistence of the contradiction for over a century as evidence that the underlying model is wrong, not that nature is inscrutable.

Abstract
A survey of light speed measurements suggests that light speed can be calibrated to be equal to the standard speed of light assumption for distances up to 12000 miles about, but that for greater distances, such as that between the Earth and spacecraft, the results are not so clear. Also that our knowledge of the speed of light delay from stars is confounded with the speed of light delay between lenses and with the effects of light intensity at the lens or ccd array etc. Thus, the actual speed of light delay from astronomical distances is not as obvious as commonly believed.
Overview
Ralph Sansbury's paper is the observational half of a long-running programme in which light is not a travelling thing at all. There are, on his account, neither aether waves nor photons crossing the gap between emitter and receiver; there are only instantaneous electrostatic forces, and what we measure as the speed of light is the time a receiver takes to build up a detectable oscillation of charge under those forces. The delay, in his formulation, is not r / c but kr / c with k ≤ 1, and c 2 is "a measure of elasticity of charge polarization inside electrons and atomic nuclei" rather than a propagation speed.
The immediate consequence is that delay should depend on signal strength as well as distance, since a stronger field drives the receiver above the noise floor sooner. Abstract
Article 1 and article 6 point out that principle of constancy of the light velocity is deficient. The conclusion of this paper is that light velocity has superposition feature: in the vacuum, light wave has no oscillating medium to propagate, and the mass of light field is zero, motion of field does not need the action of force, so the motion of light is a radiation, and it is a vector c 0 which is relative to the radiation velocity of light source, this is a relative velocity which is relative to the radiation source, but not the absolute velocity, and it obeys superposition principle of velocity vector, when the relative velocity v exists between light source and observer, the relative light velocity that observer measures is c = c 0 + v , and such conclusion indicates: light velocity obeys Galilean principle of relativity.
Overview

The Lorentz force is the force exerted on a charged particle by electric and magnetic fields, F = q ( E + v × B ). Together with Maxwell's equations , which govern the fields themselves, it constitutes classical electromagnetic theory : the equations say what the fields do, and the Lorentz force says what the fields do to charges .
The standard account
The expression is older than its name. Hermann Grassmann published the equivalent force between current elements in 1845; Maxwell gave the form in the Treatise (1873); Oliver Heaviside wrote it for a moving point charge in 1889; and Hendrik Lorentz made it the foundation of his electron theory in the 1890s, which is how it acquired his name.
Its content is straightforward and heavily used. The electric term acts along E regardless of the particle's motion. The magnetic term acts perpendicular to both the velocity and B , does no work, and bends a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field into a circle of radius mv ⁄ qB — the basis of the cyclotron, the mass spectrometer, magnetic focusing in electron optics, and the operation of every electric motor.
Two features are important for what follows. First, the Lorentz force is not derivable from Maxwell's equations; it is an independent postulate of the theory, added alongside them. Second, the Grassmann–Lorentz form is not the only candidate. The original force law of André-Marie Ampère , published between 1820 and 1825, contains a component acting along the direction of current flow, which Grassmann's does not. For a complete closed circuit the two laws give identical results, so ordinary laboratory and engineering practice cannot distinguish them. They differ only for isolated current elements — that is, where a circuit is broken, deformed, or destroyed.
On this wiki
The Lorentz force is one of the most heavily contested items in the literature collected here, and the objections are of several distinct kinds. The broader picture is set out at Electromagnetism

"Lorentz Invariance" is a short white paper by Ricardo L Carezani answering a question from a physicist at the University of Virginia: "I glanced at the page. It seemed interesting, but I see no mention of AD allowing Maxwell's equations to remain invariant. Did I miss this??"
Overview
Carezani's answer is that the question does not arise. Autodynamics discards the two frames in relative motion on which the notion of invariance is built, replaces the Lorentz equations with his own, and treats the phenomenon and the observer as forming a single physical system. Once that is done, he argues, "the concept of 'invariance' becomes meaningless."
The argument
Invariance as a semantic question
Carezani's substantive point is that "invariance" as usually stated conceals a change in what is being described. Maxwell's equations at rest, transformed to a system in relative motion, are the same as saying that the phenomenon they describe is in motion with respect to the observer. Working the classical equations into general form, he notes the standard result: an observer in motion who sees an electric field E will also see a magnetic field H . His question is whether that counts as invariance. "The equations are 'invariant,' but a different phenomenon appears when the observer, or the phenomenon, is in motion. Are the equations 'invariant'?"
The Autodynamics form
He then applies the Autodynamics treatment to the same case and reports a result that differs in one respect: "These two equations are conceptually equal with the exception that in the SR equation, the coefficient Z divides the equation and in AD, the coefficient multiplies the equation!"

Abstract
A Galilean-invarient interaction Lagrangian of a charged particle moving in an electromagnetic field in free space is obtained assuming that a natural (i.e., preferred) reference frame exists for the field and that all uniformly moving observers can determine their velocities with respect to this frame. From this Lagrangian, a Lorentz force law is derived. From this Lorentz force law, Poisson's equation, and the principle of conservation of electric charge, Lorentz's version of Maxwell's equations in free space for an observer moving uniformly through the ether is obtained. These modified Maxwell's equations, the field quantities they contain, and the wave equations derivable from them are shown to be Galilean invariant. They predict experimentally-obtained electromagnetic forces on charged particles in free space if the natural frame (i.e., ether) is entrained by the earth.

Low Level Measurements is a four-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It is the seventh part of the ten-part handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and at four pages it is one of the two longest practical articles in the set.
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
Low-level measurement is the art of measuring voltages, currents, charges and resistances small enough that the measurement apparatus is a significant part of the phenomenon. It has a substantial professional literature — the standard work is Keithley Instruments' Low Level Measurements Handbook , which shares this article's title and was in its sixth edition at the time — and it is relevant here because the anomalies claimed in this field are characteristically small differences between large numbers, which is the regime in which the errors below are decisive.
The noise floor
There is a floor below which no amount of care helps, and it is set by physics rather than by the instrument. Johnson–Nyquist noise, present in any resistance at any temperature above absolute zero, has a root-mean-square voltage of √(4 kTRB ) — about 1.3 microvolts across a one-megohm resistor in a 1 Hz bandwidth at room temperature, and growing as the square root of both resistance and bandwidth. Shot noise sets a corresponding limit on current measurement, and 1/ f or flicker noise dominates at low frequencies, which is exactly where slow drifting measurements live.

Lucy Haye , Ph.D., is a representative of the Society for the Advancement of Autodynamics (SAA), based in Long Beach, California, and a co-author of papers on Autodynamics , the alternative relativistic mechanics developed by Ricardo Carezani .
Biography
Public sources identify Lucy Haye as SAA's representative, and her papers carry a Long Beach address in the same city where Carezani lived and worked. Her published work appears through the Society and its website, autodynamics.org; no independent biographical record has been located, and the wiki does not have a date or place of birth for her.
Work
Haye's contribution to the Autodynamics literature falls into two parts: expository work on the theory's foundations, and its applications to astrophysics.
Foundations
The Superfluous System is her restatement of the central Autodynamics objection to the Lorentz transformation without algebraic machinery. Beginning from a phenomenon at A and an observer at B , she argues that relativity already holds between the two, and that the third system Lorentz introduces — in which A is at rest — carries no physical information. Her technical claim is that the transformation then divides a constant distance by a factor that shrinks with velocity, so that a fixed separation appears to grow, and that this manufactured increase is the artificial energy the neutrino was later invented to remove. The paper works a numerical example taken from Feynman 's Lectures on Physics , and a footnote records that Carezani first framed the argument this way to explain it to the photographer Herman Leonard before a portrait session.
Astrophysical applications
Three papers apply Carezani's pico-graviton theory of gravitation to observed anomalies.

"Moon Increasing Distance" , published at autodynamics.org as "Lunar Distancing" and dated 21 August 1999, is a short paper by Ricardo L Carezani and Lucy Haye applying the Autodynamics pico-graviton mechanism to the measured recession of the Moon from the Earth.
Overview
Lunar laser ranging, using the retroreflectors left by Apollo 11 and later missions, shows the Moon receding from the Earth at about 3.8 cm per year. The orthodox explanation is tidal: the Earth's tidal bulge leads the Moon, torques it forward, and transfers angular momentum from the Earth's rotation to the lunar orbit. Carezani and Haye argue instead that most of the recession is the same effect that produces the extra gravitational tug on the Pioneer spacecraft, and that only a small residue is tidal.
The argument
The Moon as a third body
The paper's framing is that the Earth–Moon–Sun system is a three-body problem with no closed solution, and that Pioneer 10/11, Galileo and Ulysses are similar: each "falls" towards the Sun–Earth direction at the anomalous 8 . 5 × 1 0 − 8 cm/s 2 reported by NASA. The Moon, on this reading, is a third body falling in the solar direction too — except that the Earth retains it, so that the fall shows up not as an acceleration towards the Sun but as a steadily increasing Earth–Moon distance.

search_text:
Mach's principle is the proposal that inertia is not a property a body possesses on its own, but an effect of that body's relation to all the other matter in the universe — so that local inertial frames are determined by the distant stars rather than by absolute space.
The standard account
The idea originates with the Austrian physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach (1838–1916), whose Die Mechanik in ihrer Entwicklung (1883) attacked Newton 's use of absolute space. Newton had argued from his rotating-bucket experiment that the curved surface of the water reveals rotation with respect to space itself. Mach replied that the experiment shows nothing of the kind: the water rotates with respect to the fixed stars, and nobody has performed — or could perform — the experiment with the rest of the universe removed. On Mach's reading, inertial resistance is a relational quantity, produced by the surrounding masses.
Einstein was strongly influenced by this argument and coined the term "Mach's principle" in 1918, hoping General Relativity would embody it. It does so only partially. General relativity does predict genuine relational effects — the Lense–Thirring frame dragging of 1918, measured by the LAGEOS satellites and by Gravity Probe B in 2011 — but it also admits solutions that are plainly non-Machian, notably Gödel's 1949 rotating universe and the empty Minkowski spacetime, in which inertial frames exist with no matter at all to define them. Brans and Dicke proposed their scalar–tensor theory in 1961 explicitly to make gravitation more Machian by tying the gravitational "constant" to the mass distribution; solar-system tests have since pushed its coupling parameter to values where it is observationally close to general relativity.
There is no agreed formulation of the principle. Physicists have catalogued a dozen or more inequivalent statements travelling under the same name, and whether general relativity satisfies any of them remains genuinely disputed inside mainstream

Abstract
The argument that Mach's principle and relativistic gravity lead to the expectation of transient fluctuations in the rest masses of objects when they are accelerated by external forces is briefly recapitulated. In appropriate circumstances such mass fluctuations can be employed to produce stationary forces (notwithstanding that in some frames of reference one may think such forces cancelled by other forces). A torsion pendulum experiment designed to search for such stationary forces is described. Small forces with the signatures expected were found. Tests of other causes that the signals might be attributed to are presented. These tests seem to rule out spurious effects as the source of the signals seen. Whether the forces seen can be brought to practical levels for rapid spacetime transport with clever engineering remains an open question.

Magnetism is the set of phenomena by which certain materials and moving charges attract or repel one another without contact: the behaviour of lodestone and iron, of the compass needle, of the electric current and the coil.
It is among the oldest observed effects in physics and among the least explained. Mainstream physics describes magnetism with great precision and declines to say what it is ; a large part of the literature catalogued on this wiki holds that this is not a limitation to be tolerated but the central problem, and that magnetism has a mechanical cause which can be shown.
The mainstream account
In the standard treatment magnetism is one aspect of a single electromagnetic field , unified with electricity by Maxwell in the 1860s.
A magnetic field B is produced by moving electric charge — a current in a wire, or the intrinsic circulation attributed to electrons within matter — and acts only on charge that is itself moving, through the Lorentz force, which is perpendicular both to the velocity and to the field. Because that force is always perpendicular to the motion, a magnetic field does no work on a moving charge; it changes direction, not speed.
Permanent magnetism in iron is attributed to electron spin rather than to orbital motion. Spin is treated as an intrinsic quantum property carrying a magnetic moment, and in a ferromagnet the exchange interaction — a quantum effect with no classical counterpart — aligns these moments across domains, so that their contributions add instead of cancelling.
There are no magnetic monopoles: cutting a magnet in half yields two magnets, and Maxwell's equations record this as ∇· B = 0. In special relativity the distinction between the electric and magnetic fields becomes frame-dependent — what one observer describes as a magnetic force another describes as electric — which is taken to show that the two are aspects of one object rather than two phenomena.

The consensus of oceanographers is that ocean waves are predominately caused by wind and supplemented by a few other sources. The following are said to be the causative forces behind ocean waves:
wind
gravitational pull of the sun and moon
wave shoaling (by entering shallower waters)
wave refractions (from bathymetry and currents)

gravity (dampening effect)
viscosity (dampening effect)
This paper intends to examine the efficacy of these forces in generating the gamut of ocean waves.

Malcolm Davidson is a researcher in electromagnetic theory and digital electronic design, known chiefly as a long-time collaborator of the British electronics engineer Ivor Catt . Together with Catt and David S. Walton he formed the "Catt, Davidson and Walton" partnership whose late-1970s papers and books challenged the conventional textbook treatment of Maxwell's displacement current.
Biography
Little biographical information about Davidson has been published. He became associated with Ivor Catt and Dr. David S. Walton during the 1970s, when the three worked jointly on the theory and practice of high-speed digital logic and on the electromagnetic behaviour of capacitors and transmission lines. As part of this research Davidson interviewed H. J. Josephs, one of the recognised authorities on the work of Oliver Heaviside, whose concept of "energy current" underlies the group's approach to electromagnetism.
Scientific contributions
Davidson's principal contribution lies in the group's re-examination of the capacitor. Walton had proposed that a capacitor is properly understood as a transmission line; Davidson argued that on this view the exponential RC charging waveform must be built up from a series of small discrete steps, a result which supported the transmission-line model of the capacitor. This line of reasoning led, in May 1976, to the group's conclusion that the concept of displacement current is unnecessary — a step central to what Catt later called "Theory C".
The resulting arguments were set out in two articles in Wireless World : "Displacement current" (December 1978) and "The History of Displacement Current" (March 1979), both co-authored by Catt, Davidson and Walton. The articles provoked considerable controversy among electrical engineers and physicists.

Manfred Geilhaupt is a German physicist associated with the Hochschule Niederrhein, the University of Applied Sciences at Krefeld and Mönchengladbach. He works on the origin of the physical constants, and in particular on the proposition that the rest mass of the electron, its charge and the fine structure constant can be derived rather than measured, by combining general relativity with the principles of thermodynamics.
Approach
Geilhaupt describes his programme as a "GR+TD" one — general relativity supplemented by thermodynamics, and specifically by the second law. He has argued that applying the second law to the action of an elementary mass-system at rest, such as a free electron, implies a mass-like uncertainty relation, and that the electron's rest mass follows from the Sommerfeld fine structure constant within such a scheme. He has extended the same treatment to the muon and the tau, under the heading of a "hidden thermodynamics" of the charged leptons, and has published a calculation of the fine structure constant from these principles.
A recurring theme is the set of large dimensionless numbers relating atomic to cosmological scales, in the tradition of Eddington and of Dirac's large numbers hypothesis. His two conference contributions recorded here address the two halves of that theme: one the relations among the measured constants themselves, the other the numerical span between the electron and the universe.

Abstract
The Earth was created in six days? This paraphrase from Genesis in the Bible may be surpassed in absurdity by fanciful "creation" theories in older civilizations of the world, but this belief has endured for 2,000 years without any physical evidence or logical reason to support it.
Overview
Myers — a retired U.S. Navy cryptologist who describes himself as "a non-scientist (cryptolinguist/codebreaker) with no degrees" — argues that the "hoax" of his title is not the Genesis account itself but its secular descendant: Kant's Nebular Hypothesis of 1755 as modified by Laplace in 1796, which holds that the Earth condensed rapidly from a cloud of gas and dust about 4.5 billion years ago and has kept the same size ever since. In his reading, a creation myth was replaced by a scientific one that shares its essential defect, a planet made all at once and thereafter fixed.
Against this he sets a growth model he calls "Accreation" — creation by accretion — in which a captured comet fragment in solar orbit grows continuously by external accretion of meteoritic mass and dust, by internal thermal expansion of a gravitationally heated core, and by volcanism that builds an atmosphere and surface water. The Earth on this account is "still a young planet and destined to continue growing forever". The paper's polemical centre is the rejection of subduction , which Myers calls "not only false, but physically impossible" and "one of the most egregious and avoidable blunders in the history of science". Its practical demand is that NOAA and the National Geodetic Survey recalculate the Earth's diameter and publish a revised datum to replace NAD83, from which a rate of expansion into the future could be computed.

Marcel Luttgens was a French independent researcher who argued that the redshift of galaxies and quasars is caused by a "gravitational braking" of light rather than by an expanding universe, and that special and general relativity are in consequence unnecessary and wrong.
He published one paper in the peer-reviewed dissident literature, and for roughly a decade ran a personal website that was as much an anthology of other people's dissident physics as a platform for his own.
Newton vs. Einstein (1998)
His one catalogued paper, Newton vs. Einstein , appeared in Apeiron 5 (1–2), January–April 1998, pages 25–30. The address given on it is Domaine de Séguret, Les Adrets-de-l'Estérel, in the Var.
The argument runs in two halves. First he takes from Steven Weinberg 's Gravitation and Cosmology (1972) the result that light leaving the centre of a static star of uniform density is redshifted, with z growing without limit as the compactness MG/R approaches its maximum value of 4/9. Then he redoes the calculation in classical mechanics, treating the universe as Euclidean, homogeneous, isotropic and static, and applying Gauss's theorem to a sphere of radius R . He obtains a redshift–distance relation
z = ( R / R 0 ) / (1 − R / R 0 ), equivalently R / R 0 = z /(1 + z )
where R 0 = c / K and K plays the part of the Hubble constant. Light loses energy in proportion to the distance travelled, so no expansion is required. He then argues that general relativity, applied to the same picture, caps the redshift at z = 2 — and since many galaxies and quasars exceed that, "general relativity is at variance with the observed facts, and thus cannot be correct."

Marek Pawłowski is a Polish theoretical physicist, associated with the Soltan Institute for Nuclear Studies in Warsaw and latterly with the University of Warsaw. He is best known for a programme developed in the 1990s with Ryszard Rączka : a unified model of the strong, electroweak and gravitational interactions built on local conformal symmetry , which reproduces the mass spectrum of the Standard Model without a dynamical Higgs field .
Unlike most figures catalogued on this wiki, Pawłowski published this work in the mainstream literature — Foundations of Physics , Physics Letters B , General Relativity and Gravitation , International Journal of Modern Physics A — and it was cited there. He appears here because of one paper given to a 1997 conference on special relativity, but that paper is a summary of a substantial published research programme rather than an isolated contribution.

The conformal programme

Taking that seriously means demanding local conformal symmetry , and the model Pawłowski and Rączka built on it is based on the symmetry group SU(3) × SU(2) L × U(1) × C , with C the local conformal group. Martin Fleischmann , FRS (born March 29, 1927 in Karlovy Vary , Czechoslovakia ) is an electrochemist at the University of Southampton and a Fellow of the Royal Society . He is best known for his controversial work with his colleague Stanley Pons on cold fusion using palladium in the 1980s and '90s. He was also the first observer of what was later called Surface Enhanced Raman Scattering .
On March 23, 1989 while they were researchers at the University of Utah , he and Stanley Pons announced "N-Fusion" which was quickly labeled by the press as cold fusion -- a result previously thought to be unattainable. After a short period of public acclaim, the pair were attacked widely for sloppy, unreproducible research and inaccurate results, as Fleischmann predicted they would be. Fleischmann, Pons and the researchers who replicated the effect remain convinced the effect is real, but sceptics who oppose them are convinced it is not.
In 1992, Fleischmann moved to France with Pons, to work at the IMRA laboratory (part of Technova Corporation, a subsidiary of Toyota); the laboratory closed in 1998 after exhausting a research investment of $12 million USD. The pair parted ways in 1995, and Fleischmann returned to Southampton, where he remained as of 1999. He has recently co-authored papers with researchers from the U.S. Navy and Italian national laboratories (INFN and ENEA)

Martin Grusenick is a German experimenter known on this wiki for a home-built Michelson–Morley interferometer experiment, documented in a 2009 online video, in which he reports that rotating the apparatus in a vertical plane produces a large fringe shift that he interprets as evidence of an aether wind directed downward into the Earth.
Biography
Little biographical detail about Grusenick is publicly available beyond his experimental work. He is described as a German experimenter who built and operated a laser interferometer in his own workshop. He came to attention within alternative-physics circles in 2009, when he published a video of his interferometer results online; the surrounding discussion took place largely on independent blogs and physics forums rather than in the academic literature.
Scientific work
Grusenick's contribution is a variation on the classic Michelson–Morley interferometer. Using a laser-based Michelson interferometer, he reports that rotating the apparatus in the horizontal plane, as in the original 1887 experiment, produces no observable shift in the interference fringes — consistent with the conventional null result.
His innovation was to mount the interferometer so that it could be rotated in a vertical plane (perpendicular to the Earth's surface). Grusenick reports that under vertical rotation a definite fringe shift becomes visible, moving in one direction and then the other over a full 360-degree rotation, with two positions (near a 45-degree angle) where the fringes appear stationary. He reports fringe shifts on the order of several to roughly eleven fringes depending on the apparatus and the time of day, and notes day–night variation in the magnitude.

Mass is the property by which a body resists being accelerated and by which it gravitates. Those are two distinct descriptions — inertial mass, defined by Newton's second law, and gravitational mass, defined by the law of gravitation — and the fact that they agree is a measured result rather than a definition.
Newton took the equality for granted; Loránd Eötvös tested it around 1900 with a torsion balance, and modern experiments, including the MICROSCOPE satellite mission, have confirmed it to roughly one part in 10 15 . Einstein made the equality a postulate, the equivalence principle, and built general relativity on it. Special relativity added a second relation: the energy content of a body at rest is E = mc 2 . In modern usage the mass of a particle means its invariant rest mass; the older notion of a "relativistic mass" increasing with speed has largely been abandoned in the professional literature in favour of speaking about relativistic momentum and energy, though it survives in textbooks.
What mass actually is remains open even on the mainstream account. The Higgs mechanism, confirmed in its broad outline by the 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson, supplies masses to the elementary particles, but the values are free parameters fitted to experiment rather than predicted. And the Higgs accounts for only a small fraction of the mass of ordinary matter: the great majority of a proton's mass is the binding energy of the field inside it. Nothing in the Standard Model explains why inertia exists at all.
On this wiki
Three arguments about mass run through the literature collected here.
Does mass increase with speed? Several researchers hold that it does not. Mass Photon Theory was a live session presented by Henri Corniere on 18 March 2023 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
A single ponderable tiny photon frees the mind of old ways of thinking and opens up new paths to a broad field of investigation where the very large can then be described and explained by the very small.
Summary
Henri Corniere 's presentation of his massive photon hypothesis, given a fortnight after James Keene previewed the paper for the society. Ian J Cowan hosted and advanced the six slides on request, Corniere having been unable to share his own screen.
He introduced himself briefly. He took a master's degree in science at Nantes and was dissatisfied enough with what he was taught — relativity, and a photon with no mass — that he did not continue in the academy, working instead as a field electronics engineer; retirement gave him the time to return to it. His statement of method was that nature does not care about our theories, that theories must fit the data rather than the reverse, and that the past mistakes have to be corrected before anything else can proceed.
The argument
The hypothesis is that the photon has a small rest mass and that space is filled with a photon gas, which he treats with the nineteenth-century kinetic theory of gases — asking explicitly whether that theory still works when the particle size drops by a factor of about a million.
He first established that the gas qualifies as ideal: stable particles in random motion, no charge, no interaction, very low pressure, very large interparticle distance.

Abstract
In (Assis 1998, pp. 241-249) and (Assis 1999, pp. 199-205) it was said that if we double the average matter density of the distant universe (galaxies), while keeping constant the matter density of the earth and all sizes and distances, the acceleration of free fall halves (that is, goes to 4.9m/s 2 instead of the usual 9.8m/s 2 ). Guala-Valverde concluded that in this case the acceleration of free fall should go to (9.8m/s 2 ) / 2, see (Guala-Valverde 1999a and 1999b, p. 25). But this was only due to a misunderstanding. Guala-Valverde was thinking on doubling the average inertial mass density of distant galaxies, while Assis was talking of doubling the average gravitational mass density of distant matter (see (Assis 1998, pp. 207, 211 and 246) or (Assis 1999, pp. 170, 174 or 204). This solves all misunderstandings. That is, Guala-Valverde and Assis agree that doubling the gravitational mass density of distant matter (while keeping unalterable Hubble's constant, the gravitational mass of the earth and its radius) will make the acceleration of free fall go to 4.9 m/s 2 . So our results are not clashing, it was all due to a misunderstanding.

The limit for the Kerr metric's horizon for non-rotating black holes is the Schwarzschild radius. By analyzing the horizon outcome for rotating and non-rotating black holes, using the Maxwell Analogy for Gravitation (or historically more correctly: the Heaviside Analogy for Gravitation, often called gravitomagnetism), I find that the Kerr metric must be incomplete in relation to the definition of 'event horizons' of rotating black holes. The Kerr metric only defines the horizons for light, but not the 'mass-horizons'. I find both the 'light-horizons' and the the 'mass-horizons' based on MAG. Moreover, I deduct the equatorial radii of rotating black holes. The probable origin of the minutes-lasting gamma bursts near black holes is unveiled as well. Finally, I deduct the spin velocity of black holes with a 'Critical Compression Radius'.
The deductions are based on the findings of my papers Did Einstein Cheat?' , On the Geometry of Rotary Stars and Black Holes , and On the Orbital Velocities Nearby Rotary Stars and Black Holes .

Abstract
In one of the earliest, and arguably the most eloquent, of the great texts advocating the systematic application of the empirical method, we find these wise words: ?Nor shall we be led to the doctrine of atoms, which implies the hypothesis of a vacuum and that of the unchangeableness of matter (both false assumptions) ...." It is only fitting that at the very outset of the scientific venture the wisest of mankind should have put his finger on what was to prove the most stubborn obstacle (I call it The Fatal Trap) to obtaining a rationally coherent, empirically grounded conception of the world. It is immediately obvious that it presents us with two baffling problems. The first is that it is wholly unable to account for change: the atoms, by definition, are unchanging, and change is totally inapplicable to a vacuum ? itself, as spatially extended nothing, an absurdity, as many of the Greeks, Aristotle among them, saw. The second is that there can exist no causal ground for attractions and repulsions between the atoms across empty space. And the attempt to resolve this by postulating a plenum merely creates further insoluble problems. Fewer than seventy years on saw the publication of Newton's ?Principia' the magnum opus which undoubtedly was to have the greatest single effect on the future course of science. Maurice Félix Charles Allais (31 May 1911 – 9 October 2010) was a French economist and physicist. He was the 1988 winner of the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics "for his pioneering contributions to the theory of markets and efficient utilization of resources." Although he is best known for his work in economics, Allais also carried out extensive experimental and theoretical work in physics, and is remembered for the Allais Effect , an anomalous behaviour of a pendulum reported during solar eclipses.
Education
École Polytechnique, Paris — graduated top of his class

Biography
Maurice Allais was born on 31 May 1911 in Paris, France, into a modest family; his father was a shopkeeper and his grandfather a carpenter. His father, taken prisoner during the First World War, died in Germany in 1915, an event that affected Allais deeply. Despite his young age, he resolved to honour his father's name.
Allais studied at the Lycée Lakanal and then entered the École Polytechnique in Paris, from which he graduated at the top of his class. He continued his studies at the École Nationale Supérieure des Mines de Paris, and later obtained a doctorate in engineering from the University of Paris (Faculty of Science) in 1949. From 1944 he served as Professor of Economics at the École Nationale Supérieure des Mines de Paris, and in 1946 he became director of its Economic Analysis Centre. He also held teaching positions at other institutions, including the University of Paris X–Nanterre.
Allais died on 9 October 2010 in Saint-Cloud, near Paris, at the age of 99.

Abstract
Based on the work of Jacobson [1] and Gibbons, [2] Schiller [3] has shown not only that a maximum force follows from general relativity, but that general relativity can be derived from the principle of maximum force. In the present paper an alternative derivation of maximum force is given. Inspired by the equivalence principle, the approach is based on a modification of the well known special relativity equation for the velocity acquired from uniform proper acceleration. Though in Schiller's derivation the existence of gravitational horizons plays a key role, in the present derivation this is not the case. In fact, though the kinematic equation that we start with does exhibit a horizon, it is not carried over to its gravitational counterpart. A few of the geometrical consequences and physical implications of this result are discussed.
Overview
Christoph Schiller had shown that a maximum force F MAX = c 4 /4 G follows from general relativity, and that general relativity can be recovered from it — the maximum force playing "the same role for general relativity as the maximum speed plays for special relativity." Richard Benish 's paper, submitted to the International Journal of Theoretical Physics in 2009, reaches exactly the same number by a different route: a modification of the special-relativistic equation for velocity under uniform proper acceleration, combined with the Equivalence Principle and the inverse-square law.
The point of the exercise is not the number, which is not in dispute, but what comes with it. In Schiller's derivation gravitational horizons are essential. In Benish's they are impossible. Displacement current was originally conceived by James Clerk Maxwell in 1861 in connection with linear polarization in a dielectric solid which he believed to pervade all of space. The official teaching today is that displacement current is a consequence of extending the original solenoidal Ampère’s Circuital Law to embrace the conservation of electric charge. Yet unless either of these two methods leads to a displacement current that is compatible with Faraday’s Law of Induction, then it cannot serve its main purpose, which is to provide a bridge between Ampère’s Circuital Law and Faraday’s Law of Induction, hence enabling the derivation of the electromagnetic wave equations. This matter will be investigated in both the Lorenz gauge and the Coulomb gauge.

Maxwell's equations are the four coupled partial differential equations that, together with the Lorentz force law , constitute classical electromagnetic theory : Gauss's law for the electric field, the absence of magnetic monopoles, Faraday's law of induction, and the Ampère–Maxwell law with its displacement-current term.
The standard account
James Clerk Maxwell built the theory in stages — "On Physical Lines of Force" (1861–62), which developed it from a mechanical model of molecular vortices in an aether ; "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field" (1865); and the Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism (1873). The decisive step was the displacement current , a term added to Ampère's circuital law which makes the system consistent with conservation of charge and, crucially, yields a wave equation. The waves travel at 1⁄√(ε₀μ₀), a quantity computable from purely electrostatic and magnetostatic measurements, and Maxwell found it equal within experimental error to the measured speed of light — the identification of light as an electromagnetic wave.
Two historical facts matter for what follows. First, the four equations universally taught today are not the ones Maxwell wrote. The Treatise presented a larger system — commonly counted as twenty equations in twenty variables, using quaternion notation — and it was Oliver Heaviside who in the mid-1880s recast them into the compact four-equation vector form, discarding the scalar and vector potentials as primary quantities. Second, the equations govern the fields only; they do not by themselves say what force a field exerts on a charge. That requires the separately postulated Lorentz force.
The equations are Lorentz-invariant as they stand, which is why they required no amendment when special relativity appeared in 1905; historically the influence ran the other way, with electromagnetism serving as the model relativity was built to match. Title Maxwell's Equations Do Not Fit Special Relativity Theory

Author(s) Janusz Dyonizy Laski
Keywords maxwell , special relativity
Published 2009

Abstract
There are two versions of Maxwell's equations. The classical version uses the Coulomb gauge and the relativistic version has electrodynamic potentials fulfilling the non-homogeneous equations for waves. With the use of the Lorenz gauge such equations have been obtained from the fourth Maxwell's equation and the equation for potentials of vector of electric intensity E . We show that the last equation after differentiation in time and multiplication by dielectric permittivity is similar to the fourth Maxwell's equation. We also show that after obvious corrections the equations are equivalent. We claim that in the fourth Maxwell's equation, instead of the vector of electric current density j , its irrotational component should only be applied. We also claim that in the equation for potentials of vector E instead of vector A there should be only its solenoidal component. It is shown that the corrected form of these two equations is fully consistent with the rest of Maxwell's equations. As the result of replacing vectors j and A by their proper components the problem of different gauges disappeared. Only one gauge i.e. that of Lorenz with a changed sign is shown to be necessary. As the result of the proposed modification in the case of waves, the wave equations for the potentials - as well as for the field vectors - are homogeneous. It is not so in the relativistic version of Maxwell's equations. We claim that the classical Maxwell's equations in the proposed version are fully consistent, satisfactory and do not fit the Special Relativity Theory.

Mayeul Arminjon (born 6 December 1954) is a French researcher who spent his career as a Chargé de Recherche of the CNRS, in its section of theoretical physics, attached to the Laboratoire « Sols, Solides, Structures – Risques » (3SR) in Grenoble.
He is unusual among the authors catalogued on this wiki in two respects. He came to gravitation in mid-career from an established position in a quite different field — the mechanics of materials, where he worked on polycrystal plasticity, homogenization and micro-macro transitions — and he has published his alternative theory in ordinary refereed journals and on arXiv rather than only in the dissident literature.
His work since 1991 falls into two connected parts: a scalar ether theory of gravitation , a preferred-frame alternative to general relativity in which gravity is treated as a pressure force, and a series of papers on the Dirac equation in curved spacetime and what it takes for quantum mechanics to be well defined there.

Overview
This is Stefan Marinov's report of his interferometric "coupled-mirrors" experiment, received by General Relativity and Gravitation in June 1979 and published in 1980 — one of the very few claims of a positive ether-drift measurement to appear in a mainstream relativity journal. Marinov reports that his apparatus in Sofia registered an absolute velocity of the Earth of 279 ± 20 km/s in July 1975 and 327 ± 20 km/s in January 1976, giving a Solar-system absolute velocity of 303 ± 20 km/s toward an apex at right ascension 14 h 17 m , declination −23°.
The design idea is to measure the Sagnac Effect along a straight line rather than around a closed loop. Mechanical Perpetual Motion is a four-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It opens the ten-part handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and it takes the oldest and simplest form of the claim: a machine of weights, wheels and levers that is supposed to run on its own arrangement.
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
The overbalanced wheel
The archetype is a wheel whose weights swing further from the axis on the descending side than on the ascending one, so that the descending side is always heavier and the wheel is always turning. It is the oldest mechanical proposal of its kind: Bhāskara II described a version with mercury-filled spokes in India around 1150, and the sketchbook of Villard de Honnecourt, from about 1230, contains a wheel hung with mallets on the same principle. Robert Fludd's water-screw mill of 1618 — a mill that pumps back its own water — is the hydraulic cousin.
The generic answer to all of them is a counting argument rather than an appeal to authority. Moving the weights out on the descending side does increase each weight's torque, but the same geometry that moves them out puts fewer of them on that side, and the two effects cancel exactly. Simon Stevin had shown the same kind of thing in 1586 with the chain draped over a pair of inclined planes: if it did not balance it would move forever, which he took as absurd, and the figure was carved on his tombstone.

Mecânica Relacional e Implementação do Princípio de Mach com a Força de Weber Gravitacional is a 2013 Portuguese-language book by the physicist André K. T. Assis , published by Apeiron (Montreal). An English edition, Relational Mechanics and Implementation of Mach's Principle with Weber's Gravitational Force , appeared in 2014.
Overview
The book develops relational mechanics , a quantitative implementation of the ideas of Leibniz, Berkeley, and Mach in which all dynamics is expressed purely through relational quantities — the distances, relative radial velocities, and relative radial accelerations between material bodies — with no reference to absolute space or time. Assis replaces Newton's gravitational force with a velocity- and acceleration-dependent Weber-type force , and shows how this implements Mach's principle, deriving inertia from the gravitational interaction of a body with the distant matter of the universe. It is an expanded successor to his earlier Mecânica Relacional (1998) and related works.
About the author
André Koch Torres Assis is a Brazilian physicist at the University of Campinas (Unicamp) known for his research on Weber's electrodynamics, the history and foundations of physics, and Mach's principle. See also his Eletrodinâmica de Ampère .

Did damage caused by a foam strike on launch cause the disaster?

Menahem Simhony (1922 – 29 June 2015) was an Israeli physicist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who developed the epola model — the electron-positron lattice theory of the vacuum. In this model what physics calls empty space is a real, crystalline solid built of alternating bound electrons and positrons, from whose measurable elastic properties Simhony derived the velocity of light, inertia and gravitation. Working outside the mainstream for more than forty years after his papers were repeatedly declined by the major physics journals, he argued that twentieth-century physics had abandoned physical explanation in favour of mathematical formalism.
Biography
Simhony was born in 1922. He joined the physics staff of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in January 1960, working in its Physics Section 5 and serving successively as Instructor, Lecturer and Senior Lecturer. His experimental background was in solid-state and semiconductor research, in particular the physics of crystals — the field from which the epola concept later grew, since it was the well-measured behaviour of ionic crystals such as sodium chloride that gave him the quantitative model for a lattice of charges.
He began work on the electron-positron lattice in 1973, submitting a thirty-page paper titled "The Electron-Positron Lattice" to Physical Review D in March of that year. It was declined, as were many subsequent submissions, generally without any specific error being identified — the stated grounds being that the work "contradicts accepted scientific knowledge" or was "too speculative." Mercury's Perihelion Advance is Caused by Our Milky Way is a four-page paper by Thierry De Mees (dated December 2004, updated July 2007), published in the General Science Journal . It restates the first result of his earlier Did Einstein Cheat?

Metaphysics of Relativity Does Not Make Sense was a live session presented by Roger J Anderton on 31 May 2025 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Among the many things missed out from being taught to physics students is metaphysics. So, they are not told that from the perspective of Newtonian physics that the metaphysics of Einstein's relativity does not make sense. Hosted by Roger Anderton.
Summary
Roger J Anderton 's subject is a gap in the physics curriculum. Metaphysics — the assumptions about time, space, causation and existence that a theory must presuppose before its equations can be interpreted — is not taught to physics students, and his contention is that the omission is what makes the disagreement about relativity irresolvable.
The metaphysics of Newton
He set out the framework a student absorbs implicitly from Newtonian mechanics. Absolute space, existing independently of the objects in it and remaining even if all matter vanished. Absolute time, flowing uniformly and, in Newton's own words, without relation to anything external. Determinism: given all positions and velocities, past and future are fixed, and the universe is a clockwork — which raises, though he did not press it, the question of who made the clock. Space and time as substances rather than relations, a view Leibniz disputed. Objects with well-defined identities and trajectories against that fixed background. And forces as real physical causes, gravity acting at a distance in a way Newton himself found puzzling and declined to frame a hypothesis about.
Anderton entered one correction on his own behalf: Newton did discuss relative space and relative time, and the assistant's presentation of him as concerned only with the absolute is not quite fair.

Michael Faraday (22 September 1791 – 25 August 1867) was an English experimentalist whose discoveries founded the practical science of electricity and whose idea of lines of force filling the space around magnets and charges became, after Maxwell gave it mathematical form, the field concept of modern physics.
Faraday came to science without a university education. Apprenticed to a bookbinder, he was taken on at the Royal Institution as Humphry Davy's laboratory assistant in 1813 and remained there for the rest of his working life. In 1821 he produced the first continuous electromagnetic rotation — a wire circling a magnetic pole — the ancestor of every electric motor. On 29 August 1831 he demonstrated electromagnetic induction: a changing current in one coil wound on an iron ring induced a transient current in a second coil, with no contact between them. Within months he had built the homopolar or "Faraday disc" generator, in which a copper disc spun between the poles of a magnet delivers a steady current. In 1833–34 he established the laws of electrolysis, showing that the mass deposited at an electrode is proportional to the quantity of charge passed — the first strong quantitative evidence for a natural unit of electricity. In 1845 he found that a magnetic field along the path of light rotates its plane of polarisation (the Faraday effect), the first demonstrated link between light and magnetism, and in the same year identified diamagnetism. His experimental notebooks were published as Experimental Researches in Electricity (1839–1855), written almost entirely without equations.

He served as a contributing editor and Thunderblog author for Thunderbolts.info, the website of The Thunderbolts Project, an organization that promotes the Electric Universe interpretation of cosmology.
Biography
Goodspeed is a freelance journalist based in the United States. He became a contributing editor to Thunderbolts.info, where his articles helped draw Internet attention to the Electric Universe model advocated by writers such as Wallace Thornhill and David Talbott . In addition to his written work, he has been involved in producing multimedia content for The Thunderbolts Project, including podcast and video material.
Work
Writing for the Thunderbolts.info "Thunderblog" between 2007 and 2011, Goodspeed authored commentary presenting Electric Universe perspectives on astronomy and cosmology and critiquing mainstream scientific views. His articles addressed subjects such as comets, planetary phenomena, and Big Bang cosmology, and included pieces critical of organized skepticism. Among his titles are "Is The Universe Electric?" (2008), "A Holistic Cosmology For the 21st Century" (2008), "The Skeptical Inquirer Embarrasses Itself" (2008), "Electric Comets Re-write Space Science" (2010), and "The Electric Comet: The Elephant in NASA's Living Room?" Michael Jefferson Lawrence is a British theoretical physicist based in Ipswich, Suffolk, who writes under the banner of the Maldwyn Centre for Theoretical Physics. His work is centred on dimensional analysis and the construction of unit systems, from which he argues that the fundamental constants and the observable properties of matter stand in simple algebraic relationships that conventional SI units obscure.
Work
Adjusted Planck units
Lawrence's method is to rebuild the Planck system with the factors of 2π removed and the gravitational constant absorbed into the base units, producing what he calls Adjusted and then Double Adjusted Planck Units. In " A Toolkit for Improving the Understanding of Relationships between Physical Parameters based on Adjusted SI units and a New Planck Unit Framework " (2009) he sets out the framework; in " A Reinterpretation of the von Klitzing and Josephson constants " (2009) he applies it to the two quantum electrical standards, arguing that they emerge as natural maxima of resistance and inverse magnetic flux, and that many parameters can then be expressed as simple powers of h and c alone. He supports the construction with a dimensional grading in which every fundamental constant except c carries zero net dimension.
" Interpreting Why Triple-Adjusted Planck Unit Observable Fundamental Properties Are Simple Powers " (2013) extends the same programme a further step.
Velocity addition
A separate 2013 paper, " Accepted Relativistic Addition of Velocities and Energies are Only Two-Variable Versions of a New Infinite Variables Formula ", argues that the standard relativistic velocity- and energy-addition formulae are special cases of a more general expression admitting arbitrarily many terms.

Michael Meade Steinbacher was an American photographer, based at Whitewater in the California desert, who applied a camera and a great deal of fieldwork to geology. He contributed two papers to the Natural Philosophy Alliance and led its geology field tours , taking participants through the mountains and deserts of the American west to look at landforms in the light of his own reading of them.
His thesis, set out in " A New Approach to Mountain Formation " (2011), is that mountain ranges are lithified dunes. He proposes that a transient high-energy plasma discharge once enveloped the Earth, filling the air with dust and sand driven by extreme winds; that higher ground acted as a snow fence, so that material drifted behind it in self-perpetuating deposits; and that electromagnetic effects — he names the Bennett pinch — gathered and hardened the airborne material. Rain and floodwater then cut the dunes into a slurry which slumped into stratified alluvial fans, and further electrical discharge converted the fresh deposits into granite, sandstone, schist and basalt. The "rivers of fire" of ancient legend he reads as discharges cutting drainage channels by something like industrial electrical discharge machining. A companion paper, " The Consequences of a Reversal of the Rotation of Earth " (2012), pursues a related line.
The approach draws on two sources. One is the worldwide similarity of catastrophe traditions, which Steinbacher — following Velikovsky — takes to record an event within human memory; he opens the 2011 paper by noting that he is not religious and that a single such story would not have interested him. The other is Electric Universe plasma cosmology, and in particular Anthony Peratt's comparison of petroglyph forms with instabilities observed in high-energy laboratory discharges.

Michael Holdt Twichell is an American electrical and software engineer and a self-published theorist, known in the New Energy and Tesla-research community for Aether Gravity — a proposal that gravity is not a property of space curvature but the observable consequence of matter absorbing the aether around it . He has set the theory out in two self-published volumes, The Twichell Manuscript — Volume I: Aether Gravity (2011) and Physics of the Dark Matter: The Proton Magnet (2017), and has presented it four times at the TeslaTech ExtraOrdinary Technology Conference.
His position is a full-space one: he holds that the replacement of the nineteenth-century aether by the empty-space model of relativity was a wrong turn, and that restoring a material medium removes the need for much of what he regards as the over-complication of modern physics.
Aether Gravity
The central claim of the first volume is a mechanism rather than a field equation. Matter, on Twichell's account, continuously absorbs the aether in which it sits; the resulting inflow towards a mass is what is observed as gravitational attraction. Weight is therefore a consequence of a flow, not of a geometric property of spacetime.
From that single mechanism he argues for explanations of a range of otherwise unconnected phenomena, among them plate tectonics and the inner–outer core structure of the Earth, supernovae and black holes, the Pioneer anomaly , the Allais effect and the Coriolis effect . He also treats the theory as the route to gravity control, and has argued that the same principle was known to ancient civilizations — a theme he developed in a 2015 interview with Open Minds TV and in his later conference talks.

title: Michelson interferometer
content_preview: The Michelson interferometer is an optical instrument that splits a single beam of light into two paths, sends them along separate arms to mirrors, recombines t
search_text:
The Michelson interferometer is an optical instrument that splits a single beam of light into two paths, sends them along separate arms to mirrors, recombines them, and reads the resulting interference fringes. Because the fringe pattern responds to differences in the optical path travelled by the two beams, the instrument converts a change far smaller than a wavelength of light into a visible shift — which is what has made it, for more than a century, the most sensitive general-purpose measuring device in physics.
How it works
A half-silvered beam splitter divides the incoming light. One part travels to a mirror at the end of arm 1 and returns; the other travels to a mirror at the end of arm 2 and returns. The two returning beams recombine at the splitter and are observed together. If the two round trips take exactly the same time the beams arrive in phase; any difference produces a proportional displacement of the fringes. Rotating the whole apparatus, changing an arm length, changing the medium in an arm, or changing the speed of the instrument through whatever the light propagates in will all, on one theory or another, alter the fringe position.
Albert A. Michelson built the first version in 1881 in Potsdam and, with Edward Morley , a far more sensitive one mounted on a stone slab floating in mercury for the 1887 Michelson–Morley experiment at the Case School of Applied Science in Cleveland. That instrument had an effective arm length of about 11 metres, achieved by multiple reflections, and was expected to show a fringe shift of roughly 0.4 of a fringe as it was turned.
The design has outlived the question it was built to answer. Fourier-transform infrared spectrometers are Michelson interferometers with one moving mirror. Michelson himself used the principle to measure stellar diameters — the first was Betelgeuse in 1920 — and to define the metre in terms of the wavelength of cadmium light.
