Saturday Morning Science Chat with David de Hilster
Summary
David de Hilster hosted a second week in Franklin Hu 's absence, again streaming to both the society's channel and his own Dissident Science , and set the topic deliberately: is charge real?
The case against charge
De Hilster opened with a question few could answer — who first put the plus and minus signs on things? — and gave the answer as Benjamin Franklin. His argument follows from that. The signs are a notation adopted to record which things attract and which repel; they have since become so ingrained that people take charge for an innate property of matter. He regards it instead as a magical attribute imposed on a particle, and asks anyone who uses it for a physical account of what a field actually is. The model he and his father Robert de Hilster are writing up needs no charge at all: the nucleus holds what orbits it for mechanical reasons, everything is Newtonian, and by Occam's razor the burden falls on whoever wants the extra ingredient. He noted that Glenn Borchardt 's neomechanics likewise dispenses with it.
Hu, watching from the road, wrote in twice. First that charge is too complex a phenomenon to be an assumption — which de Hilster read back as an argument for his own side, since an assumption is precisely what one declines to explain. Then that charge needs to emerge as the result of something like ordinary Newtonian physics, at which de Hilster cheerfully declared they agreed.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene , Bob Gray , Ian Cohen, Alistair Riddoch , Carl and Phil, and comments from Cornelis Verhey and viewers. It became the most direct confrontation between Hu and Keene the series has recorded, and it was conducted without rancour on either side.
Keene's Physicist's Survival Guide
Keene opened with the video he is planning: clicking through the physics literature at random and noting what it says. His complaint is not that the accounts are wrong so much as that they contradict each other. Elementary particles are defined as those with no smaller constituents — and then CERN papers openly track the breakdown products of the heavy quarks. Grand unification presumes a weak force which he does not regard as a force at all: on his account the weak interactions all rest on the unconditional bit operation, and calling it a force is like calling rust one. The speed of light is listed as a constant of vacuum, whereas his own work has it varying, and requires a minimum quantity of quanta present for light to be conducted at all.
He also gave his reading of magnetic monopoles, which he says need not be a new kind of particle: on his model the L bits are magnetic monopoles, and the reason a divided bar magnet always yields a north and a south is that the division never gets down to the fundamental length constant.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Ian Cohen, James Keene , Bob Gray , Carl and Alex, the whole of it on dark matter. Hu's microphone was barely audible for the first half — a Windows update had reset the level — so Ian carried much of the discussion, and Hu twice handed the chair over while attending to his mother.
Ian: are spiral galaxies spiral?
Ian's proposal, which he has raised before and thinks neglected, is that what we see in the night sky is not a contemporaneous snapshot. An object is visible only if it happened to be at a distance of X light years at the moment X years ago when it emitted the light; if it was elsewhere then, the light has already passed us or has not yet arrived. Looking at a nebula whose near side is a million light years away and whose far side is two million, we are combining events separated by a million years.
From that he draws two conclusions. First, that the gravitational effects attributed to dark matter may simply be matter we cannot see — ordinary matter, of the kind found in a laboratory, that is not at the right distance for its light to reach us now. He prefers to call this dark stuff , declining the mainstream term. Second, and more provocatively, that spiral galaxies may not be spiral. His tentative position is that they are elliptical or spherical bodies whose apparent shape is the composite of parts seen at different epochs as the object rotates.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Bill Lucas , James Keene , Bob Gray and a new participant, Toby. The theme was set by Lucas — how to judge between competing theories — and it turned into a sustained cross-examination of his own.
Distinti, and the case for polytheism
Lucas had found a YouTube channel by Robert Distinti, an electrical engineer with a couple of hundred videos, and recommended it as a third party critical of everyone's theories rather than of any one of them. Hu played David de Hilster 's review of Distinti's latest.
The point that stuck was Distinti's rule that a theory's ability does not prove its exclusivity: that a model gives good answers does not show no other model would give the same ones. De Hilster's illustration from his own experience was a dean telling him his thesis was ridiculous because Maxwell's equations are irrefutable — which, he said, misses that there may be another way to arrive at the same place. Distinti's remedy for what he calls polytheism — several theories fitting the same data — is to increase the sampling footprint until the candidates can be told apart, his example being two sine waves of different frequency that both pass through every measured point until one measures more finely.
Lucas drew from it the moral he cared about: a theory is never finished. General relativity was put forward to explain gravity, and when the Pioneer trajectories and the spiral arms did not fit, the response was to add dark matter and dark energy rather than to falsify anything.

Saturday Morning Science Chats
Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Ian Cohen, Bob Gray , Dennis Allen , Harry Ricker and Jim, given over entirely to unipolar induction — the Faraday disc. An email storm had been running all week on the subject, with messages arriving several times an hour, and this session was the attempt to settle it against the experimental record.
The question
When a cylindrical magnet is rotated about its own magnetic axis, does its field rotate with it?
Hu says no: put a compass beside the magnet, spin the magnet about its axis, and the compass will not move; nothing about the space around it changes. Field lines, on his account, are a mathematical device with no physical realization, so there is nothing there to be traced from one angular position to another. He predicted that iron filings on a paper over a spinning magnet would sit perfectly still.
Ian says yes, and gave an analogy worth keeping: a member under stress viewed in polarized light shows stress lines; rotate the member and the lines rotate with it. To hold that the lines of force stay fixed while their source turns is, he said, to claim the stress lines would remain static in some absolute frame, which he thinks absurd. He also noted the history — Faraday first introduced the idea of the lines not following the magnet, to explain the homopolar result by having the magnet cut its own lines of force, and changed his mind some twenty years later.

Saturday Morning Science Chats was a live session on 18 January 2020 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Saturday Morning Science Chats with Franklin Hu
Summary
Bob Gray presented an update on his classical electrodynamics research, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bill Lucas , Ian Cohen, James Keene and Alistair Riddoch taking part.
Gray: from Weber to a generalized Maxwell system
Gray is looking for the simplest and most complete route to classical electrodynamics. His starting point is Weber electrodynamics, which is conventionally presented without fields at all: everything follows from a single potential energy function. He has taken that function and defined fields and potentials from it, arriving at four equations that look much like Maxwell's but carry three extra terms. Those terms come from the time derivative of the charge density, which appears in Weber's approach and, for reasons he cannot see, not in Maxwell's; set them to zero and the two systems coincide. He treats this as evidence that Maxwell's system comes up short.
What he wants and cannot yet get is the expression for the electrodynamic field that he was taught comes from special relativity. He would rather not import relativity into Weber to obtain it, and he reported a correction to his own understanding: Heaviside derived that same expression from Maxwell's equations in 1888, seventeen years before the relativity paper, so it does not depend on relativity at all. Lucas's The Universal Force derives it too, from six empirical laws of electrodynamics — more assumptions than Weber's one potential function, which is why Gray keeps looking.

Saturday Morning Science Chats
Summary
A small chat over the Christmas week — Franklin Hu and Ian Cohen for most of it, joined by James Keene and, on a poor line, Harry Ricker . It was given over almost entirely to Ian's report of attending a public lecture on the 1919 eclipse expeditions, and to what he learned there.
Ian at Astronomy Ireland
Ian had gone to a lecture by Professor Peter Coles of Maynooth, given to Astronomy Ireland, on the centenary of the Eddington–Dyson eclipse measurement. He asked from the floor why no terrestrial experiment had been contemplated, and then put his own position: that general relativity as such — the space-time account — has not been verified, only certain peripheral anomalies. Coles replied that if one neglects all the evidence then of course there is no evidence, and the audience applauded. Ian's own description of the moment was fair to both sides: the speaker had said all the right things about science being open to question, was not hostile, and was courteous afterwards in the pub, but was plainly reluctant to engage, and the applause was for putting down a crank at the back.
He pressed two further points privately. On the standard rejoinder that GPS confirms general relativity daily, he answered that what GPS shows is the variation of atomic clock rates with gravitational potential, which is not general relativity as such; and he said that GPS contradicts special relativity, since the speed of light there is not independent of the observer's motion. He got no reply to the second.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Alistair Riddoch , Ian Cohen, James Keene , Bill Lucas , Harry Ricker and Toby. It began with Riddoch's model of the vacuum and turned into an argument about what would count as doing science at all.
Infinity, and immutability
Riddoch opened with two things he had been turning over. The first was density: he had learned that relativity has the centre of a black hole infinitely dense, and wanted to know whether infinite density is even a possible thing. Hu's answer was that an infinity in a result is a red flag that something has gone wrong, and he made the same complaint about renormalization, which he calls dividing one infinity by another and keeping the answer. Ian agreed — thou shalt not divide by zero — and extended it to the big bang's infinitely small interval and infinitely great density, and to the Copenhagen picture, which appears to require an infinite speed of transmission where relativity has a finite one.
The second was the word immutable . Riddoch's own model has Planck-scale building blocks that have always existed and never change: not permeable, not compressible, not flexible. What changes is only their relative orientation, spin polarity and rate of rotation. Because they are not perfect spheres — their surfaces are wave-deformed — the gaps between them do change, alternating between hyperbolic tetrahedra and hyperbolic octahedra as the blocks turn. Those gaps are genuine void, with no properties at all except a shape, and the shape is defined entirely from outside: as he put it, it is the doughnut that defines the hole, not the hole.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Bill Lucas , James Keene , Stefan and a guest, Eugene, who had written asking to present a paper. The first stretch was domestic — Hu's indoor winter garden under cheap LED lamps, aluminium recycling, and a discussion of commercial maize, the density at which it is planted, its inedibility, and the Roundup litigation.
Eugene: a biogenic origin for earthquakes
Eugene presented what he calls the biogenic earthquake hypothesis, posted as a preprint on EarthArXiv: that microbial life beneath the surface may trigger earthquakes.
His argument runs in stages. The accepted limit on the depth of the biosphere — twelve to fifteen kilometres — rests on temperature and pressure limits he thinks badly underestimated: the most extreme organism known before 2018 tolerated 122 to 130 °C, and a strain found that year survives well beyond it. Set against models of the earth's interior composition, he arrives at a possible limit near seventy-five kilometres, which is deep enough to matter for earthquakes.
For how such organisms would feed, he pointed to a documented case: bacterial chains beneath the ocean floor that perform a distributed respiration, the deeper cells taking electrons from sulphur and passing them up the chain to cells at the surface that attach them to oxygen — effectively feeding on an electric current. He suggests telluric currents could do the same tens of kilometres down. He also gave energy estimates that he says are adequate even for a magnitude nine event.

Summary
A short session over the Thanksgiving weekend, with Franklin Hu and James Keene the only participants and Keene's connection failing badly in the last quarter hour, which ended the chat early. It was a two-way conversation throughout, and the better for it.
Keene's density ranges
Keene reported extending an earlier study by parsing the whole range of initial quanta density in his simulator, from absolute vacuum — no one-state bits at all — up to maximum, where every locus is occupied. The ranges he now identifies: above about 0.75 a lepton–quark soup; between roughly 0.66 and 0.75, plasma; and below that, down to about 0.1, the range in which atoms occur. He noted that the higher end of the atomic range appears to favour higher- Z atoms, which he takes as consistent with the astrophysical account of heavy elements forming in large explosions.
Hu queried that immediately, and the question was a good one: if all atoms are made of the same protons, neutrons and electrons, why should their bit density differ? Keene did not evade it but did not settle it either; his answer went by way of the simulation's behaviour rather than the chemistry.
Run in vacuum mode, anything with momentum leaves the volume and is lost, so the volume cools to what he calls absolute zero — no radiation out, no particle motion — a state unreachable in the laboratory but exact in simulation. Plotting the final density against the initial, he finds that at very high initial densities the final density is near zero: the simulation shows an explosion in every direction, and what is left is almost nothing. Saturday Morning Science Chats
Summary
Bob Gray presented on the internal consistency of Maxwell's equations, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bill Lucas , Harry Ricker , James Keene , Cornelis Verhey , Carl and, later, David de Hilster .
Gray's claim
Gray had been working from Frederick David Tombe 's account of Maxwell's original equations, drawn from the 1861 and 1864 papers — twenty equations, presented in vector notation as eight. His question is not whether the equations agree with experiment but whether they are mathematically consistent among themselves: can one show, for a given equation, that the left-hand side genuinely equals the right?
To ask that he had to add assumptions, which he listed and offered for challenge: vacuum permittivity and permeability, one constitutive relation Tombe omits, point charges as an adequate approximation to their positions, the charge density as a sum of delta functions, the current density as charge density times a velocity, and expressions for the scalar and vector potentials for discrete charges. Everything then stands in fundamental quantities and the check can be made.
His result: it fails. Working out the divergence of E with those substitutions yields, on the right, a term containing the accelerations of the charges — the vector potential involves the current density, hence velocity, hence a time derivative giving acceleration — and there is nothing corresponding on the left. So the two sides cannot be equal in general.

Saturday Morning Video Chats with Franklin Hu
Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Bill Lucas , James Keene , Ian Cohen, Alistair Riddoch , Bob Gray and Michael Teske. It opened on an email storm and settled into the best-focused argument the series has had about gravity: is it a property of the mass itself or something acting from outside?
The email storm
The previous week's brief mention of evolution had taken over the list, and Hu was plainly irritated by where it went — theological argument about Adam and Eve rather than science. He put the substantive points that had emerged: that what Darwin observed is variation within a species, beaks and colours and sizes, and that selection experiments run into a limit past which the organism cannot reproduce, so that a bird remains a bird; that the automobile analogy offered on the list fails because car design is intelligent selection, not a random process; and that chimpanzees have twenty-four chromosome pairs to our twenty-three, which someone had taken to mean they are the more evolved.
Ian's reply was measured on both counts. On the theology, he declined to take part: one either believes or one does not, and arguing about the Abrahamic god is no more physics than arguing about what Thor or Odin did. On the biology he made two corrections — chromosome count does not track development, and the orthodox view is not that humans descend from chimpanzees but that both descend from a common primate ancestor. Riddoch added that many small organisms have far more chromosomes than we do.

Saturday Science Chat sponsored by the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society
Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Ian Cohen, James Keene and Bill Lucas — after a brief exchange of non-scientific news, given over to a single item from the week's physics headlines and where it led.
The neutron lifetime measured from orbit
The paper reported the first space-based measurement: the MESSENGER spacecraft carries a neutron detector, and neutrons knocked out of Venus and Mercury by cosmic rays and counted at altitude give an estimate of how long they survive.
Hu set out why the item matters. The two laboratory methods — the bottle and the beam — do not agree: the beam gives about nine seconds longer than the bottle, against a lifetime near fourteen and a half minutes. If both are equally valid and give different answers, what is being measured? He returned to this as his standing test case, alongside the gravitational constant. He also noted how remarkable the number itself is: fourteen minutes is an age for a subatomic particle, closer to the decay of an atomic nucleus than to a muon. And he explained why the measurement is hard at all: a free neutron is nearly undetectable, and a detector is essentially a counter tube wrapped in a large block of wax, registering what the neutrons produce rather than the neutrons.
The verdict on the new result was that its uncertainty — something like ten to seventeen minutes — is far too wide to choose between the two laboratory values, though the group hopes to build a more precise instrument.

Saturday Science Chat was a live session on 14 March 2020 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Saturday Science Chat
Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene , Ian Cohen, Alistair Riddoch , Carl and Bob Gray . It began with the clocks — Ian had arrived an hour early, the American and European changeovers being a fortnight apart — and with his account of daylight saving as a German wartime measure of 1916 to save coal, copied by Britain a month later. From the clocks it went to time itself and stayed there.
Is time quantized?
Keene holds that space, time and energy are all quantized, and that this is what makes his binary mechanics work: with those three quantities discrete, the quantities usually presented to students as fundamental physical constants become derivable rather than merely measured. He put the criterion plainly — by their fruits ye shall know them — and treated the quantization as a postulate justified by its utility, declining to go behind it. Asked why the world should be quantized, he said that is where science shades into philosophy and religion, and that he would leave it to others; he noted that Bill Lucas , asked the same, answers that God made it so, and that this is not where he himself will go.
Hu wanted a physical cause rather than a postulate, and offered one: that we are inside a computer. Nothing in a computer happens faster than the clock; each tick fixes a state; a bit is here or there and never half-way. Keene was sympathetic but said this is only another way of saying that space, time and energy are quantized.

Saturday Science Chat hosted by Franklin Hu and sponsored by the Chappell Natural Philosophy Society.
Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu , with Dennis Allen , Harry Ricker , Ian Cohen and others, running on two threads: what a photon is, and how the earliest radio detector worked.
The shape of the photon
Hu repeated the claim he had made the previous week — that a photon occupies the space of a rod, still a compression wave, with the rod's orientation carrying the polarisation — and drew from it the distinction he thinks matters. At the high-frequency end everything looks like particles; at the radio end everything looks like waves; and that, he argued, is not a continuum of behaviour but two different things. Light generated by atomic electron transitions comes in these rod-like packets of fixed energy; a radio wave is more like an ocean wave, broad and of any amplitude.
Harry Ricker pressed the obvious objection: the electromagnetic spectrum appears continuous, from the very low frequencies once used to reach submerged submarines up to the extreme high frequencies — so where does one behaviour stop and the other begin? Hu's answer was that the boundary is technological, set by how fast electrons can be made to oscillate in a circuit, and he asked repeatedly what the highest radio frequency actually achievable is and where it sits on the spectrum. Ricker's own answer was that the spectrum is one thing described by two different models at the two ends, that the choice is a matter of which model one is using, and that this does not answer what either a photon or a radio wave physically is.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Dennis Allen , Bob Gray , Alistair Riddoch and Ian Cohen, given over almost entirely to inertial propulsion.
Allen's fourth edition
Allen reported a fourth edition of his book, now on Amazon and downloadable free from ResearchGate and Academia, adding two appendices.
His substantive point concerns the mechanics the book treats, which is built on complex numbers and is therefore two-dimensional — the real and imaginary parts — and which its author, an electrical engineer, prefers because complex multiplication fits alternating current theory hand in glove. Allen's argument is that this cannot reach the case he cares about: Boeing's arrangement uses two rotors spinning oppositely at the same angular velocity with their axes moved relative to each other, which is a three-dimensional situation.
He proposed two routes out. Quaternions, which are three vectors and a scalar and form a skew field, multiplication not commuting — noting that when a researcher in the west published a two-volume work on tesla-style transmission, a correspondent pointed out that it was quaternions and he had not known. And the Frenet–Serret apparatus of differential curve theory: the uniform circular motion in the book is what one gets by setting the torsion to zero, and restoring it would give the third dimension.
Boeing's control moment gyros
The session's centrepiece was a set of slides from a 2015 Tesla Tech talk by Mike Gamble of Boeing, which Allen had circulated and James Keene put on screen.

Saturday Science Chat
Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene , Ian Cohen, Dennis Allen , Cornelis Verhey and Bob. Bob had circulated a paper titled Something is Rotten in the State of QED and, disclaiming any expertise in the subject, put it up for others; it set the session's course.
What is wrong with QED
Bob's summary of the paper's complaint was mathematical. Any QED calculation runs into infinities, and what is done with them depends on how the sums are taken and what is subtracted from what. The paper's first equation is the assignment of −1/12 to the sum of all the positive integers — traceable, through its references, to Euler — and this is used in the course of a calculation held up as physics' most accurate. Hu made the same complaint about renormalization: dividing infinity by infinity and keeping the answer.
The session then worked through the encyclopaedia articles on quantum electrodynamics, the quantum vacuum and the anomalous magnetic moment, reading them aloud. Hu could make nothing of the Feynman diagram — an electron and positron annihilating to a gamma ray which then produces a quark, an antiquark and a gluon, three things he takes not to exist — and said it looked like a cartoon.
Keene's objection went to the physics rather than the arithmetic. Most of what is going on, he said, is hidden in the diagram's vertices: when he derives Planck's constant from first principles it comes out as an elemental action divided by the fine structure constant, which implies well over a hundred events inside what is treated as a single Planck-constant event.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Dennis Allen , Bob and James Keene , beginning on gyroscopes and ending on what is actually in a particle accelerator beam.
Gyroscopes
Bob had raised a Buckminster Fuller piece explaining why a gyroscope pushed one way moves at right angles, and Allen added two experimentalists who report that classical mechanics does not give the right numbers for gyroscopic motion — one in Kyrgyzstan working with a precision gyroscope and a stopwatch and no grant, and an engineer, now dead, some of whose experimental material is still online. Allen expects it to disappear in due course, remarking drily that the modern way is not to refute people but to take down their videos after they die.
The room agreed on what a gyroscope does — hold its axis in space, which is why spacecraft use them — and disagreed about why. Allen's account: in free space with no fields, striking the axis produces transient behaviour and the axis settles fixed again, though not necessarily parallel to the old one. Hu offered a mechanical picture from a rolling bicycle wheel, which resists being pushed over because it can only roll straight while upright.
Keene's first answer — that the translation of angular momentum into linear momentum opposes the gradient of the gravitational potential — he immediately called unsatisfying, and said it needed more thought.

Saturday Science Chat was a live session on 5 December 2020 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Summary
A general science chat hosted by Franklin Hu , standing in with no speaker scheduled, and used to make the first public presentation of an idea he had arrived at two or three months earlier. He stated it without preamble: the shape of a photon is a rod.
Why a shape at all
Hu's argument for insisting on one is that he is a physicalist — if it cannot be shown on a billiard table he does not believe it — and that the history of the DNA molecule is the model. The components were known long before anyone found the arrangement that fitted the data, and the helix ended the mystery. He wants the same for light rather than talk of a photon whose shape nobody will state.
A rod that is a wave
His second claim is that light is strictly a wave: he does not accept wave–particle duality, and says so rather than working around it. What he means by a rod is the wavelet one would get by dipping a rectangular object into a very narrow wave tank — a single pulse with a fixed width and height travelling in a straight line, not the great circular waves one normally makes.
He listed the properties this has to account for: light travels in rays, it does not disperse, and it is localised. His example was pair annihilation, where two back-to-back gamma rays strike specific spots in a silicon detector rather than smearing across it. A rod, he argued, has all three particle-like properties and remains a wave.
The inverse square law he handled by distinguishing the individual photon from the population: a photon from Alpha Centauri arrives at full amplitude, and it is only the number per unit area that thins with distance.

Summary
A session cut short by the technology. The live room had been set up wrongly, so nobody could join — participants who tried found themselves connected to an already-ended broadcast — and Franklin Hu spoke alone for the hour, answering typed comments, before ending the stream to restart it. What survives is therefore a monologue and a set of replies, but the monologue is a clear statement of his position on the nature of light.
Clumps against waves
Hu was answering a YouTube correspondent, Gary, who holds that light consists of discrete clumps travelling independently, with frequency given by the spacing between them and no medium required. Hu set the two pictures against each other and proposed to score them against what is actually observed, using Lego bricks and sticky notes for want of a whiteboard.
Non-collision. Two beams crossed at right angles do not scatter each other. On the clump view they should: colliding is what particles do. The available escape — that the clumps are so small that collisions are effectively never — he thought strained, since the interaction appears to be not nearly zero but exactly zero. On a wave view it follows without effort: the medium's particles have more than one degree of freedom, so a displacement from one direction and a displacement from another can be carried at once. He added the stronger version: two water waves meeting head-on rise together and pass straight through each other, which no two solid objects do — a white brick meeting a red brick stops.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene and Bob Gray , most of it a sustained and good-tempered argument between Hu and Keene about what counts as an explanation.
Deriving the constants
Keene's claim for binary mechanics is that it derives what are called the fundamental constants — the speed of light, Planck's constant, the electron mass and others — from first principles, and that nobody else does. His first principles he described as minimal: the full quantisation of space, time and energy, quantisation being already accepted for charge.
The distinction he insisted on, and which Hu eventually accepted as a clean statement of where they differ, is between deriving a constant and showing interrelationships among constants. The literature is full of formulae relating the fine structure constant, the charge, the speed of light and the rest to one another, and Keene has no quarrel with that work — it is simply, as he put it, a different cage in the zoo. His rule is that unexplained data may not be explained by reference to other unexplained data. He noted, as support rather than opposition, that the standard model concedes it cannot derive any of these constants from its own principles.
Hu's counter, pressed several times, was that binary mechanics grounds out the same way one level down: it takes fundamental quantities of length, time and mass, and cannot say where those come from. Keene agreed without embarrassment — he has not attempted to, and there is an empty slot for anyone who wants to. Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Dennis Allen , Bob, Roger, Bill Lucas , Alistair Riddoch and Ian Cohen, taking up an argument running on the society's email list.
Do a heavy and a light object really fall together?
Ian Cohen set out the case, carefully and at length, that they do not quite. The textbook derivation cancels the small mass from both sides and leaves the acceleration as GM/r ²; but the earth is not stationary, and the object attracts it too, so the relative acceleration is G(M+m)/r ². Two consequences follow. The heavier object accelerates very slightly faster. And, if the two experiments are run one after the other, the heavier object has slightly less distance to cover, because the earth has moved further to meet it. He was emphatic that this is not Aristotle vindicated — the difference is of the order of the object's mass to the earth's — but that it is not exactly zero either.
Hu accepted the distance argument readily and resisted the acceleration one, on the ground that inertial resistance rises in proportion to the force. Ian took him through it again, and the disagreement did not resolve.
Riddoch made the observation that clarified the case: if both objects are released at the same moment, the earth's movement toward them is common to both, so that effect drops out and only the acceleration difference remains — which is exactly the thought experiment Ian had proposed. He then scaled it up memorably: if the whole human population jumped a metre at once, the earth would move about a twelve-trillionth of a metre the other way, and when one person alone jumps, it moves eight billion times less.

Weber against Lorentz
Bob brought a paper he thought the group should see: a Liverpool group's experimental test of electron beam deflection in the fringing field of a solenoid, comparing three predictions — Weber's force equation, the Maxwell–Lorentz field treatment, and a commercial boundary-element package.
The result, which he showed from the plotted data, is that in the low velocity regime the Weber prediction tracks the measured deflections closely across three solenoid sizes while the Lorentz prediction is well off. Bob was careful to keep his own enthusiasm in check: he is a Weber partisan and said so, and added that Weber does not fit everything — at velocities near the speed of light it fails and the Lorentz treatment with the relativistic factor does better. His own standing question was why there is not one equation that works everywhere.
Hu found the more striking point to be that a law as basic as the Lorentz force is not confirmed here, and asked whether the paper had done the high-speed experiments itself. Bob was scrupulous: the paper cites others for that and he did not know how those were set up, so he would not speak for the authors.
The two then drew out the methodological difference. Summary
Franklin Hu hosting, with James Keene , Ian Cohen and Alistair Riddoch , working through a video reply from the Draft Science channel — run by a critic, Gary, who had been banned from the chats and whom Hu argued should be let back in. The exchange had been running for some weeks and this session was Hu's response to the response.
The disagreement
Gary's position, as Hu set it out from the video, is that light is strictly a particle: photons drawn as circles, with the polarisation an inherent property of each, no waves anywhere, and radio behaving the same way. Hu's is that a photon is a wavelet in a medium.
Hu was at pains to say how much he agrees. Treating photons as discrete clumps travelling through space with a definite volume and length is right; so is the account of what they do on arrival, jostling electrons; so is the photoelectric explanation, that what matters is the energy delivered per unit time rather than the total, with the fixed quantum hv per packet. His own picture of the photon as a rod maps onto Gary's circles, the rod's orientation supplying the polarisation.
His criticism is that the account is incomplete rather than wrong: it has to postulate a photon that stands in no relation to anything else known, and cannot say what it is made of. He used his standing image for this — the socks disappearing from the dryer, which little elves would explain perfectly consistently and without any way of being tested. Logical consistency, he said, is grossly insufficient. His own theory, he argued, sits one level below Gary's and says what the clump is.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu on the Fourth of July, with Ian Cohen, Alistair Riddoch , James Keene and Bob, who had prepared slides on the question Hu had been putting to the group for some weeks: what is a magnetic field, and why does an electron deflect in one?
Bob's answer: there is no magnetic field
Bob's case, developed over a long presentation, is that the magnetic field is not a physical field at all.
He began with terminology — field means several different things, and if one defines an electrodynamic field as force per unit charge on a test body, then B does not qualify, its units being wrong.
His alternative comes from Weber electrodynamics, where the force between two charged bodies is the Coulomb force multiplied by a coupling coefficient with a constant term, a velocity-dependent term and an acceleration-dependent term. His analogy was static against kinetic friction: nobody finds it strange that the coupling between two objects differs according to their relative motion. On this reading the magnetic field is simply that dynamic coupling, and the Coulomb field is the only real physical field.
He applied Occam's razor twice. First to William J Hooper , who identifies three electric fields — Coulomb, motional and transformer — which Bob tabulated to show that they differ precisely in how many time derivatives they carry: none, one, two. Second to the multipole expansion of the scalar potential, whose infinite series of terms would, on the same logic, give an infinite series of fields.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Dennis Allen , Ian Cohen, Bill Lucas and James Keene , prompted by a popular article on warp drive in the week's physics headlines.
Is faster-than-light travel possible?
Hu put the question round the room before showing the article.
Ian Cohen had no objection in principle: the speed of light is an arbitrary speed much as the speed of sound in air is, being the speed of electromagnetic radiation in the ether, and there is no reason nothing should exceed it. He drew a distinction that ran through the session — between exceeding c by orders of magnitude, which is the science-fiction case, and exceeding it slightly, which needs only a refractive index below unity. His own example is the total internal reflection of radio waves at the ionosphere, where the phase speed exceeds c by a few per cent. He also holds, as a standing position, that gravitational interaction propagates far faster than light.
Bill Lucas framed it as a question about the medium: c reflects the tensile strength of the electromagnetic field, as measured by Hooper , so the question is whether that strength can differ — and he has seen no answer.
Dennis Allen brought a 1995 Galilean Electrodynamics paper by a NACA physicist whose manuscript had been supplied by his daughter, arguing that classical physics extended without curved spacetime reproduces the results credited to general relativity. Its relevant claim is a distinction he thought decisive: a body cannot be accelerated past c by forces applied from without , but may be by propulsion from within . Covid
The first quarter hour was the participants' own views on the pandemic, offered as opinion. Carl's argument was that lockdowns slow the case rate without changing how many are ultimately infected, that the justification is keeping hospitals from being overrun, and that sequestering the vulnerable while the rest of the population acquired immunity would have reached the same place. Ian drew the parallel with the 1918 influenza, which came in successive waves and then subsided of its own accord, and added the cynical reading that governments needed to be seen doing something. Hu described his own experience of a covid ward when his mother died, which he found calm and well within capacity, and noted that the ventilator shortage feared in the United States had not materialised.

The substance of the session was an argument running on the email list between Hu, Akinbo Ojo , Cornelius, Harry Ricker and David de Hilster about displacement current and what an electromagnetic wave is.
Hu set out the background from a first reading. The greater part of it is Ian's account of how he came to the subject, which is the most complete the series has recorded, followed by Ricker on unipolar induction and de Hilster on where the society might go.
Ian Cohen's account
Asked for his background, Ian gave it at length. He is an engineering scientist from Dublin with degrees in engineering and mathematics, and a doctorate in mathematical modelling and computer simulation of the thermal response of buildings, done during the first energy crisis. He remembers being struck at eighteen, in a first-year physics course, by the reciprocity paradox in special relativity — the question Dingle put, how a clock can be both faster and slower — and finding the answers unsatisfactory; but he went on with the mainstream.
What turned him was Al Kelly . In the early to mid nineties Kelly gave lectures in Dublin, the first at Trinity College, Ian's own university, arguing from the Sagnac effect that the postulates of special relativity are suspect — an effect Ian had never been taught. He went, found colleagues in the audience dismissive, and was struck enough to look into it: the alternative readings of Michelson–Morley, an ether travelling with the earth in its orbit. There followed a correspondence in the Irish Times between Kelly and the academic community, including the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies — founded in 1940 by de Valera on the model of Princeton's — whose replies Ian described as hostile and insulting.

Saturday: Cosmology & Expansion Tectonics was a live session presented by John B Eichler on 12 December 2020 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
John will present his worldview of Cosmology and how it relates to the geophysics of Expansion Tectonics. He weaves together the concepts of many famous scientists into an understandable framework based more on laboratory experimentation than abstract theory.
Summary
John B Eichler — a computer scientist from the Illinois Institute of Technology who worked on Univac machines in the vacuum-tube era and designed blast shields for the Atomic Energy Commission — presenting the connection he sees between cosmology and expansion tectonics: that one must know how the solar system was assembled to understand what is happening to the earth.
Method
He began with what he thinks goes wrong. Where hands-on experiment is possible, results repeat; the earth and the universe do not allow it, and the strongest evidence is where laboratory work backs the theoretical construct. So one should question any proposed esoteric law that has no empirical verification, and remember that a concept being visualisable does not make it obey the laws of physics.
He then defined worldview as what the scientist brings to the table — the paradigms absorbed from classes and books. These are two-edged: without a framework we could not make sense of anything, and with one we cannot see past it. To a hammer, everything looks like a nail.
Alfvén's plasma universe

Abstract
A new cosmological theory is presented based on the proposition that all four metrical coefficients of space and time change with the cosmological expansion. Such a universal scale expansion would preserve the four-dimensional spacetime geometry and therefore by general relativity most physical relationships. In addition, if the scale expansion were exponential with time, all epochs would be equivalent. The theory resolves several outstanding problems with the Big Bang theory and better agrees with four observational programs. It also provides a simple explanation to the Pioneer anomaly.
Overview
This is the first of a projected four-part series in Apeiron in which C Johan Masreliez sets out the Scale Expanding Cosmos (SEC) theory. Its founding proposition is a single change to the standard cosmological line element: instead of expanding only the three spatial metrical coefficients, as Friedmann's choice of coordinates does, let all four — space and time together — expand by a common exponential factor. The result is the SEC line element ds 2 = e 2 t / T ( dt 2 − dx 2 − dy 2 − dz 2 ), where T is the Hubble time. Science Chat was a live session on 5 September 2020 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Summary
Franklin Hu hosting alone, with technical trouble at the start — the usual live link was broken and his camera failed partway through — and with a session built around a single discipline: what a dissident should do when confronted with experimental evidence against their own hypothesis.
He opened by putting a question to the audience, which nobody took up: if you met a civilisation a billion years ahead of us who knew all the physics there is, what one question would you ask?
A falsifiable experiment
Hu first reported an exchange with the Draft Science channel, whose author holds that light and radio arrive in clumps rather than as waves. Hu had suggested he would not accept a disproving experiment, was told that was nonsense, and welcomed that — because it means the two can agree in advance on what would settle it.
The test he proposes is simple: transmit a raw square-wave carrier, put a bare receiving antenna next to it and look at an oscilloscope. His own hypothesis predicts something recognisably square; the clump hypothesis predicts a sine wave whatever is transmitted. Searching for the experiment, he found only people asserting what one would expect — that a perfect square is impossible because of the bandwidth required, or that nobody would broadcast that way because a sine wave is more efficient — and no record of anyone having actually done it. His complaint was that this is crowd expectation rather than a physical experiment, and that the thing would not be hard to do.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Bill Lucas , Ian Cohen and Roger, opening on the pandemic and its restrictions — Ian describing the confinement of the over-seventies in Ireland, which he criticised, and the two-kilometre limit — before turning to physics.
Mass increase and photon mass
Ian reported on an exchange with Dennis Allen about relativistic mass increase. Allen had pointed to an article which Ian concluded really is self-contradictory: it cites a cyclotron result telling against the effect and then treats Einstein's relation as confirmed. Ian noted that longitudinal and transverse mass vary differently — one as the cube of the gamma factor, the other as its square or as gamma itself depending on whose treatment one takes — and that positing them at all seems to require the force to be resolved into electric and magnetic components.
He also corrected himself on photon mass from the previous week. One can divide hν by c ² to get an equivalent mass of order 10 −19 grams. If instead one postulates a zero rest mass and puts it into the gamma relation, both numerator and denominator go to zero at v = c , so the expression is undefined rather than infinite; whereas postulating a non-zero rest mass and accelerating to c makes the equation blow up and is illegitimate.
Laithwaite, and what Lucas claims follows from him

Science Chat Saturday was a live session on 18 April 2020 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Science Chat Saturday sponsored by the Chappell Natural Philosophy Society
Summary
James Keene on quantum entanglement and Bell's theorem, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bob Gray , Ian Cohen, Roger, Carl and Bill Lucas present.
The argument
Keene's paper takes its stand on a remark of Bell's own: that there is a way to escape the inference of superluminal speeds and spooky action at a distance, but that it involves absolute determinism. That escape is the freedom loophole , and Keene's claim is that binary mechanics occupies it — a local realist theory with exact time development laws, in which all action occurs over one length constant in one time constant, and in which the one-state quanta exist whether observed or not.
The consequence he draws is that entanglement experiments cannot settle the matter by themselves. Closing every other loophole leaves this one; to close it one would have to falsify the local realist theory directly — that is, falsify the quantisation of space, time and energy.
He was scathing about how the loophole is discussed, and this was the liveliest part of the paper: not merely deterministic but super -deterministic; not merely determinism but absolute determinism; not merely hard to imagine but impossible; not merely a question about free will but a loss of freedom to choose ; not merely a new question but unscientific. He called the vocabulary a propaganda ploy — believe in superluminal effects or be an anti-freedom jerk — and said the reason for it is precisely that the experiments alone cannot exclude the alternative.

Science Chat Saturday was a live session on 27 June 2020 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Science Chat Saturday sponsored by the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society
Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene , Dennis Allen and others, given over to a set of experiments Keene had just been corresponding about — and to a long, patient and unresolved argument about whether his theory accounts for them.
Dmitriev's weight measurements
The experiments are Alexander Dmitriev's, at the technical university in St Petersburg, and Keene presented them as work that stands or falls on its own merits whatever anyone thinks of his interpretation.
They are all high-precision weighings of sealed containers in which something is stimulated. A brass rod heated ultrasonically loses weight over the period of heating. A piezoceramic pile heated by one degree shows the container's apparent mass fall while the temperature is held up, and stay down as long as it is held. Coils of optical fibre illuminated by helium and semiconductor lasers lose weight while the light is passing, and recover it a few seconds after the laser is switched off. And a container holding two rotors spinning in opposite directions — so that the total angular momentum is about zero — shows a mass difference that grows with the frequency of rotation.
On the last, Keene had written to Dmitriev because he could not tell from the paper which orientation weighed less, having predicted in the same email that it would be the horizontal rotor; the reply arrived a quarter of an hour before the session and confirmed it. Hu pressed him repeatedly and with some exasperation on what horizontal means — the plane of the spinning disc or the axis — and the answer settled on the axis lying parallel to the earth's surface.

Science Chat Saturday sponsored by the CNPS - John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society.
Summary
John W Kierein presenting Gravity and the Redshift: Why the Big Bang is Wrong , hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bill Lucas , Ian Cohen, Roger, Carl and James Keene present. The first quarter hour went on getting the slides shared, Kierein working from an unfamiliar computer.
Before the talk
Lucas gave his own reasons for rejecting the big bang while the sharing was sorted out. His derivation of gravity from electrodynamics has it arise from the force between vibrating neutral multipoles, which decay slowly — and that decay, on his account, produces the cosmic microwave background, so the observation usually taken as the strongest evidence for the big bang has another explanation. The same decay weakens the earth's field and causes it to expand, which he reads in the stretch marks on the ocean floor.
He then made a much larger claim, which should be read as his own: that of sixteen radiometric methods for dating the earth, only three gave an old age before radiohalos were understood, and that taking the halo patterns properly into account brings all sixteen into agreement at ten thousand years or less. He explained the mechanism he relies on — alpha particles from a decaying inclusion travelling a distance fixed by their energy and etching rings into the surrounding mineral, so that one can read off which isotopes were originally present rather than assuming all the lead came from uranium — and said the work was done at Oak Ridge and then ignored. Hu queried it against the accepted four-billion-year figure and did not get further than restating the disagreement.

Science Chat Saturday was a live session on 9 May 2020 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Science Chat Saturday sponsored by the CNPS
Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Dennis Allen , James Keene , Ian Cohen and Bill Lucas , intended as a mailbag session and diverted when Hu's screen sharing crashed his browser repeatedly.
Keene opened by pointing to a new video on the inertial propulsion mechanism, correcting his presentation of the previous week, and credited Allen by name for his contribution to the argument.
Lucas on the length of the year
Lucas — audible only with difficulty throughout — described work on coral and limestone. Coral lays down annual rings and, within them, ripples marking the days, so the oldest coral records years of some 486 days against the present 365. He reads this as the earth having expanded, on his own account through a decay in gravity, which he says he can predict; and he identifies two intervals in the record where the rate of change was different, which he associates with events in the biblical narrative.
He also reported that papers on the subject, some produced under NOAA contract, have been taken down from the internet, and that he has kept downloaded copies — drawing the parallel with what he sees in other fields the group works in.
Asked what causes the decay, he gave his own mechanism: within an atom each proton vibrates with respect to an electron, giving dipole, quadrupole or higher oscillations, and the net force between two atoms is proportional to the number of multipoles and the amplitude — most terms cancelling under spherical symmetry, which is why gravity is so many orders weaker. He noted a further consequence he had seen reported: that an atom's mass changes measurably when a single electron is removed or excited.

Science Chat Saturdays was a live session on 8 February 2020 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Science Chat Saturdays
Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Bill Lucas , Ian Cohen, James Keene , Alistair Riddoch and Dennis Allen . Hu opened with a question rather than a topic: it is February 2020, a date that once sounded futuristic — why are there still such holes in physics, and why does nobody, orthodox or otherwise, know what gravity is?
Lucas on why
Lucas's answer was historical and political. He traced it to the American settlement between the established colonial churches and the revival movements, and argued that from about 1850 the separation of church and state was used to license a science defined by opposition to religion: what Maxwell and Ampère had called the Spirit of God became the electric field, and quantum mechanics took the universal wave function rather than the field as its object. He credited Poincaré with a meta-theory of theorems from logic applicable to all scientific theories, said Poincaré published relativity a year before Einstein and then showed by those theorems that it was false, and that this was why the theory was carried elsewhere.
He gave his own experience as evidence of the cost. He had held the highest-paid postdoctoral position in the country at Catholic University, running a National Science Foundation grant to treat a thousand inoperable brain tumours with negative pion beams made at Los Alamos — the pion stopping in the brain, replacing an electron, entering the nucleus and breaking it up — with 990 of the thousand tumours destroyed and no notable side effects; and he was dismissed by the NSF and the Department of Energy after giving a paper to the American Physical Society arguing that logic falsifies special and general relativity. Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene and Dennis Allen , given over to a paper Keene had posted the night before on the fine structure constant.
Alpha as a variable
Keene's proposal is to define alpha as the probability of an electromagnetic interaction with a charged particle — in his simulator, the proportion of charge-carrying quanta accelerated by scalar (electrostatic) or vector (magnetic) events during a tick.
The correction that prompted the new paper was small and he explained it precisely: he had been counting the quanta as displayed at the end of each tick, where the relevant number is the count at the beginning, before the time development laws are applied, since those are the quanta available to be acted on.
The result is that alpha is not constant in the simulator but varies with the density of quanta in the volume, with a regression accounting for about ninety-seven per cent of the variance across seven runs. He noted this is not a foreign idea to the mainstream, the running of coupling constants with energy being the whole basis of the unification programme.
The check he thought most interesting: the accepted value of alpha appears at a quanta density of about 0.237 of the maximum possible, and running the same seven files for the proton–electron mass ratio puts the observed 1836 at about 0.238. He asked whether the coincidence indicates that this density range corresponds to ordinary laboratory conditions — standard temperature and pressure — which is where those measurements have been made, the Hall effect among them.

Abstract
The World Wide Web is a source of social encounter occurring over undefined distances. If physical parameters of social encounter are considered uncontrollable for studies in a natural setting, the internet world, when dissected philosophically with respect to physical witnessibility of engaged identities, provides a model in which distance is absent. Upon comparison of meaning in science method and theory as it is necessarily rooted to common perceptional experience, it is proposed that established criteria of virtual, real, and actual employed for description in internet studies not only constitute 'world', but 'universe' in which the gap between the actual and virtual has a physical meaning. Philosophical analogy is made from a proposed universal model to theory proposed by Albert Einstein, Karl Popper and Thomas Kuhn and applied in an attempt to bridge conceptually the social and natural sciences . A release of identity-funding inhibition to the extension of the range of witness beyond the immediate environment, associated with cognitive generalization of phenomenon involving a null hypothesis, seen universally to singularly account for cognitive and behavioral trends towards modern times, is proposed to be the consequence of physical factors that are external to cultures. A universal "paradox of the injuring concept" is rendered in terms of a physical divide between the virtual and the actual.

Scott A. Mainwaring is an American consultant and philanthropist based in Helena, Montana, who is known within Electric Universe circles as a principal supporter and co-founder of the SAFIRE Project, an experimental effort to test the Electric Sun model.
Biography
Mainwaring resides in Helena, Montana, where he has worked as a consultant and part-time lecturer. He is the son of Bruce Mainwaring, a longtime advocate of the Electric Universe idea, and together they have directed the Mainwaring Archive Foundation, the philanthropic vehicle through which the family has funded independent scientific research.
Mainwaring became involved in Electric Universe research after attending the 2012 Electric Universe conference, where he encountered the proposal of engineer Montgomery Childs to build an apparatus capable of testing the Electric Sun hypothesis empirically.
Work
Mainwaring recognized in Montgomery Childs' proposal a pragmatic, empirical method for testing the Electric Universe hypothesis, and in particular the Electric Sun model. He introduced the proposal to his father, Bruce Mainwaring, and the two decided to support the initiative through the Mainwaring Archive Foundation.
The resulting effort became the SAFIRE Project, which sought to reproduce and study, in the laboratory, plasma conditions resembling those proposed for the Sun. The project proceeded through a bench-top proof-of-concept phase, a full-scale laboratory phase built around the "SAFIRE Plasma Engine," and subsequent research into the molecular and atomic-scale reactions observed in its plasma environments. Beyond financing the work, Mainwaring consulted regularly with Childs and contributed hands-on assistance during construction of the Phase 2 apparatus.
The SAFIRE Project was later carried forward as a commercial enterprise under Aureon Energy Ltd.

Scott R. Chubb (30 January 1953 – 25 March 2011) was an American theoretical and computational physicist at the Naval Research Laboratory, and for the last two decades of his life one of the principal theoreticians working on low energy nuclear reactions.
Education and early career
A.B. in physics — Princeton University, 1975
Ph.D. in physics — State University of New York at Stony Brook, 1982, with research carried out at Brookhaven National Laboratory
After his doctorate Chubb received several offers and went first to Northwestern University as a postdoctoral researcher, then to the Naval Research Laboratory on a National Research Council postdoctoral appointment, joining Barry Klein's Condensed Matter Theory Branch. David J Nagel , then head of the Condensed Matter and Radiation Sciences division, later recalled that Chubb "stood out immediately after his arrival at the Lab".
Career
Chubb's NRL work covered an unusually wide range of scales. His early appointment was in solid-state physics, chiefly surface-science computation. He then moved to the Remote Sensing Division, where he worked on computational analysis of satellite data on ocean waves, including measurements of currents at the edge of the Gulf Stream in the western Atlantic. He also wrote on the relativistic corrections required by the Global Positioning System — where the gravitational and kinematic terms combine to about +38.6 microseconds per day, enough to accumulate some 11.6 km of ranging error daily if uncorrected — and obtained a patent on a device to correct for them.

Abstract
Gravitational waves, like EM waves , can be used to transport intelligent signals. Alien civilizations may be advanced enough to have discovered how to generate (and/or modulate ) gravitational waves. These waves could be detected using gravitational wave detector technology. Gravitational waves would probably be the preferred method of extraterrestrial communication for the following reasons:
They can be monitored 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, regardless of weather conditions.
Gravitational waves are more like sound waves, which can be detected (or heard), regardless of detector orientation.
Gravitational waves are not impeded by interstellar dust.
Gravitational waves produced by natural sources have a relatively low frequency (< 5 kHz). Intelligent signals are likely to be much higher.
Only the most advanced civilizations would have the technology to receive gravitational waves.
Currently, there are no terrestrial sources of gravitational waves that we know of.
Since the demand for wireless (EM) services is constantly growing, radio interference will become more and more of a problem. Satellites orbiting the earth also cause major interference. For this reason, advanced civilizations will be forced to use gravitational waves as a method of extraterrestrial communication and reserve EM waves for terrestrial communication. I predict that once we develop the technology to transmit and receive gravitational waves, we will also use it for interplanetary communication.

Shane B. Claggett is an American biochemist and scientific software developer based in Los Angeles, California. His published research spans the structure and function of the F 1 F o ATP synthase enzyme and the development of automated instrumentation and control software for radiochemistry . He has expressed interests in computational protein design , the role of water in biological systems, and connections between quantum mechanics and consciousness .

Work

Should Spacetime be Discarded? was a live session presented by Roger J Anderton on 4 May 2024 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
There are problems unifying Einstein's relativity with quantum physics as is well-known. One proposal for unifying them is to discard spacetime. Introducing spacetime into modern physics has created many problems.
Summary
Roger J Anderton hosted this himself, continuing from his sessions on Minkowski spacetime. The question is whether adding spacetime to physics was a mistake, and his angle is that the answer is now being given inside the mainstream as well as outside it: one proposal for unifying relativity with quantum theory is to discard spacetime altogether.
His framing is the historical one he uses repeatedly. The 1905 paper contains no spacetime; Minkowski added it in 1908; general relativity followed in 1915; and between those dates the theory turned into something else. He cited Alexander Unzicker as holding that the development went wrong in exactly that decade.
Two videos
The first was Sabine Hossenfelder on whether gravity is a force, played to set out the position he disputes. Her account: weight is a force and mass a scalar, a distinction that does not matter in daily life; in general relativity there is no force acting on masses at all, only masses navigating a curved spacetime whose curvature we see indirectly as gravity; the equivalence principle makes the effects of gravity locally the same as acceleration in flat space, so that Einstein and Newton differ over the man who jumps off a roof — Newton says gravity pulls him down, Einstein that the force which had been pushing him up has been removed. Sithamalli K. Balasubramanian is an Indian researcher based in Pune, Maharashtra, who has proposed an alternative, non-quantum-mechanical model of atomic structure. His work argues for a definite geometric structure at the nuclear level and a compulsory link between nuclear geometry and covalent molecular geometry, which he applies to explain the bonding and shapes of compounds of carbon, silicon and boron.
Biography
Balasubramanian is a retired researcher living in Pune, Maharashtra, India. Over several decades he developed and privately circulated a model of atomic structure that departs from mainstream quantum theory. His manuscripts were submitted to established chemistry journals but were not accepted for publication because they questioned the fundamental assumptions of current chemical theory rather than reporting conventional experimental discoveries.
Scientific contributions
Balasubramanian proposes a deterministic, non-mathematical model for atomic structure that differs from the accepted quantum model by assuming a definite structure at the nuclear level and assigning a compulsive link between nuclear and atomic structures. In this model there is an integral relation between the nuclear geometry and the covalent molecular geometry, which he holds to be consistent with the complex covalent chemistry of carbon.
According to the model, the known geometry of a number of covalent molecules can be explained, the inverted bond is accounted for, and additional bonding types are permitted: a new type of double bond with tetrahedral geometry, and a new triple bond, termed the benzyne triple bond, that is said to display cis–trans isomerism. The model has been extended in a series of three papers to the atomic structures of carbon, silicon and boron.

Sjaak Uitterdijk is a Dutch electronics engineer and independent critic of modern theoretical physics. Trained in electronics rather than in academic physics, he has published a long series of papers on the viXra e-print archive arguing that Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity rests on manipulative mathematics, and that a great deal of twentieth-century physics built on it — space-time, black holes, gravitational waves, E = mc 2 , quark models of the nucleus and the particle–wave duality — must be rejected along with it. His critiques are collected in the freely distributed book Physics since Einstein .
Biography
Little biographical detail is publicly documented. In the prologue to Physics since Einstein Uitterdijk writes that he first heard, at about sixteen years of age, the claim that only a handful of extremely intelligent scientists could understand Einstein's 1905 theory, and that "after having successfully completed my academic study Electronics" he decided to take up that challenge and investigate the Special Theory of Relativity for himself. Having read the first ten pages of Einstein's paper "for the umpteenth time", he concluded that either the theory was comprehensible only to geniuses or it was simply wrong — and set out to test the second possibility. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey ( SDSS ) is a long-running imaging and spectroscopic survey of the sky, begun in 2000 and named for the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, which funded it. It is the source of much of the observational material that arguments about redshift , quasars and large-scale structure have been conducted on for the past twenty-five years — including a number of the arguments recorded on this wiki.
This article is a short account of the survey oriented to that use. It describes what SDSS is and where it now stands, and then sets out the particular data products that pages on this wiki draw on, and what the disputes over them have been.
The survey
SDSS observes with two telescopes: the Sloan Foundation 2.5 m telescope at Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico, which has carried the survey since the beginning, and the du Pont 2.5 m telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, which extends it to the southern sky.
Its work divides into two kinds. Imaging records the positions, brightnesses and colours of objects; the imaging camera was retired in 2009, by which time the survey had photometered several hundred million objects over roughly a third of the sky. Spectroscopy — now the whole of the survey's activity — measures the spectrum of a selected object, which is what yields a redshift and hence, on the standard interpretation, a distance.
The survey has run in five phases:
SDSS-I (2000–2005) — the original imaging and redshift survey
SDSS-II (2005–2008) — adding a Milky Way structure survey and the Sloan Supernova Survey
SDSS-III (2008–2014) — including BOSS, the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey
SDSS-IV (2014–2020) — extending to the southern hemisphere
SDSS-V (2020– ) — the current phase, organised as three "mappers": the Milky Way Mapper , the Black Hole Mapper (a time-domain spectroscopic survey of quasars and X-ray sources) and the Local Volume Mapper

The Society for the Advancement of Autodynamics (SAA) was founded in 1994 in Southern California by David de Hilster , Dr. Ricardo Carezani , Amnon Meyers and others, with the purpose of advancing the theory of Autodynamics as developed by Carezani. It later had a chapter in the United Kingdom, and it remains the publisher of essentially the whole Autodynamics literature.
Activities
Publishing
The Society produced a book early on but sold only a few copies. Its two substantial titles are Autodynamics: Fundamental Basis for a New Relativistic Mechanics (1998), the first comprehensive statement of the theory, and Autodynamics: Storm in Physics (2005). The 1998 book was the first to be mass-printed, putting copies into the thousands.
Beyond the books, the Society publishes Carezani's papers, derivations and expository notes at autodynamics.org . That collection is indexed at Ricardo L Carezani and grouped by subject at Autodynamics ; it includes the derivations ( Frames Derivation , Galilean Simplification , The Superfluous System ), the decay papers ( Muon Decay and Autodynamics , Pion Decay and Autodynamics , Nucleus-Nucleus Collision , The Compton Effect and Autodynamics ), the gravitational programme ( Universal Gravitation in Autodynamics and its four applications), and the neutrino papers ( Origin of the Neutrino , Super-Kamiokande: Super-Proof for Neutrino Non-existence , Neutrinos at Fermi Lab , SN 1987A and the Neutrino ).
Several members appear as authors or editors across that body of work: Lucy Haye as co-author of the astrophysical papers, de Hilster and Meyers as editors, and Brian F. Hall as editor of the Pioneer paper.
Public advocacy
The Society has twice intervened publicly against the neutrino hypothesis. Sol Aisenberg (1928 – March 24, 2014) was an American physicist and inventor. He held a Ph.D. in physics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (M.I.T.) and is credited, with R. Chabot, with the pioneering deposition of diamond-like carbon films, a field of research he helped originate in 1971. He was president of the International Technology Group in Natick, Massachusetts.
Biography
Aisenberg was born in 1928 in Brooklyn, New York. He also held part-time appointments as a staff member at M.I.T., as a lecturer at Harvard Medical School, and as a Visiting Research Professor in the Bioengineering Department of Boston University. Over a long career as a physicist and inventor, he accumulated numerous patents and publications. He resided in Natick, Massachusetts, and died on March 24, 2014, at the age of 85.
Education
Graduated — Brooklyn College
Ph.D. in physics — Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Work
In 1971, Aisenberg and R. Chabot reported the preparation of hard, amorphous carbon films by direct deposition from low-energy carbon ion beams, work that is generally regarded as the beginning of research into what became known as diamond-like carbon (DLC). Aisenberg is credited with coining the term "diamond-like" to describe these films. Such films are noted for their high hardness, wear resistance, low friction, chemical stability, and infrared transparency, and have since found broad application in coatings and optics.

"Solution to the Tired Light Theory" is an article by Glenn Borchardt published on 29 December 2025 on The Scientific Worldview , prompted by a reader's questions about how redshift is calculated.
Borchardt sets out his own account of why the cosmological redshift occurs, distinguishing it from the classic tired light proposal. His argument rests on the claim that the speed of light, like the speed of sound and every other wave motion, depends on the medium it travels through — so a wavelength stretched over intergalactic distance needs no expanding universe to explain it.

Author(s) James G Gilson

Published 2008
No. of pages 17
Read the full paper here (archived copy — the original link is no longer available)
Abstract
In an earlier paper, it was shown that the cosmological model that was introduced in a sequence of three earlier papers under the title A Dust Universe Solution to the Dark Energy Problem, originally described by the Friedman equations, can be expressed as a solution to a non-linear Schrödinger equation. In this paper, a large collection of solutions to this Schrödinger equation are found and discussed in the context of relaxing the uniform mass density condition usually employed in cosmology theory. The surprising result is obtained that this non-linear equation can have its many solutions linearly superposed to obtain solution of the cosmology theory problem of great generality and applicability.
Presented at
Physical Interpretations of Relativity Theory XI (12 September 2008)

Abstract
Revised version (20.12.2008). Accepting clock retardation as an empirical fact, we provisionally adopt Whitrow's derivation of the Robertson-Walker Metric (RWM) of Cosmology from the gamma-factor of SR. Recalling the fact that the principle of cosmic isotropy can be used as an argument for the definability of an all-embracing universal time, at least statistically, we propose to reverse this procedure by postulating such time as a regulative idea in the sense of Kant. Taking RWM as our formal point of departure we next investigate the properties of two standard models of modern cosmology: !) the uniform expansion model of Milne & Prokhovnik, which is the simplest model of a cosmic "big bang", and 2) the exponential expansion model of Bondi & Gold, supposed to be the simplest model of a cosmic "steady state". Rejecting the so-called "perfect cosmological principle" of the latter, it is easy to show that the ideas of "big bang" and "steady state" may not be mutually exclusive after all: a universe starting with a "big bang" at the dawn of creation may approximate to a "steady state" in the course of infinite time. We further consider the relationship between our choice of time scale for a particular model of the universe and its corresponding space metric. As it turns out, there are at least two important ways of mapping the expansion of the universe: a) that which keeps atomic sizes constant while light is being stretched, and b) that which keeps distances between fundamental particles constant while their constituents are shrinking. Finally a new model of the universe is proposed which deviates from RWM by allowing the curvature of space to vary with distance. Abstract
Still more shocking than the metaphysical assumption of some initial singularity, is the constant insistence upon the so-called cosmological principle of "homogeneity" and "isotropy" of the Universe. Observations do contradict this principle. And to me, the inhomogeneous, fractal at least on a certain scale range, of the distribution of matter is in itself an important cosmological fact, hitherto almost neglected. Moreover difficultties as to the applicability of the second principle of thermodynamics, observations of abnormal redshifts, etc., are casting large doubts not only upon the standard cosmological models, but even on the interpretation of the observed redshift as due solely to a universal expansion.
Overview
Pecker's paper is a conference contribution — delivered to a meeting at which Halton Arp , Jayant Narlikar and Geoffrey Burbidge also spoke — setting out, from the standpoint of a senior professional astronomer at the Collège de France, why he had never accepted the Big Bang . It is not a paper proposing an alternative model. It is a catalogue of the assumptions he regards as unearned, arranged as five complaints: the initial singularity, the cosmological principle, the arbitrary selection of "significant" facts, the unexamined application of the second law of thermodynamics to the universe as a whole, and the accumulating evidence of anomalous Redshifts .
His central objection is methodological. The standard model, he argues, rests less on observation than on a demand for simplicity — "the argument of simplicity is a Pythagorician argument, which cannot convince" — and Occam's razor is being used not to prune hypotheses but to forbid them.
